abstract: \Ve describe a series of careful llumerical experiments which measure the average generalization capability of neural networks trained on a variety of simple functions. These experiments are designed to test whether average generalization performance can surpass the worst-case bounds obtained from formal learning theory using the Vapnik-Chervonenkis dimension (Blumer et al., 1989). We indeed find that, in some cases, the average generalization is significantly better than the VC bound: the approach to perfect performance is exponential in the number of examples m, rather than the 11m result of the bound. In other cases, we do find the 11m behavior of the VC bound, and in these cases, the numerical prefactor is closely related to prefactor contained in the bound.

paragraphs: The paper asks how closely average neural-network generalization follows worst-case guarantees from Vapnik-Chervonenkis theory. The authors conduct numerical experiments on a variety of simple functions, measuring how performance on unseen cases improves as the number of training examples increases. The distinction between an average observation and a worst-case bound is central to the question.

In some cases, performance approaches perfection exponentially with the number of examples, m. This is faster than the inverse-m behavior associated with the bound examined in the paper. Such results do not contradict a worst-case guarantee: a guarantee can allow substantially better behavior on particular learning problems.

Other cases exhibit the inverse-m pattern, and their numerical prefactors are closely related to the prefactor in the theoretical bound. The findings therefore support both possibilities. Worst-case theory can be conservative for some tasks, yet informative about the rate and scale of learning for others. The paper's contribution is an experimental examination of that relationship across the tested functions.
summary.tldr: Numerical experiments find that average generalization sometimes improves much faster than VC bounds suggest and sometimes closely follows them.

title: Can neural networks do better than the Vapnik-Chervonenkis bounds?

paragraphs: The paper asks when observed frequencies can reliably approximate true probabilities for every event in a family at once. It studies distributions over binary vectors of length n. The desired guarantee is that the largest estimation error across the event family stays below a chosen tolerance with sufficiently high probability.

Polynomial uniform convergence means that this guarantee requires a sample size growing only polynomially with the vector length, inverse error tolerance, and inverse failure probability. The distribution is part of the setting, so the analysis can account for which observations it tends to produce. This makes the question sensitive to the actual sampling distribution.

The main result gives a necessary and sufficient condition using the expected VC dimension of the event family restricted to sampled points, normalized by sample size. An appropriate polynomial decay of that quantity characterizes polynomial uniform convergence. This connects a probability-estimation guarantee to the effective complexity visible in random samples, and the paper discusses applications to distribution-dependent PAC learning.
summary.tldr: A sample-dependent VC-dimension condition exactly characterizes polynomial uniform convergence under a specified distribution.

paragraphs: Saccade combines locating handwritten characters with recognizing them. A single network learns to classify the character centered in its input window and estimate the distances from the window's center to the current and next characters. Recognition and movement guidance are therefore learned together as parts of reading a line.

During testing, the system uses those classifications and distance estimates with jumping rules to move between characters. The design draws on large and corrective eye movements: the system moves toward an informative location and uses positioning information to guide its progress. The network learns distance estimates despite differences in character width, spacing, writing style, and other factors.

The paper reports accurate and efficient recognition of handwritten digits and describes locating characters whether they touch or remain separate. This matters because identifying character boundaries and interpreting characters are closely connected tasks. Saccade makes the classifier contribute directly to navigation, allowing its learned view of the text to help determine where the system should look next.
summary.tldr: Saccade trains one network to recognize handwritten characters and guide jumps along a line using learned position estimates.

title: Learning to See Where and What: Training a Net to Make Saccades and Recognize Handwritten Characters

abstract: This paper relates the computational power of Fahlman' s Recurrent Cascade Correlation (RCC) architecture to that of fInite state automata (FSA). While some recurrent networks are FSA equivalent, RCC is not. The paper presents a theoretical analysis of the RCC architecture in the form of a proof describing a large class of FSA which cannot be realized by RCC.
originalAbstract: This paper relates the computational power of Fahlman' s Recurrent Cascade Correlation (RCC) architecture to that of fInite state automata (FSA). While some recurrent networks are FSA equivalent, RCC is not. paragraphs: This paper examines the computational capabilities of Recurrent Cascade-Correlation, or RCC, by comparing it with finite-state automata. A finite-state automaton processes inputs through transitions among a finite collection of states. It therefore supplies a precise reference for asking which state-dependent computations a recurrent neural architecture can represent.

The authors present a theoretical analysis establishing that a large class of finite-state automata cannot be realized by RCC. The contribution is a proof about the architecture's representational capacity. It identifies computations that fall outside what the model can express, rather than reporting difficulty encountered by a particular training run.

The finding matters because some recurrent networks are equivalent in computational power to finite-state automata, but that property does not carry over to RCC. Having recurrent connections alone does not establish the same representational capabilities across architectures. The paper therefore supplies a structural limit that must be considered when choosing RCC for tasks requiring particular finite-state behavior.
summary.tldr: A theoretical proof shows that Recurrent Cascade-Correlation cannot represent a large class of finite-state automata.

title: Finite State Automata that Recurrent Cascade-Correlation Cannot Represent

paragraphs: The paper addresses a memory problem in learning probabilistic transducers represented by suffix trees. These models use contexts to describe conditional output distributions, but the existing learning approach can build very large trees. Storing the resulting representation can therefore require a great deal of computer memory.

The proposed model makes the representation more compact by sharing distribution parameters across contexts that produce similar conditional outputs. Different contexts can retain their role in describing the input while relying on common parameters when their output behavior is alike. The central idea is to organize storage around similarities in predictive behavior, reducing the need for separate parameter sets.

The authors illustrate the approach through comparative experiments on learning a noun phrase recognizer. This application tests the compact transducer in a language-processing setting where context helps determine output. The stated contribution is a more economical model and learning algorithm, with the experiments demonstrating advantages of sharing parameters among contexts instead of allowing the tree representation to grow so large.
summary.tldr: Sharing parameters among contexts with similar output distributions makes learned probabilistic transducers more compact.

title: Shared Context Probabilistic Transducers

We show how to compute a stopping criterion, give bounds on the approximation error, and show applications to large scale problems.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a sparse, greedy approximation to the maximum a posteriori estimate in Gaussian process regression. Its aim is to improve how computation scales with the number of training examples. The approximation uses a size parameter n that is much smaller than the full sample size m, making sparsity central to the computational savings.

The stated computational requirement is O(n²m), with O(nm) storage. Prediction costs O(n), while computing confidence bounds costs O(nm). These separate costs clarify where the smaller representation helps: producing a prediction depends on n, whereas the reported confidence-bound calculation still depends on the training sample size as well. Keeping n small is therefore important to the proposed scaling behavior.

The authors also provide a computable stopping criterion and bounds on approximation error. These address how to decide when the greedy procedure has done enough work and how to characterize the resulting approximation. Applications to large-scale problems accompany the analysis, connecting the method's computational motivation with its use beyond small training sets.
summary.tldr: A sparse greedy Gaussian process approximation improves scaling and includes a stopping criterion and approximation-error bounds.

title: Sparse Greedy Gaussian Process Regression

abstract: We develop an approach to object recognition based on match(cid:173) ing shapes and using a resulting measure of similarity in a nearest neighbor classifier. The key algorithmic problem here is that of finding pointwise correspondences between an image shape and a stored prototype shape. We introduce a new shape descriptor, the shape context, which makes this possible, using a simple and robust algorithm. The shape context at a point captures the distri(cid:173) bution over relative positions of other shape points and thus sum(cid:173) marizes global shape in a rich, local descriptor. We demonstrate that shape contexts greatly simplify recovery of correspondences between points of two given shapes. Once shapes are aligned, shape contexts are used to define a robust score for measuring shape sim(cid:173) ilarity. We have used this score in a nearest-neighbor classifier for recognition of hand written digits as well as 3D objects, using exactly the same distance function. On the benchmark MNIST dataset of handwritten digits, this yields an error rate of 0.63%, outperforming other published techniques.

paragraphs: The paper recognizes objects by comparing their shapes with stored examples. The main challenge is finding which points on one shape correspond to points on another. Its proposed descriptor, the shape context, characterizes a point using the distribution of the other shape points relative to it.

Each descriptor is attached to one point but summarizes information about the shape as a whole. The authors show that this makes point correspondences substantially easier to recover. After aligning the shapes, they use shape contexts to calculate a robust similarity score, connecting point matching to the final decision about which shapes resemble one another.

That score is used in a nearest-neighbor classifier for both handwritten digits and three-dimensional objects, with the same distance function in both applications. On MNIST, the reported error rate is 0.63%, outperforming other published techniques in the paper's comparison. The contribution is a descriptor that supports correspondence, alignment, and recognition within one shape-matching approach.
summary.tldr: Shape contexts summarize surrounding shape points to simplify matching and achieve a reported 0.63% MNIST error with nearest-neighbor recognition.

title: Shape Context: A New Descriptor for Shape Matching and Object Recognition

abstract: We present a novel connectionist model for acquiring the semantics of a simple language through the behavioral experiences of a real robot. We focus on the “compositionality” of semantics, a fundamental character- istic of human language, which is the ability to understand the meaning of a sentence as a combination of the meanings of words. We also pay much attention to the “embodiment” of a robot, which means that the robot should acquire semantics which matches its body, or sensory-motor system. The essential claim is that an embodied compositional semantic representation can be self-organized from generalized correspondences between sentences and behavioral patterns. This claim is examined and conﬁrmed through simple experiments in which a robot generates corre- sponding behaviors from unlearned sentences by analogy with the corre- spondences between learned sentences and behaviors.

paragraphs: This paper studies how a robot can learn the meanings of sentences through its own behavior. The focus is compositionality: understanding a sentence by combining the meanings of its words. The proposed connectionist model links this linguistic ability to embodiment, so that learned meanings fit the robot’s particular sensory and motor capabilities.

The central proposal is that these meanings can organize themselves through general relationships between sentences and behavioral patterns. Sentence meanings are therefore connected to what the robot experiences and does. Learning correspondences across examples is intended to provide a basis for interpreting combinations of words that the robot has not previously encountered.

Simple experiments with a real robot support this claim. The robot produces corresponding behaviors for unlearned sentences by drawing analogies with previously learned sentence–behavior relationships. This demonstrates the proposed form of generalization within the simple language and experiments studied. Its significance is that compositional understanding and bodily experience can develop together within one learned representation.
summary.tldr: A connectionist model learns embodied sentence meanings that let a real robot respond to previously unlearned sentences in simple experiments.

title: A Holistic Approach to Compositional Semantics: a connectionist model and robot experiments

abstract: We propose the hierarchical Dirichlet process (HDP), a nonparametric Bayesian model for clustering problems involving multiple groups of data. Each group of data is modeled with a mixture, with the number of components being open-ended and inferred automatically by the model. Further, components can be shared across groups, allowing dependencies across groups to be modeled effectively as well as conferring generaliza- tion to new groups. Such grouped clustering problems occur often in practice, e.g. in the problem of topic discovery in document corpora. We report experimental results on three text corpora showing the effective and superior performance of the HDP over previous models.

paragraphs: Grouped datasets often contain recurring clusters shared across groups, but the number of clusters may be unknown. A document collection, for example, can reuse topics in different proportions. The Hierarchical Dirichlet Process models that structure without fixing the number of mixture components beforehand.

Each group has its own mixture, while a hierarchy allows components to be shared across groups. The model infers how many components are needed and which ones recur. This combines group-specific variation with statistical connections that would be lost if every group were clustered independently.

Experiments on three text corpora show effective performance beyond previous models. The contribution is a Bayesian nonparametric framework that lets complexity grow with the evidence while retaining a common vocabulary of latent components. Shared clusters also support generalization to new groups, making the hierarchy useful for both describing existing collections and extending their organization.
summary.tldr: Hierarchical Dirichlet Processes infer an open-ended set of mixture components that can be shared across related groups.

title: Sharing Clusters among Related Groups: Hierarchical Dirichlet Processes

abstract: Humans are extremely adept at learning new skills by imitating the actions of others. A progression of imitative abilities has been observed in children, ranging from imitation of simple body movements to goalbased imitation based on inferring intent. In this paper, we show that the problem of goal-based imitation can be formulated as one of inferring goals and selecting actions using a learned probabilistic graphical model of the environment. We first describe algorithms for planning actions to achieve a goal state using probabilistic inference. We then describe how planning can be used to bootstrap the learning of goal-dependent policies by utilizing feedback from the environment. The resulting graphical model is then shown to be powerful enough to allow goal-based imitation. Using a simple maze navigation task, we illustrate how an agent can infer the goals of an observed teacher and imitate the teacher even when the goals are uncertain and the demonstration is incomplete.

paragraphs: This paper treats imitation as a problem of understanding another agent's goal and choosing actions to achieve it. The proposed framework uses a learned probabilistic graphical model of the environment. Within that model, uncertainty about what a teacher intends can be handled alongside the problem of deciding what the learner should do.

The authors first develop planning algorithms that use probabilistic inference to find actions leading to a goal state. Planning then helps initiate the learning of policies conditioned on goals, with feedback from the environment supporting that learning. This connects an ability to plan for an explicit goal with an ability to act toward goals inferred from observation.

A simple maze-navigation task illustrates the resulting imitation behavior. The agent can infer a teacher's goals and imitate the teacher even when the demonstration is incomplete and the goals remain uncertain. The demonstration supports the framework's capacity for goal-based imitation in that setting, showing how planning, learning, and interpreting demonstrations can share one probabilistic representation.
summary.tldr: A learned graphical model enables an agent to infer a teacher's goals and plan imitative actions despite incomplete demonstrations.

title: Goal-Based Imitation as Probabilistic Inference over Graphical Models

abstract: The computational modelling of the primary auditory cortex (A1) has been less fruitful than that of the primary visual cortex (V1) due to the less organized properties of A1. Greater disorder has recently been demonstrated for the tonotopy of A1 that has traditionally been considered to be as ordered as the retinotopy of V1. This disorder appears to be incongruous, given the uniformity of the neocortex; however, we hypothesized that both A1 and V1 would adopt an efficient coding strategy and that the disorder in A1 reflects natural sound statistics. To provide a computational model of the tonotopic disorder in A1, we used a model that was originally proposed for the smooth V1 map. In contrast to natural images, natural sounds exhibit distant correlations, which were learned and reflected in the disordered map. The auditory model predicted harmonic relationships among neighbouring A1 cells; furthermore, the same mechanism used to model V1 complex cells reproduced nonlinear responses similar to the pitch selectivity. These results contribute to the understanding of the sensory cortices of different modalities in a novel and integrated manner.

paragraphs: The organization of primary auditory cortex appears less orderly than that of primary visual cortex. This paper asks whether both could nevertheless follow the same efficient-coding principle. The authors hypothesize that auditory disorder reflects the statistical structure of natural sounds, rather than requiring a fundamentally different organizing strategy.

To investigate, they apply to sound a model originally proposed for smooth maps in visual cortex. Natural sounds contain distant correlations, and learning those relationships produces a disordered map in the auditory model. The result connects differences in the learned spatial organization to differences in the statistics of the sensory inputs.

The model also predicts harmonic relationships among neighboring auditory cells. In addition, the mechanism used to model visual complex cells generates nonlinear auditory responses resembling pitch selectivity. These are model-based predictions and reproductions of response properties. Together, they support an integrated computational account in which a shared learning principle can yield different cortical organizations and response patterns across sensory modalities.
summary.tldr: An efficient-coding model links auditory-map disorder to natural sound statistics and predicts harmonic relationships and pitch-like selectivity.

title: The topographic unsupervised learning of natural sounds in the auditory cortex

abstract: In the superset label learning problem (SLL), each training instance provides a set of candidate labels of which one is the true label of the instance. As in ordinary regression, the candidate label set is a noisy version of the true label. In this work, we solve the problem by maximizing the likelihood of the candidate label sets of training instances. We propose a probabilistic model, the Logistic Stick- Breaking Conditional Multinomial Model (LSB-CMM), to do the job. The LSB- CMM is derived from the logistic stick-breaking process. It ﬁrst maps data points to mixture components and then assigns to each mixture component a label drawn from a component-speciﬁc multinomial distribution. The mixture components can capture underlying structure in the data, which is very useful when the model is weakly supervised. This advantage comes at little cost, since the model introduces few additional parameters. Experimental tests on several real-world problems with superset labels show results that are competitive or superior to the state of the art. The discovered underlying structures also provide improved explanations of the classiﬁcation predictions.

paragraphs: Superset label learning addresses training data where each example comes with several candidate labels, exactly one of which is correct. The challenge is to learn from that ambiguity without knowing which candidate to trust. This paper treats the candidate set as a noisy observation of the true label and learns by maximizing the likelihood of the observed sets.

Its model, LSB-CMM, uses a logistic stick-breaking construction to connect input examples to mixture components. Each component then supplies its own probability distribution over labels. These components give the learner a way to capture structure shared by examples, which can be especially useful when the labels provide only weak supervision. The abstract states that this requires few additional parameters.

Experiments on several real-world problems report performance competitive with or better than existing methods. The discovered components also improve explanations of classification predictions. The contribution therefore combines a probabilistic treatment of ambiguous labels with a representation of underlying data structure that supports both prediction and interpretation.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic mixture model learns from candidate label sets while discovering structure that helps explain its predictions.

title: A Conditional Multinomial Mixture Model for Superset Label Learning

abstract: We study stochastic optimization problems when the \emph{data} is sparse, which is in a sense dual to the current understanding of high-dimensional statistical learning and optimization. We highlight both the difficulties---in terms of increased sample complexity that sparse data necessitates---and the potential benefits, in terms of allowing parallelism and asynchrony in the design of algorithms. Concretely, we derive matching upper and lower bounds on the minimax rate for optimization and learning with sparse data, and we exhibit algorithms achieving these rates. Our algorithms are adaptive: they achieve the best possible rate for the data observed. We also show how leveraging sparsity leads to (still minimax optimal) parallel and asynchronous algorithms, providing experimental evidence complementing our theoretical results on medium to large-scale learning tasks.

paragraphs: The paper examines stochastic learning and optimization when sparsity is a property of the observed data. It identifies a tradeoff: sparse observations can require more samples for accurate learning, yet their structure can also make computation more amenable to parallel and asynchronous execution. Both effects belong in an assessment of sparse-data methods.

The authors derive matching upper and lower bounds on minimax rates. These bounds characterize the best worst-case performance available in the studied setting, and the paper supplies algorithms that attain those rates. The algorithms are adaptive, achieving the best possible rate for the data actually observed.

The computational contribution builds on the same sparsity structure. The authors construct parallel and asynchronous algorithms that retain minimax optimality, so the benefits of those execution styles are compatible with the statistical guarantees. Experiments on medium- to large-scale learning tasks complement the theory. The result connects the extra information needed for sparse-data learning with opportunities to organize its computation more efficiently.
summary.tldr: Sparse data can increase sample requirements while enabling adaptive, parallel, and asynchronous algorithms that attain optimal minimax rates.

title: Estimation, Optimization, and Parallelism when Data is Sparse

abstract: We study optimal image encoding based on a generative approach with non-linear feature combinations and explicit position encoding. By far most approaches to unsupervised learning learning of visual features, such as sparse coding or ICA, account for translations by representing the same features at different positions. Some earlier models used a separate encoding of features and their positions to facilitate invariant data encoding and recognition. All probabilistic generative models with explicit position encoding have so far assumed a linear superposition of components to encode image patches. Here, we for the first time apply a model with non-linear feature superposition and explicit position encoding. By avoiding linear superpositions, the studied model represents a closer match to component occlusions which are ubiquitous in natural images. In order to account for occlusions, the non-linear model encodes patches qualitatively very different from linear models by using component representations separated into mask and feature parameters. We first investigated encodings learned by the model using artificial data with mutually occluding components. We find that the model extracts the components, and that it can correctly identify the occlusive components with the hidden variables of the model. On natural image patches, the model learns component masks and features for typical image components. By using reverse correlation, we estimate the receptive fields associated with the model's hidden units. We find many Gabor-like or globular receptive fields as well as fields sensitive to more complex structures. Our results show that probabilistic models that capture occlusions and invariances can be trained efficiently on image patches, and that the resulting encoding represents an alternative model for the neural encoding of images in the primary visual cortex.

paragraphs: Image components can move and hide one another, yet many feature-learning models represent position through repeated features and combine components by addition. This paper studies a probabilistic generative model that explicitly encodes position while combining features nonlinearly. The nonlinear combination better matches occlusion, where one component blocks another rather than simply adding its appearance.

The model separates each component into mask and feature parameters. On artificial data containing mutually occluding components, it extracts the components and identifies the occluding elements through its hidden variables. On natural image patches, it learns masks and features corresponding to typical image components, giving a different representation from linear superposition models.

The authors also use reverse correlation to estimate receptive fields associated with hidden units. They find Gabor-like and globular fields, along with fields sensitive to more complex structures. The results show that models combining occlusion and invariance can be trained efficiently on image patches. They offer an alternative model of image encoding in primary visual cortex, rather than establishing that the brain implements this particular generative mechanism.
summary.tldr: A generative image model combines explicit position with nonlinear occlusion to learn components and varied receptive-field structures.

title: What Are the Invariant Occlusive Components of Image Patches? A Probabilistic Generative Approach

abstract: Motivated by the problem of robust factorization of a low-rank tensor, we study the question of sparse and low-rank tensor decomposition. We present an efficient computational algorithm that modifies Leurgans' algoirthm for tensor factorization. Our method relies on a reduction of the problem to sparse and low-rank matrix decomposition via the notion of tensor contraction. We use well-understood convex techniques for solving the reduced matrix sub-problem which then allows us to perform the full decomposition of the tensor. We delineate situations where the problem is recoverable and provide theoretical guarantees for our algorithm. We validate our algorithm with numerical experiments.

We present an efficient computational algorithm that modifies Leurgans' algoirthm for tensor factorization. Our method relies on a reduction of the problem to sparse and low-rank matrix decomposition via the notion of tensor contraction. paragraphs: The paper studies how to separate sparse and low-rank components of a tensor, motivated by robust factorization. These components represent different kinds of structure: low rank describes a compact factorized representation, while sparsity concerns a component with relatively few nonzero entries. Recovering them separately is the central computational problem.

The proposed efficient algorithm modifies Leurgans' tensor-factorization method. Its main move is to use tensor contraction to reduce the task to sparse and low-rank matrix decomposition. The authors then solve this matrix subproblem with established convex techniques and use the result to carry out the full tensor decomposition.

This reduction matters because it brings well-understood matrix methods into a tensor problem, supplying a concrete route from the reduced computation back to the desired factors. The paper identifies situations in which recovery is possible and gives theoretical guarantees for the algorithm in those settings. Numerical experiments validate the approach. The recoverability claims are conditional on the situations analyzed, rather than a guarantee for every sparse-plus-low-rank tensor.
summary.tldr: Tensor contraction reduces sparse and low-rank tensor decomposition to convex matrix subproblems, with recovery guarantees in specified settings.

title: Sparse and Low-Rank Tensor Decomposition

abstract: Deep dynamic generative models are developed to learn sequential dependencies in time-series data. The multi-layered model is designed by constructing a hierarchy of temporal sigmoid belief networks (TSBNs), defined as a sequential stack of sigmoid belief networks (SBNs). Each SBN has a contextual hidden state, inherited from the previous SBNs in the sequence, and is used to regulate its hidden bias. Scalable learning and inference algorithms are derived by introducing a recognition model that yields fast sampling from the variational posterior. This recognition model is trained jointly with the generative model, by maximizing its variational lower bound on the log-likelihood. Experimental results on bouncing balls, polyphonic music, motion capture, and text streams show that the proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art predictive performance, and has the capacity to synthesize various sequences.

This recognition model is trained jointly with the generative model, by maximizing its variational lower bound on the log-likelihood. paragraphs: The paper develops deep generative models for sequences, with the goal of learning how observations depend on earlier parts of a time series. Its architecture builds a hierarchy of temporal sigmoid belief networks. Each temporal network is itself a sequence of sigmoid belief networks, giving the model both temporal organization and multiple layers.

Information from preceding networks enters through a contextual hidden state that regulates the current network's hidden bias. This provides a mechanism for past context to influence the model's present behavior. To make learning and inference scalable, the authors introduce a recognition model that quickly samples from an approximate, variational posterior. It is trained jointly with the generative model by maximizing a lower bound on log-likelihood.

The experiments span bouncing balls, polyphonic music, motion capture, and text streams. The authors report state-of-the-art predictive performance on these evaluations and show that the model can synthesize different sequences. The contribution combines a temporal generative architecture with an inference mechanism intended to make that architecture practical to train.
summary.tldr: Hierarchies of temporal sigmoid belief networks combine contextual sequence modeling with fast variational inference for prediction and synthesis.

title: Deep Temporal Sigmoid Belief Networks for Sequence Modeling

abstract: We propose a class of nonparametric two-sample tests with a cost linear in the sample size. Two tests are given, both based on an ensemble of distances between analytic functions representing each of the distributions. The first test uses smoothed empirical characteristic functions to represent the distributions, the second uses distribution embeddings in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Analyticity implies that differences in the distributions may be detected almost surely at a finite number of randomly chosen locations/frequencies. The new tests are consistent against a larger class of alternatives than the previous linear-time tests based on the (non-smoothed) empirical characteristic functions, while being much faster than the current state-of-the-art quadratic-time kernel-based or energy distance-based tests. Experiments on artificial benchmarks and on challenging real-world testing problems demonstrate that our tests give a better power/time tradeoff than competing approaches, and in some cases, better outright power than even the most expensive quadratic-time tests. This performance advantage is retained even in high dimensions, and in cases where the difference in distributions is not observable with low order statistics.

paragraphs: The paper proposes two nonparametric tests for deciding whether two samples come from different distributions. Their computational cost grows linearly with sample size. Both represent distributions through analytic functions and compare those representations at a finite collection of locations, making the testing procedure inexpensive as datasets grow.

One test uses smoothed empirical characteristic functions; the other uses distribution embeddings in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Analyticity is the key property: differences between distributions can be detected almost surely at finitely many randomly selected locations or frequencies. The authors establish consistency against a broader class of alternatives than earlier linear-time tests using unsmoothed empirical characteristic functions.

Experiments show a better tradeoff between detection power and runtime than competing approaches. In some cases, the tests also have higher outright power than expensive quadratic-time tests. The reported advantage persists in high-dimensional settings and when low-order statistics do not reveal the distributional difference, suggesting that computational efficiency need not require focusing only on simple differences.
summary.tldr: Two linear-time distribution tests use analytic representations to achieve strong empirical detection power at low computational cost.

title: Fast Two-Sample Testing with Analytic Representations of Probability Measures

abstract: We introduce an unsupervised learning algorithmthat combines probabilistic modeling with solver-based techniques for program synthesis.We apply our techniques to both a visual learning domain and a language learning problem,showing that our algorithm can learn many visual concepts from only a few examplesand that it can recover some English inflectional morphology.Taken together, these results give both a new approach to unsupervised learning of symbolic compositional structures,and a technique for applying program synthesis tools to noisy data.
originalAbstract: We introduce an unsupervised learning algorithmthat combines probabilistic modeling with solver-based techniques for program synthesis.We apply our techniques to both a visual learning domain and a language learning problem,showing that our algorithm can learn many visual concepts from only a few examplesand that it can recover some English inflectional morphology.Taken together, these results give both a new approach to unsupervised learning of symbolic compositional structures,and a technique for applying program synthesis tools to noisy data.

paragraphs: The paper introduces an unsupervised learning algorithm that combines probabilistic modeling with solver-based program synthesis. Its goal is to learn symbolic, compositional structures from observations. In such a representation, learned concepts have components that can be combined, giving program synthesis a role in discovering the structure behind data.

The two ingredients address complementary parts of this task. Probabilistic modeling supplies a way to work with uncertainty and noisy observations, while synthesis tools support the construction of symbolic programs. The resulting approach brings program synthesis into a learning setting where the evidence need not be perfectly clean.

The authors apply the algorithm to visual concepts and a language-learning problem. They show that it learns many visual concepts from only a few examples and recovers some English inflectional morphology. These are specific demonstrations of learning structured concepts across two domains. Together, they support the approach as a method for unsupervised symbolic learning and as a technique for applying synthesis tools to noisy data.
summary.tldr: Combining probabilistic modeling with program synthesis enables unsupervised learning of visual concepts and some English morphology.

title: Unsupervised Learning by Program Synthesis

abstract: Most existing approaches to distributed sparse regression assume the data is partitioned by samples. However, for high-dimensional data (D >> N), it is more natural to partition the data by features. We propose an algorithm to distributed sparse regression when the data is partitioned by features rather than samples. Our approach allows the user to tailor our general method to various distributed computing platforms by trading-off the total amount of data (in bits) sent over the communication network and the number of rounds of communication. We show that an implementation of our approach is capable of solving L1-regularized L2 regression problems with millions of features in minutes.
originalAbstract: Most existing approaches to distributed sparse regression assume the data is partitioned by samples. However, for high-dimensional data (D >> N), it is more natural to partition the data by features. We propose an algorithm to distributed sparse regression when the data is partitioned by features rather than samples. Our approach allows the user to tailor our general method to various distributed computing platforms by trading-off the total amount of data (in bits) sent over the communication network and the number of rounds of communication. We show that an implementation of our approach is capable of solving L1-regularized L2 regression problems with millions of features in minutes.

paragraphs: Distributed regression usually splits a dataset across machines by observations, giving each machine a subset of the samples. This paper addresses a different arrangement: splitting by features. That arrangement is particularly natural when the number of features greatly exceeds the number of observations, so the dataset is much wider than it is tall.

The proposed sparse-regression algorithm is designed for this feature partition. Its general method lets users trade the total number of bits transmitted across the network against the number of communication rounds. These are separate costs: exchanging less data overall and coordinating fewer exchanges need not be the same objective. Making that tradeoff adjustable helps adapt the method to different distributed computing platforms.

The authors report an implementation that solves regression problems combining squared-error loss with an L1 penalty on millions of features in minutes. This demonstrates practical capability at a large feature count. The broader contribution is an approach to distributed sparse regression whose data layout and communication choices explicitly address high-dimensional datasets.
summary.tldr: The paper makes sparse regression practical on feature-partitioned data by allowing communication volume and communication rounds to be traded off.

title: Feature-distributed sparse regression: a screen-and-clean approach

abstract: We develop efficient solution methods for a robust empirical risk minimization problem designed to give calibrated confidence intervals on performance and provide optimal tradeoffs between bias and variance. Our methods apply to distributionally robust optimization problems proposed by Ben-Tal et al., which put more weight on observations inducing high loss via a worst-case approach over a non-parametric uncertainty set on the underlying data distribution. Our algorithm solves the resulting minimax problems with nearly the same computational cost of stochastic gradient descent through the use of several carefully designed data structures. For a sample of size n, the per-iteration cost of our method scales as O(log n), which allows us to give optimality certificates that distributionally robust optimization provides at little extra cost compared to empirical risk minimization and stochastic gradient methods.

Our methods apply to distributionally robust optimization problems proposed by Ben-Tal et al., which put more weight on observations inducing high loss via a worst-case approach over a non-parametric uncertainty set on the underlying data distribution. Our algorithm solves the resulting minimax problems with nearly the same computational cost of stochastic gradient descent through the use of several carefully designed data structures. paragraphs: Ordinary empirical risk minimization fits a model to the observed sample distribution. This paper develops efficient methods for a robust version designed to provide calibrated performance confidence intervals and optimal bias–variance tradeoffs. The robust objective considers a nonparametric uncertainty set of possible data distributions rather than relying on one fixed weighting of observations.

Within that uncertainty set, a worst-case calculation gives greater weight to observations with high loss. Learning therefore becomes a minimax problem: the model is optimized against an adverse reweighting of the data. The paper’s computational contribution is to solve this more demanding objective using carefully designed data structures that keep the expense close to stochastic gradient descent.

For n observations, the stated per-iteration cost is O(log n). This makes the distributionally robust formulation accessible with little additional computational cost relative to standard empirical risk minimization and stochastic gradient methods. The approach also supplies optimality certificates associated with the robust problem. Its significance is that statistical robustness and certification need not require a large increase in the cost of each optimization step.
summary.tldr: Specialized data structures enable distributionally robust minimax optimization with O(log n) per-iteration cost and little overhead over stochastic gradient methods.

title: Stochastic Gradient Methods for Distributionally Robust Optimization with f-divergences

abstract: Variational autoencoders are powerful models for unsupervised learning. However deep models with several layers of dependent stochastic variables are difficult to train which limits the improvements obtained using these highly expressive models. We propose a new inference model, the Ladder Variational Autoencoder, that recursively corrects the generative distribution by a data dependent approximate likelihood in a process resembling the recently proposed Ladder Network. We show that this model provides state of the art predictive log-likelihood and tighter log-likelihood lower bound compared to the purely bottom-up inference in layered Variational Autoencoders and other generative models. We provide a detailed analysis of the learned hierarchical latent representation and show that our new inference model is qualitatively different and utilizes a deeper more distributed hierarchy of latent variables. Finally, we observe that batch-normalization and deterministic warm-up (gradually turning on the KL-term) are crucial for training variational models with many stochastic layers.

We show that this model provides state of the art predictive log-likelihood and tighter log-likelihood lower bound compared to the purely bottom-up inference in layered Variational Autoencoders and other generative models. We provide a detailed analysis of the learned hierarchical latent representation and show that our new inference model is qualitatively different and utilizes a deeper more distributed hierarchy of latent variables. Finally, we observe that batch-normalization and deterministic warm-up (gradually turning on the KL-term) are crucial for training variational models with many stochastic layers.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders can learn representations without labels, but adding multiple dependent stochastic layers makes training difficult. This limits the benefit of their increased expressive capacity. The Ladder Variational Autoencoder addresses the inference side of that problem: how observations are used to estimate the hidden variables in a deep generative model.

Its inference procedure recursively corrects the generative distribution using a data-dependent approximate likelihood. The process resembles the Ladder Network and differs from inference that proceeds purely from the input upward. By combining the generative distribution with observation-dependent corrections, the method provides a different way to use the hierarchy during inference.

The authors report state-of-the-art predictive log-likelihood and a tighter likelihood lower bound compared with bottom-up layered variational autoencoders and other generative models. Their representation analysis finds a deeper, more distributed use of latent variables. They also observe that batch normalization and gradually introducing the KL term are crucial for training models with many stochastic layers, tying the reported success to both inference design and training procedure.
summary.tldr: Ladder Variational Autoencoders recursively combine generative structure with data-dependent corrections to train deeper, more distributed latent hierarchies.

title: Ladder Variational Autoencoders

abstract: We present a new model, Predictive State Recurrent Neural Networks (PSRNNs), for filtering and prediction in dynamical systems. PSRNNs draw on insights from both Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) and Predictive State Representations (PSRs), and inherit advantages from both types of models. Like many successful RNN architectures, PSRNNs use (potentially deeply composed) bilinear transfer functions to combine information from multiple sources. We show that such bilinear functions arise naturally from state updates in Bayes filters like PSRs, in which observations can be viewed as gating belief states. We also show that PSRNNs can be learned effectively by combining Backpropogation Through Time (BPTT) with an initialization derived from a statistically consistent learning algorithm for PSRs called two-stage regression (2SR). Finally, we show that PSRNNs can be factorized using tensor decomposition, reducing model size and suggesting interesting connections to existing multiplicative architectures such as LSTMs and GRUs. We apply PSRNNs to 4 datasets, and show that we outperform several popular alternative approaches to modeling dynamical systems in all cases.

paragraphs: Predictive State Recurrent Neural Networks combine ideas from recurrent neural networks and predictive state representations to filter observations and predict dynamical systems. The paper seeks to connect flexible recurrent computation with the structure of probabilistic state updates, bringing insights from both modeling traditions into one architecture.

PSRNNs combine information using bilinear transfer functions, which can be composed deeply. The authors show that these operations arise naturally in Bayes-filter state updates: observations can act as gates on belief states. Training combines backpropagation through time with initialization from two-stage regression, a statistically consistent learning algorithm for predictive state representations. This links the starting parameters to a structured statistical procedure before recurrent training.

The model can also be factorized using tensor decomposition, reducing its size and suggesting connections to multiplicative architectures such as LSTMs and GRUs. Across four datasets, the authors report better performance than several popular alternatives for dynamical-system modeling. These findings support the proposed combination of architecture, initialization, and training in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: PSRNNs connect recurrent neural computation with predictive-state filtering, combining statistical initialization, recurrent training, and compact tensor factorization.

title: Predictive State Recurrent Neural Networks

abstract: Decision trees and random forests are well established models that not only offer good predictive performance, but also provide rich feature importance information. While practitioners often employ variable importance methods that rely on this impurity-based information, these methods remain poorly characterized from a theoretical perspective. We provide novel insights into the performance of these methods by deriving finite sample performance guarantees in a high-dimensional setting under various modeling assumptions. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of these impurity-based methods via an extensive set of simulations.
originalAbstract: Decision trees and random forests are well established models that not only offer good predictive performance, but also provide rich feature importance information. We provide novel insights into the performance of these methods by deriving finite sample performance guarantees in a high-dimensional setting under various modeling assumptions. We further demonstrate the effectiveness of these impurity-based methods via an extensive set of simulations.

paragraphs: Decision trees and random forests provide information about which input variables matter alongside their predictions. Practitioners commonly use importance measures based on the impurity information produced by these models. This paper examines the theoretical performance of those methods, addressing a gap between their widespread use and their mathematical characterization.

The main contribution is a set of finite-sample performance guarantees in a high-dimensional setting. These guarantees concern behavior with a limited amount of data, rather than only in an unlimited-data limit. They are derived under various modeling assumptions, so the paper's conclusions connect the usefulness of impurity-based importance to the statistical setting in which it is applied.

An extensive collection of simulations provides additional evidence of the methods' effectiveness. The theoretical and empirical components serve complementary purposes: the guarantees characterize performance under assumptions, while the simulations demonstrate behavior in the cases studied. Together, they provide a firmer basis for understanding a feature-importance tool already commonly used with predictive tree models.
summary.tldr: The paper gives finite-sample guarantees and simulation evidence for impurity-based variable importance in high-dimensional tree models.

title: Variable Importance Using Decision Trees

abstract: We consider the problem of solving a large-scale Quadratically Constrained Quadratic Program. Such problems occur naturally in many scientific and web applications. Although there are efficient methods which tackle this problem, they are mostly not scalable. In this paper, we develop a method that transforms the quadratic constraint into a linear form by a sampling a set of low-discrepancy points. The transformed problem can then be solved by applying any state-of-the-art large-scale solvers. We show the convergence of our approximate solution to the true solution as well as some finite sample error bounds. Experimental results are also shown to prove scalability in practice.

Although there are efficient methods which tackle this problem, they are mostly not scalable. In this paper, we develop a method that transforms the quadratic constraint into a linear form by a sampling a set of low-discrepancy points. The transformed problem can then be solved by applying any state-of-the-art large-scale solvers. We show the convergence of our approximate solution to the true solution as well as some finite sample error bounds. Experimental results are also shown to prove scalability in practice.

paragraphs: A quadratically constrained quadratic program optimizes a quadratic objective subject to quadratic restrictions. Such problems arise in scientific and web applications, but methods that work efficiently at smaller scales may struggle as the problem grows. This paper addresses that scaling challenge by changing how the quadratic constraint is represented.

The method samples a set of low-discrepancy points and uses them to transform the constraint into a linear form. The transformed problem can then be handled by existing solvers designed for large-scale optimization. This separates the task of approximating the difficult constraint from the task of solving the resulting optimization problem.

The authors show convergence of their approximate solution to the true solution and provide finite-sample error bounds. These results connect the sampled formulation to the original problem, rather than treating the transformation as an unsupported shortcut. Experiments also demonstrate scalability in practice. The contribution is therefore both computational and analytical: a sampled constraint representation opens access to large-scale solvers, while error bounds describe the accuracy of the approximation.
summary.tldr: Low-discrepancy sampling converts a quadratic constraint into a linear approximation that existing large-scale solvers can handle.

title: Large-Scale Quadratically Constrained Quadratic Program via Low-Discrepancy Sequences

abstract: Extreme multi-label classification (XMLC) is a problem of tagging an instance with a small subset of relevant labels chosen from an extremely large pool of possible labels. Large label spaces can be efficiently handled by organizing labels as a tree, like in the hierarchical softmax (HSM) approach commonly used for multi-class problems. In this paper, we investigate probabilistic label trees (PLTs) that have been recently devised for tackling XMLC problems. We show that PLTs are a no-regret multi-label generalization of HSM when precision@$k$ is used as a model evaluation metric. Critically, we prove that pick-one-label heuristic---a reduction technique from multi-label to multi-class that is routinely used along with HSM---is not consistent in general. We also show that our implementation of PLTs, referred to as extremeText (XT), obtains significantly better results than HSM with the pick-one-label heuristic and XML-CNN, a deep network specifically designed for XMLC problems. Moreover, XT is competitive to many state-of-the-art approaches in terms of statistical performance, model size and prediction time which makes it amenable to deploy in an online system.

Moreover, XT is competitive to many state-of-the-art approaches in terms of statistical performance, model size and prediction time which makes it amenable to deploy in an online system.

paragraphs: Extreme multi-label classification assigns a few relevant labels from a very large collection. Organizing those labels in a tree can make prediction manageable, but a tree method designed for choosing one class does not automatically handle several correct labels. This paper examines probabilistic label trees as a principled way to make that transition.

The authors show that probabilistic label trees generalize hierarchical softmax to the multi-label setting with a no-regret result for precision at k, which evaluates relevance among the top k predictions. They also prove that the common shortcut of selecting one label and treating the task as multi-class classification is not generally consistent. That result identifies a theoretical problem with an otherwise convenient reduction.

Their implementation, extremeText, performs significantly better than hierarchical softmax with that shortcut and XML-CNN in the reported comparisons. It is also competitive with several leading approaches in predictive performance, model size, and prediction time. Together, the theory and experiments support tree-based multi-label prediction that preserves the task’s multiple-label structure while remaining practical for online deployment.
summary.tldr: Probabilistic label trees provide a theoretically justified and efficient multi-label extension of hierarchical softmax.

title: A no-regret generalization of hierarchical softmax to extreme multi-label classification

abstract: Deep reinforcement learning could be used to learn dexterous robotic policies but it is challenging to transfer them to new robots with vastly different hardware properties. It is also prohibitively expensive to learn a new policy from scratch for each robot hardware due to the high sample complexity of modern state-of-the-art algorithms. We propose a novel approach called Hardware Conditioned Policies where we train a universal policy conditioned on a vector representation of robot hardware. We considered robots in simulation with varied dynamics, kinematic structure, kinematic lengths and degrees-of-freedom. First, we use the kinematic structure directly as the hardware encoding and show great zero-shot transfer to completely novel robots not seen during training. For robots with lower zero-shot success rate, we also demonstrate that fine-tuning the policy network is significantly more sample-efficient than training a model from scratch. In tasks where knowing the agent dynamics is important for success, we learn an embedding for robot hardware and show that policies conditioned on the encoding of hardware tend to generalize and transfer well. Videos of experiments are available at: https://sites.google.com/view/robot-transfer-hcp.

paragraphs: Training a separate reinforcement learning policy for every robot can require substantial experience, especially when robots differ greatly in their hardware. This paper instead trains a shared policy that receives a vector describing the robot. The policy can therefore condition its behavior on hardware properties while reusing learning across multiple robots.

The study uses simulated robots with different dynamics, kinematic structures, lengths, and degrees of freedom. One approach directly encodes the kinematic structure. The authors report strong transfer to previously unseen robots without additional training. When this zero-shot transfer has lower success, fine-tuning the shared network requires significantly fewer samples than training from scratch.

For tasks where dynamics information is important, the authors also learn a hardware embedding rather than relying only on the direct structural encoding. Policies using this representation tend to generalize and transfer well. The findings support hardware information as a useful input for shared robot policies, with both immediate transfer and efficient adaptation demonstrated in simulation.
summary.tldr: Conditioning a shared policy on robot hardware enables transfer to unseen simulated robots and more sample-efficient fine-tuning.

title: Hardware Conditioned Policies for Multi-Robot Transfer Learning

abstract: How humans make repeated choices among options with imperfectly known reward outcomes is an important problem in psychology and neuroscience. This is often studied using multi-armed bandits, which is also frequently studied in machine learning. We present data from a human stationary bandit experiment, in which we vary the average abundance and variability of reward availability (mean and variance of reward rate distributions). Surprisingly, we find subjects significantly underestimate prior mean of reward rates -- based on their self-report, at the end of a game, on their reward expectation of non-chosen arms. Previously, human learning in the bandit task was found to be well captured by a Bayesian ideal learning model, the Dynamic Belief Model (DBM), albeit under an incorrect generative assumption of the temporal structure - humans assume reward rates can change over time even though they are actually fixed. We find that the "pessimism bias" in the bandit task is well captured by the prior mean of DBM when fitted to human choices; but it is poorly captured by the prior mean of the Fixed Belief Model (FBM), an alternative Bayesian model that (correctly) assumes reward rates to be constants. This pessimism bias is also incompletely captured by a simple reinforcement learning model (RL) commonly used in neuroscience and psychology, in terms of fitted initial Q-values. While it seems sub-optimal, and thus mysterious, that humans have an underestimated prior reward expectation, our simulations show that an underestimated prior mean helps to maximize long-term gain, if the observer assumes volatility when reward rates are stable and utilizes a softmax decision policy instead of the optimal one (obtainable by dynamic programming). This raises the intriguing possibility that the brain underestimates reward rates to compensate for the incorrect non-stationarity assumption in the generative model and a simplified decision policy.

paragraphs: The authors study repeated human choices among options with uncertain rewards in a stationary bandit experiment. They vary the average abundance and variability of rewards. At the end of a game, participants' reported expectations for unchosen options reveal a significant underestimate of the prior mean reward rate, which the paper calls pessimism bias.

The comparison links the observed pessimism to how participants may represent the environment.

Simulations show that an underestimated prior mean can improve long-term gain when an observer assumes volatility in a stable environment and uses a softmax decision policy. This conditional result suggests that pessimism might compensate for an incorrect environmental assumption and a simplified choice rule. It offers a possible explanation of the behavior rather than establishing that pessimism is generally optimal.
summary.tldr: Human reward pessimism may compensate for assumed environmental volatility and a simplified decision policy in stationary bandit tasks.

title: Why so gloomy? A Bayesian explanation of human pessimism bias in the multi-armed bandit task

abstract: Knowledge distillation is to transfer the knowledge of a large neural network into a smaller one and has been shown to be effective especially when the amount of training data is limited or the size of the student model is very small. To transfer the knowledge, it is essential to observe the data that have been used to train the network since its knowledge is concentrated on a narrow manifold rather than the whole input space. However, the data are not accessible in many cases due to the privacy or confidentiality issues in medical, industrial, and military domains. To the best of our knowledge, there has been no approach that distills the knowledge of a neural network when no data are observable. In this work, we propose KegNet (Knowledge Extraction with Generative Networks), a novel approach to extract the knowledge of a trained deep neural network and to generate artificial data points that replace the missing training data in knowledge distillation. Experiments show that KegNet outperforms all baselines for data-free knowledge distillation. We provide the source code of our paper in https://github.com/snudatalab/KegNet.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers the behavior of a large trained network into a smaller student. The paper focuses on cases where the original training data cannot be accessed, including settings involving confidential or private information. This removes the examples normally used to expose the teacher's useful knowledge during the transfer process.

The difficulty is that a trained network's knowledge is concentrated in a narrow portion of the input space. Merely having the network does not supply representative examples from that region. KegNet addresses this problem using generative networks to extract knowledge from the trained model and produce artificial data points that substitute for the missing training examples.

Those generated examples provide the data used for distillation into a student. The authors report that KegNet outperforms all baselines in their data-free distillation experiments. The stated contribution is a way to perform knowledge transfer without observable training data, with experimental support for the usefulness of the generated replacements. It establishes an alternative source of distillation examples when direct access to the original data is unavailable.
summary.tldr: KegNet generates artificial examples from a trained network to support knowledge distillation when original training data are unavailable.

title: Knowledge Extraction with No Observable Data

abstract: The history of learning for control has been an exciting back and forth between two broad classes of algorithms: planning and reinforcement learning. Planning algorithms effectively reason over long horizons, but assume access to a local policy and distance metric over collision-free paths. Reinforcement learning excels at learning policies and relative values of states, but fails to plan over long horizons. Despite the successes of each method on various tasks, long horizon, sparse reward tasks with high-dimensional observations remain exceedingly challenging for both planning and reinforcement learning algorithms. Frustratingly, these sorts of tasks are potentially the most useful, as they are simple to design (a human only need to provide an example goal state) and avoid injecting bias through reward shaping. We introduce a general-purpose control algorithm that combines the strengths of planning and reinforcement learning to effectively solve these tasks. Our main idea is to decompose the task of reaching a distant goal state into a sequence of easier tasks, each of which corresponds to reaching a particular subgoal. We use goal-conditioned RL to learn a policy to reach each waypoint and to learn a distance metric for search. Using graph search over our replay buffer, we can automatically generate this sequence of subgoals, even in image-based environments. Our algorithm, search on the replay buffer (SoRB), enables agents to solve sparse reward tasks over hundreds of steps, and generalizes substantially better than standard RL algorithms.

paragraphs: Reaching a distant goal is difficult when rewards are sparse and observations are high-dimensional. Planning can reason over long routes but needs ways to measure distances and execute local movements. Reinforcement learning can learn those capabilities, yet struggles with long horizons. Search on the Replay Buffer combines these strengths by breaking a distant goal into reachable subgoals.

The method uses goal-conditioned reinforcement learning to learn a policy for reaching waypoints and a distance measure for search. It then performs graph search over states in the replay buffer to select a sequence of subgoals. Stored experience thereby supplies the states used for planning, while the learned policy carries out the shorter tasks.

The authors report that SoRB solves sparse-reward tasks requiring hundreds of steps and generalizes substantially better than standard reinforcement learning algorithms. It also generates subgoal sequences in image-based environments. The contribution is a way to organize learned local capabilities into longer plans, allowing a distant example goal to be approached through a sequence of easier objectives.
summary.tldr: SoRB searches stored experience for subgoals and uses goal-conditioned reinforcement learning to solve long-horizon, sparse-reward tasks.

title: Search on the Replay Buffer: Bridging Planning and Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Learning causal structure from observational data has attracted much attention, and it is notoriously challenging to find the underlying structure in the presence of confounders (hidden direct common causes of two variables). In this paper, by properly leveraging the non-Gaussianity of the data, we propose to estimate the structure over latent variables with the so-called Triad constraints: we design a form of "pseudo-residual" from three variables, and show that when causal relations are linear and noise terms are non-Gaussian, the causal direction between the latent variables for the three observed variables is identifiable by checking a certain kind of independence relationship. In other words, the Triad constraints help us to locate latent confounders and determine the causal direction between them. This goes far beyond the Tetrad constraints and reveals more information about the underlying structure from non-Gaussian data. Finally, based on the Triad constraints, we develop a two-step algorithm to learn the causal structure corresponding to measurement models. Experimental results on both synthetic and real data demonstrate the effectiveness and reliability of our method.

paragraphs: Hidden common causes make causal discovery from observational data especially difficult. This paper investigates how to recover relationships among latent variables using information in observed measurements. Its central tool is a family of Triad constraints that exploits non-Gaussian structure in the data to locate hidden confounders and determine causal directions between them.

The authors construct a pseudo-residual from three observed variables and test a particular independence relationship. They show that this can identify the direction between the relevant latent variables when causal relations are linear and noise terms are non-Gaussian. These assumptions are essential to the stated identifiability result and explain where the directional information comes from.

The authors argue that Triad constraints reveal more underlying structure than Tetrad constraints in this setting. They use the new constraints in a two-step algorithm for learning causal structure corresponding to measurement models. Experiments on synthetic and real data support the method's effectiveness and reliability, complementing the theoretical result about what the specified independence checks can identify.
summary.tldr: Triad constraints identify latent causal directions through independence tests under linear relations and non-Gaussian noise.

title: Triad Constraints for Learning Causal Structure of Latent Variables

abstract: We provide a differentially private algorithm for hypothesis selection. Given samples from an unknown probability distribution $P$ and a set of $m$ probability distributions $\mathcal{H}$, the goal is to output, in a $\varepsilon$-differentially private manner, a distribution from $\mathcal{H}$ whose total variation distance to $P$ is comparable to that of the best such distribution (which we denote by $\alpha$). The sample complexity of our basic algorithm is $O\left(\frac{\log m}{\alpha^2} + \frac{\log m}{\alpha \varepsilon}\right)$, representing a minimal cost for privacy when compared to the non-private algorithm. We also can handle infinite hypothesis classes $\mathcal{H}$ by relaxing to $(\varepsilon,\delta)$-differential privacy. We apply our hypothesis selection algorithm to give learning algorithms for a number of natural distribution classes, including Gaussians, product distributions, sums of independent random variables, piecewise polynomials, and mixture classes. Our hypothesis selection procedure allows us to generically convert a cover for a class to a learning algorithm, complementing known learning lower bounds which are in terms of the size of the packing number of the class. As the covering and packing numbers are often closely related, for constant $\alpha$, our algorithms achieve the optimal sample complexity for many classes of interest. Finally, we describe an application to private distribution-free PAC learning.

paragraphs: Private hypothesis selection chooses a probability distribution from a candidate collection using samples from an unknown distribution. The aim is to select a candidate whose total variation distance to the truth is comparable to the best available candidate, while satisfying differential privacy. This turns private distribution learning into a carefully controlled selection problem.

For m candidates, best-candidate error α, and privacy parameter ε, the basic algorithm uses O(log(m)/α² + log(m)/(αε)) samples. The authors characterize the added privacy cost as minimal relative to nonprivate selection. They also address infinite candidate classes by relaxing the requirement to approximate, or (ε,δ), differential privacy.

The procedure converts a cover of a distribution class into a learning algorithm. Applications include Gaussians, product distributions, sums of independent random variables, piecewise polynomials, and mixtures. Because covering and packing sizes are often closely related, the authors obtain optimal sample complexity for many classes at constant α. They also describe an application to private distribution-free PAC learning.
summary.tldr: A differentially private selection procedure finds nearly best-fitting candidate distributions with a small additional sample cost for privacy.

title: Private Hypothesis Selection

abstract: Compression is at the heart of effective representation learning. However, lossy compression is typically achieved through simple parametric models like Gaussian noise to preserve analytic tractability, and the limitations this imposes on learning are largely unexplored. Further, the Gaussian prior assumptions in models such as variational autoencoders (VAEs) provide only an upper bound on the compression rate in general. We introduce a new noise channel, Echo noise, that admits a simple, exact expression for mutual information for arbitrary input distributions. The noise is constructed in a data-driven fashion that does not require restrictive distributional assumptions. With its complex encoding mechanism and exact rate regularization, Echo leads to improved bounds on log-likelihood and dominates beta-VAEs across the achievable range of rate-distortion trade-offs. Further, we show that Echo noise can outperform flow-based methods without the need to train additional distributional transformations.

paragraphs: Representation learning often compresses an input while retaining enough information to reconstruct it. This creates a trade-off between the information preserved, called the rate, and reconstruction error, called distortion. The paper argues that familiar Gaussian assumptions make this trade-off tractable but can restrict the encoding, while generally providing only an upper bound on the actual compression rate.

Echo noise is a new, data-driven noise channel with a simple exact expression for mutual information for arbitrary input distributions. Mutual information measures how much information about the input survives in the representation. Having an exact expression lets the model regularize that quantity directly without relying on restrictive distributional assumptions of the kind highlighted in the paper.

The authors report improved log-likelihood bounds and rate-distortion performance that dominates beta-VAEs across the achievable trade-off range. They also show that Echo can outperform flow-based methods without training additional distributional transformations. These findings connect the encoding mechanism and exact rate control to improved representation learning, rather than treating the noise distribution merely as a mathematical convenience.
summary.tldr: Echo noise enables exact information-rate regularization in autoencoders and improves the reported trade-off between compression and reconstruction.

title: Exact Rate-Distortion in Autoencoders via Echo Noise

abstract: Minimizing a non-smooth function over the Grassmannian appears in many applications in machine learning. In this paper we show that if the objective satisfies a certain Riemannian regularity condition with respect to some point in the Grassmannian, then a Riemannian subgradient method with appropriate initialization and geometrically diminishing step size converges at a linear rate to that point. We show that for both the robust subspace learning method Dual Principal Component Pursuit (DPCP) and the Orthogonal Dictionary Learning (ODL) problem, the Riemannian regularity condition is satisfied with respect to appropriate points of interest, namely the subspace orthogonal to the sought subspace for DPCP and the orthonormal dictionary atoms for ODL. Consequently, we obtain in a unified framework significant improvements for the convergence theory of both methods.
