paragraphs: This paper studies optimization problems whose solutions are subspaces, represented as points on the Grassmannian. The objective can be both nonsmooth and nonconvex, making convergence guarantees challenging. The authors identify a geometric regularity condition that allows a Riemannian subgradient method to approach a particular target point at a linear rate.

The guarantee is conditional: the objective must satisfy the stated regularity condition, the method must start from an appropriate initialization, and its step sizes must decrease geometrically. Under these requirements, the distance to the target contracts at a geometric pace. The result therefore connects a property of the objective's geometry with a concrete choice of optimization procedure.

The authors then establish the required condition for two applications. For Dual Principal Component Pursuit, the relevant target is the subspace orthogonal to the desired subspace. For Orthogonal Dictionary Learning, the targets are the orthonormal dictionary atoms. Bringing both problems into the same framework strengthens their convergence theory and explains how a shared geometric argument supports efficient progress in each.
summary.tldr: A geometric regularity condition yields linear convergence for appropriately initialized subgradient methods in robust subspace and orthogonal dictionary learning.

title: A Linearly Convergent Method for Non-Smooth Non-Convex Optimization on the Grassmannian with Applications to Robust Subspace and Dictionary Learning

abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning often requires decentralised policies, which severely limit the agents' ability to coordinate their behaviour. In this paper, we show that common knowledge between agents allows for complex decentralised coordination. Common knowledge arises naturally in a large number of decentralised cooperative multi-agent tasks, for example, when agents can reconstruct parts of each others' observations. Since agents can independently agree on their common knowledge, they can execute complex coordinated policies that condition on this knowledge in a fully decentralised fashion. We propose multi-agent common knowledge reinforcement learning (MACKRL), a novel stochastic actor-critic algorithm that learns a hierarchical policy tree. Higher levels in the hierarchy coordinate groups of agents by conditioning on their common knowledge, or delegate to lower levels with smaller subgroups but potentially richer common knowledge. The entire policy tree can be executed in a fully decentralised fashion. As the lowest policy tree level consists of independent policies for each agent, MACKRL reduces to independently learnt decentralised policies as a special case. We demonstrate that our method can exploit common knowledge for superior performance on complex decentralised coordination tasks, including a stochastic matrix game and challenging problems in StarCraft II unit micromanagement.

paragraphs: Agents acting without centralized control can struggle to coordinate because each has only partial information. This paper uses common knowledge: information on which agents can independently agree. Such knowledge can arise when agents reconstruct parts of one another’s observations, providing a shared basis for coordinated decisions without centralized execution.

MACKRL learns a hierarchical policy tree through a stochastic actor-critic algorithm. Higher levels coordinate groups using their common knowledge. They can also delegate decisions to smaller subgroups, which may share richer information. This hierarchy lets the policy vary the scope of coordination according to the knowledge available among the participating agents.

The entire tree supports decentralized execution. Its lowest level contains independent policies for individual agents, so independently learned decentralized behavior is included as a special case. Experiments on a stochastic matrix game and StarCraft II unit micromanagement demonstrate superior performance through exploiting common knowledge. The findings show how shared information can support complex coordination even when agents must execute their policies separately.
summary.tldr: MACKRL learns a hierarchy of policies that uses common knowledge to coordinate groups while preserving fully decentralized execution.

title: Multi-Agent Common Knowledge Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Neural networks are nowadays highly successful despite strong hardness results. The existing hardness results focus on the network architecture, and assume that the network's weights are arbitrary. A natural approach to settle the discrepancy is to assume that the network's weights are ``well-behaved" and posses some generic properties that may allow efficient learning. This approach is supported by the intuition that the weights in real-world networks are not arbitrary, but exhibit some ''random-like" properties with respect to some ''natural" distributions. We prove negative results in this regard, and show that for depth-$2$ networks, and many ``natural" weights distributions such as the normal and the uniform distribution, most networks are hard to learn. Namely, there is no efficient learning algorithm that is provably successful for most weights, and every input distribution. It implies that there is no generic property that holds with high probability in such random networks and allows efficient learning.

paragraphs: Neural networks work well in practice despite theoretical results showing that learning them can be computationally hard. One possible explanation is that earlier hardness results allow arbitrary weights, whereas realistic weights might possess helpful regularities. This paper investigates whether weights drawn from familiar, natural distributions provide a general escape from those learning difficulties.

The authors prove negative results for depth-two networks with weights from distributions including the normal and uniform distributions. Their conclusion concerns algorithms that would be provably successful for most weight choices and every input distribution. Within that scope, simply making weights random according to these natural distributions does not yield an efficient learning guarantee.

The distinction between weights and inputs is central to interpreting the result. The networks need not have specially selected unusual weights, but the desired guarantee still covers every distribution of inputs. Consequently, a property shared by most networks under the studied weight distributions cannot by itself establish that broad guarantee. The result narrows a proposed explanation for practical success without asserting that every concrete learning task involving such networks is difficult.
summary.tldr: Natural random weight distributions alone do not make depth-two networks efficiently learnable with guarantees covering every input distribution.

title: Hardness of Learning Neural Networks with Natural Weights

abstract: Content creation, central to applications such as virtual reality, can be tedious and time-consuming. Recent image synthesis methods simplify this task by offering tools to generate new views from as little as a single input image, or by converting a semantic map into a photorealistic image. We propose to push the envelope further, and introduce Generative View Synthesis (GVS) that can synthesize multiple photorealistic views of a scene given a single semantic map. We show that the sequential application of existing techniques, e.g., semantics-to-image translation followed by monocular view synthesis, fail at capturing the scene's structure. In contrast, we solve the semantics-to-image translation in concert with the estimation of the 3D layout of the scene, thus producing geometrically consistent novel views that preserve semantic structures. We first lift the input 2D semantic map onto a 3D layered representation of the scene in feature space, thereby preserving the semantic labels of 3D geometric structures. We then project the layered features onto the target views to generate the final novel-view images. We verify the strengths of our method and compare it with several advanced baselines on three different datasets. Our approach also allows for style manipulation and image editing operations, such as the addition or removal of objects, with simple manipulations of the input style images and semantic maps respectively. For code and additional results, visit the project page at https://gvsnet.github.io

paragraphs: Generative View Synthesis creates multiple photorealistic views of a scene from a single semantic map, an input describing the arrangement of semantic categories. The task combines generating visual appearance with inferring a scene layout that supports changes in viewpoint. It targets content creation settings where manually producing those views is time-consuming.

The authors find that applying image generation and single-image view synthesis in sequence fails to capture scene structure adequately. Their method instead solves appearance generation together with three-dimensional layout estimation. It lifts the input map into a layered 3D feature representation that preserves semantic labels, then projects those features into target viewpoints to generate images.

This shared representation supports geometrically consistent views while preserving semantic structures. Comparisons with advanced baselines across three datasets support the method's strengths. The approach also allows changes to visual style through style images and edits such as adding or removing objects through semantic maps. These controls connect the generated views to inputs that users can manipulate directly.
summary.tldr: Generative View Synthesis jointly learns scene layout and appearance to produce consistent novel views from a single semantic map.

title: Generative View Synthesis: From Single-view Semantics to Novel-view Images

abstract: Random forests have been one of the successful ensemble algorithms in machine learning. The basic idea is to construct a large number of random trees individually and make prediction based on an average of their predictions. The great successes have attracted much attention on the consistency of random forests, mostly focusing on regression. This work takes one step towards convergence rates of random forests for classification. We present the first finite-sample rate O(n^{-1/(8d+2)}) on the convergence of pure random forests for classification, which can be improved to be of O(n^{-1/(3.87d+2)}) by considering the midpoint splitting mechanism. We introduce another variant of random forests, which follow Breiman's original random forests but with different mechanisms on splitting dimensions and positions. We get a convergence rate O(n^{-{1}/(d+2)}(\ln n)^{{1}/(d+2)}) for the variant of random forests, which reaches the minimax rate, except for a factor (\ln n)^{{1}/(d+2)}, of the optimal plug-in classifier under the L-Lipschitz assumption. We achieve tighter convergence rate O(\sqrt{\ln n/n}) under proper assumptions over structural data.

paragraphs: Random forests combine predictions from many randomized trees. Although their consistency has received substantial theoretical attention, much of that work concerns regression. This paper studies classification and derives finite-sample convergence rates, quantifying how the analyzed forests improve as the number of observations increases.

For pure random forests, the authors obtain a rate of O(n^(-1/(8d+2))), where n is sample size and d is dimension. Using midpoint splitting improves this to O(n^(-1/(3.87d+2))). They also analyze a variant resembling Breiman's original forest but with changed rules for selecting split dimensions and positions. Its rate is O(n^(-1/(d+2))(ln n)^(1/(d+2))).

Under the stated Lipschitz assumption, the latter rate matches the optimal plug-in classifier's minimax rate up to a logarithmic factor. With suitable additional assumptions on data structure, the paper obtains the tighter rate O(√(ln n/n)). These results show how splitting mechanisms and structural assumptions affect theoretical classification rates, with each guarantee attached to its particular forest and assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper derives classification convergence rates for several random forest variants, including a near-minimax rate under a Lipschitz assumption.

title: Towards Convergence Rate Analysis of Random Forests for Classification

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are widely used deep learning models that learn meaningful representations from graph-structured data. Due to the finite nature of the underlying recurrent structure, current GNN methods may struggle to capture long-range dependencies in underlying graphs. To overcome this difficulty, we propose a graph learning framework, called Implicit Graph Neural Networks (IGNN), where predictions are based on the solution of a fixed-point equilibrium equation involving implicitly defined "state" vectors. We use the Perron-Frobenius theory to derive sufficient conditions that ensure well-posedness of the framework. Leveraging implicit differentiation, we derive a tractable projected gradient descent method to train the framework. Experiments on a comprehensive range of tasks show that IGNNs consistently capture long-range dependencies and outperform state-of-the-art GNN models.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks learn representations from connected data, but their finite recurrent structure can make distant relationships difficult to capture. This paper introduces Implicit Graph Neural Networks, which base predictions on an equilibrium of graph-dependent state vectors. The representation is defined through a fixed-point equation rather than solely through a finite sequence of recurrent updates.

An equilibrium formulation raises the question of whether the resulting states are well defined. The authors use Perron-Frobenius theory to derive sufficient conditions for well-posedness. They then use implicit differentiation to construct a tractable training method based on projected gradient descent. The framework therefore addresses both the mathematical definition of the representation and how to optimize it.

Across a comprehensive set of experimental tasks, the authors report that IGNNs consistently capture long-range dependencies and outperform the compared state-of-the-art graph models. These findings support equilibrium-based representations as a practical approach to distant graph relationships. The theoretical conditions remain sufficient conditions, while the performance advantage is an experimental result over the tasks studied.
summary.tldr: IGNNs learn graph representations through fixed-point equilibria and show strong experimental performance on long-range dependencies.

title: Implicit Graph Neural Networks

abstract: The Gumbel-Softmax is a continuous distribution over the simplex that is often used as a relaxation of discrete distributions. Because it can be readily interpreted and easily reparameterized, it enjoys widespread use. We propose a modular and more flexible family of reparameterizable distributions where Gaussian noise is transformed into a one-hot approximation through an invertible function. This invertible function is composed of a modified softmax and can incorporate diverse transformations that serve different specific purposes. For example, the stick-breaking procedure allows us to extend the reparameterization trick to distributions with countably infinite support, thus enabling the use of our distribution along nonparametric models, or normalizing flows let us increase the flexibility of the distribution. Our construction enjoys theoretical advantages over the Gumbel-Softmax, such as closed form KL, and significantly outperforms it in a variety of experiments. Our code is available at https://github.com/cunningham-lab/igr.

paragraphs: Discrete choices are often approximated by continuous distributions so that learning can use reparameterization. Gumbel-Softmax is a popular construction of this kind, producing continuous values on the simplex that approximate discrete outcomes. This paper introduces a more modular family that transforms Gaussian noise into an approximation of a one-hot vector through an invertible function.

The transformation includes a modified softmax and can incorporate additional components for different purposes. A stick-breaking construction extends reparameterization to distributions with countably infinite support, making the approach usable with nonparametric models. Normalizing flows provide another option, increasing the flexibility of the resulting distribution.

The construction has theoretical advantages over Gumbel-Softmax, including a closed-form KL divergence, and significantly outperforms it in a variety of experiments reported by the authors. Its broader contribution is a configurable way to build continuous approximations to discrete distributions. The same framework can therefore address both greater distributional flexibility and settings with infinitely many possible outcomes, depending on the chosen transformation.
summary.tldr: Invertible Gaussian transformations provide flexible, reparameterizable approximations to discrete distributions, including constructions with countably infinite support.

title: Invertible Gaussian Reparameterization: Revisiting the Gumbel-Softmax

abstract: Existing research on continual learning of a sequence of tasks focused on dealing with catastrophic forgetting, where the tasks are assumed to be dissimilar and have little shared knowledge. Some work has also been done to transfer previously learned knowledge to the new task when the tasks are similar and have shared knowledge. %However, in the most general case, a CL system not only should have the above two capabilities, but also the \textit{backward knowledge transfer} capability so that future tasks may help improve the past models whenever possible. To the best of our knowledge, no technique has been proposed to learn a sequence of mixed similar and dissimilar tasks that can deal with forgetting and also transfer knowledge forward and backward. This paper proposes such a technique to learn both types of tasks in the same network. For dissimilar tasks, the algorithm focuses on dealing with forgetting, and for similar tasks, the algorithm focuses on selectively transferring the knowledge learned from some similar previous tasks to improve the new task learning. Additionally, the algorithm automatically detects whether a new task is similar to any previous tasks. Empirical evaluation using sequences of mixed tasks demonstrates the effectiveness of the proposed model.

paragraphs: A system learning tasks sequentially faces two different needs. It should preserve earlier knowledge when a new task is unrelated, and reuse useful knowledge when tasks are similar. This paper addresses sequences containing both types, bringing protection against forgetting and knowledge transfer into the same network.

The proposed algorithm automatically detects whether an incoming task resembles any earlier tasks. For dissimilar tasks, it focuses on limiting forgetting. For similar tasks, it selectively transfers knowledge from relevant previous tasks to improve learning of the new one. Selectivity matters because the sequence can contain a mixture of useful and unrelated prior experience.

The paper also frames backward transfer, where later learning can help earlier models, as part of the combined capability it seeks to provide. Its empirical evaluation uses mixed task sequences and demonstrates the proposed model's effectiveness. The central contribution is therefore a continual-learning approach that responds to task relationships, rather than treating every new task as requiring the same balance between preserving and sharing knowledge.
summary.tldr: The method automatically detects task similarity to combine forgetting prevention with selective knowledge transfer in mixed continual-learning sequences.

title: Continual Learning of a Mixed Sequence of Similar and Dissimilar Tasks

abstract: By chaining a sequence of differentiable invertible transformations, normalizing flows (NF) provide an expressive method of posterior approximation, exact density evaluation, and sampling. The trend in normalizing flow literature has been to devise deeper, more complex transformations to achieve greater flexibility. We propose an alternative: Gradient Boosted Normalizing Flows (GBNF) model a density by successively adding new NF components with gradient boosting. Under the boosting framework, each new NF component optimizes a weighted likelihood objective, resulting in new components that are fit to the suitable residuals of the previously trained components. The GBNF formulation results in a mixture model structure, whose flexibility increases as more components are added. Moreover, GBNFs offer a wider, as opposed to strictly deeper, approach that improves existing NFs at the cost of additional training---not more complex transformations. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique for density estimation and, by coupling GBNF with a variational autoencoder, generative modeling of images. Our results show that GBNFs outperform their non-boosted analog, and, in some cases, produce better results with smaller, simpler flows.

paragraphs: Normalizing flows describe probability distributions through sequences of differentiable, invertible transformations. They support density evaluation, sampling, and posterior approximation. Increasing their flexibility often involves making those transformations deeper or more complex. This paper develops another way to expand a flow model: add separately trained flow components through gradient boosting.

Each new component optimizes a weighted likelihood objective that directs it toward suitable residuals left by previously trained components. The resulting model is a mixture whose flexibility grows as components are added. This expands the model across components while keeping the individual transformations relatively simple, at the cost of additional training.

The authors evaluate the method on density estimation and on image generation by combining it with a variational autoencoder. Boosted models outperform their corresponding non-boosted versions in the reported results. In some cases, smaller and simpler flows also produce better results. The findings support boosting as a useful route to stronger flow models without requiring every component to become more elaborate.
summary.tldr: Gradient boosting builds a mixture of normalizing flows that improves density estimation and image generation by adding components trained on remaining errors.

title: Gradient Boosted Normalizing Flows

abstract: Label noise generally degenerates the performance of deep learning algorithms because deep neural networks easily overfit label errors. Let $X$ and $Y$ denote the instance and clean label, respectively. When $Y$ is a cause of $X$, according to which many datasets have been constructed, e.g., \textit{SVHN} and \textit{CIFAR}, the distributions of $P(X)$ and $P(Y|X)$ are generally entangled. This means that the unsupervised instances are helpful to learn the classifier and thus reduce the side effect of label noise. However, it remains elusive on how to exploit the causal information to handle the label-noise problem. We propose to model and make use of the causal process in order to correct the label-noise effect.Empirically, the proposed method outperforms all state-of-the-art methods on both synthetic and real-world label-noise datasets.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can damage deep learning because neural networks readily fit the errors themselves. This paper approaches the problem through a causal model of how examples arise. It focuses on the setting where the clean label is a cause of the observed instance, a construction the authors associate with datasets such as SVHN and CIFAR.

Under that causal relationship, the distribution of inputs and the rule relating inputs to clean labels are generally entangled. Consequently, examples without trustworthy labels can still contain information useful for learning the classifier. The proposed method explicitly models and uses the causal generation process to reduce the effect of label noise.

The authors report that their method outperforms the state-of-the-art approaches they evaluate on both synthetic and real-world label-noise datasets. The central idea is to extract guidance from the structure of the inputs as well as their supplied labels. Its motivation is tied to the stated direction of causation, rather than claiming that every label-noise problem has the same causal structure.
summary.tldr: A causal model of labels generating inputs provides additional information for learning classifiers from instance-dependent noisy labels.

title: Instance-dependent Label-noise Learning under a Structural Causal Model

abstract: Gradient-based hyperparameter optimization has earned a widespread popularity in the context of few-shot meta-learning, but remains broadly impractical for tasks with long horizons (many gradient steps), due to memory scaling and gradient degradation issues. A common workaround is to learn hyperparameters online, but this introduces greediness which comes with a significant performance drop. We propose forward-mode differentiation with sharing (FDS), a simple and efficient algorithm which tackles memory scaling issues with forward-mode differentiation, and gradient degradation issues by sharing hyperparameters that are contiguous in time. We provide theoretical guarantees about the noise reduction properties of our algorithm, and demonstrate its efficiency empirically by differentiating through $\sim 10^4$ gradient steps of unrolled optimization. We consider large hyperparameter search ranges on CIFAR-10 where we significantly outperform greedy gradient-based alternatives, while achieving $\times 20$ speedups compared to the state-of-the-art black-box methods.

paragraphs: Gradient-based hyperparameter optimization adjusts training choices by differentiating through the learning process. Over many training steps, this becomes difficult because memory requirements grow and the gradients can degrade. Updating hyperparameters online avoids some of that burden, but the paper describes a performance cost from making overly short-term choices.

Forward-mode differentiation with sharing, or FDS, addresses the two obstacles together. Forward-mode differentiation tackles memory scaling, while sharing hyperparameters across neighboring training steps addresses gradient degradation. This makes the temporal organization of hyperparameters part of the optimization method. The authors also provide theoretical guarantees about the resulting reduction in noise.

The empirical evaluation differentiates through approximately ten thousand optimization steps, demonstrating operation over long training horizons. On CIFAR-10 with large hyperparameter search ranges, FDS significantly outperforms greedy gradient-based alternatives and achieves twentyfold speedups relative to the compared state-of-the-art black-box methods. These findings show that considering longer-term training effects can be computationally practical in the studied setting, without relying on exclusively local hyperparameter updates.
summary.tldr: FDS combines forward-mode differentiation and temporal hyperparameter sharing to make gradient-based tuning practical across thousands of training steps.

title: Gradient-based Hyperparameter Optimization Over Long Horizons

abstract: The key objective of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) is to generate new data with the same statistics as the provided training data. However, multiple recent works show that state-of-the-art architectures yet struggle to achieve this goal. In particular, they report an elevated amount of high frequencies in the spectral statistics which makes it straightforward to distinguish real and generated images. Explanations for this phenomenon are controversial: While most works attribute the artifacts to the generator, other works point to the discriminator. We take a sober look at those explanations and provide insights on what makes proposed measures against high-frequency artifacts effective. To achieve this, we first independently assess the architectures of both the generator and discriminator and investigate if they exhibit a frequency bias that makes learning the distribution of high-frequency content particularly problematic. Based on these experiments, we make the following four observations: 1) Different upsampling operations bias the generator towards different spectral properties. 2) Checkerboard artifacts introduced by upsampling cannot explain the spectral discrepancies alone as the generator is able to compensate for these artifacts. 3) The discriminator does not struggle with detecting high frequencies per se but rather struggles with frequencies of low magnitude. 4) The downsampling operations in the discriminator can impair the quality of the training signal it provides.In light of these findings, we analyze proposed measures against high-frequency artifacts in state-of-the-art GAN training but find that none of the existing approaches can fully resolve spectral artifacts yet. Our results suggest that there is great potential in improving the discriminator and that this could be key to match the distribution of the training data more closely.

paragraphs: Generated images can look convincing while still having frequency statistics that differ from real images. This paper investigates why GANs exhibit these spectral artifacts, separating the roles of the generator and discriminator. The goal is to understand which architectural choices cause difficulties and why proposed remedies help.

The experiments find that different upsampling operations push generators toward different spectral properties. However, checkerboard artifacts from upsampling do not explain the entire mismatch, because generators can compensate for them. On the discriminator side, the difficulty is detecting frequency components with small magnitudes, rather than high frequencies themselves. Downsampling can also weaken the training signal that the discriminator supplies.

These distinctions matter because they challenge explanations that assign the problem solely to generator upsampling or assume that discriminators are inherently unable to recognize high frequencies. The authors examine existing countermeasures and find that none fully eliminates spectral artifacts in their analysis. Their results suggest that improving the discriminator could help generated data match training-data statistics more closely, while leaving complete resolution as an open outcome.
summary.tldr: GAN spectral artifacts reflect both generator and discriminator behavior, with weak-frequency detection and discriminator downsampling emerging as promising targets for improvement.

title: On the Frequency Bias of Generative Models

abstract: Multi-task learning aims to explore task relatedness to improve individual tasks, which is of particular significance in the challenging scenario that only limited data is available for each task. To tackle this challenge, we propose variational multi-task learning (VMTL), a general probabilistic inference framework for learning multiple related tasks. We cast multi-task learning as a variational Bayesian inference problem, in which task relatedness is explored in a unified manner by specifying priors. To incorporate shared knowledge into each task, we design the prior of a task to be a learnable mixture of the variational posteriors of other related tasks, which is learned by the Gumbel-Softmax technique. In contrast to previous methods, our VMTL can exploit task relatedness for both representations and classifiers in a principled way by jointly inferring their posteriors. This enables individual tasks to fully leverage inductive biases provided by related tasks, therefore improving the overall performance of all tasks. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed VMTL is able to effectively tackle a variety of challenging multi-task learning settings with limited training data for both classification and regression. Our method consistently surpasses previous methods, including strong Bayesian approaches, and achieves state-of-the-art performance on five benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: Related tasks can help one another learn, particularly when each has limited training data. This paper develops variational multi-task learning, a probabilistic framework that expresses task relationships through priors. It casts learning several tasks as a joint variational Bayesian inference problem, giving knowledge sharing an explicit role in the probabilistic model.

For each task, the prior is a learnable mixture of approximate posterior distributions from other related tasks. The mixture is learned using the Gumbel-Softmax technique. This allows the framework to determine how knowledge from other tasks contributes to a particular task's prior. Sharing extends to both learned representations and classifiers through joint inference of their posteriors.

Experiments cover challenging classification and regression settings with limited data. The authors report consistent improvements over previous approaches, including strong Bayesian methods, and state-of-the-art performance on five benchmark datasets. The contribution is a unified mechanism for borrowing information across tasks at multiple parts of the model, with empirical evidence that this sharing helps when individual tasks have little data.
summary.tldr: VMTL learns task-specific priors from other tasks' posteriors, sharing information across representations and classifiers to improve limited-data learning.

title: Variational Multi-Task Learning with Gumbel-Softmax Priors

abstract: We study the problem of learning revenue-optimal multi-bidder auctions from samples when the samples of bidders' valuations can be adversarially corrupted or drawn from distributions that are adversarially perturbed. First, we prove tight upper bounds on the revenue we can obtain with a corrupted distribution under a population model, for both regular valuation distributions and distributions with monotone hazard rate (MHR). We then propose new algorithms that, given only an ``approximate distribution'' for the bidder's valuation, can learn a mechanism whose revenue is nearly optimal simultaneously for all ``true distributions'' that are $\alpha$-close to the original distribution in Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance. The proposed algorithms operate beyond the setting of bounded distributions that have been studied in prior works, and are guaranteed to obtain a fraction $1-O(\alpha)$ of the optimal revenue under the true distribution when the distributions are MHR. Moreover, they are guaranteed to yield at least a fraction $1-O(\sqrt{\alpha})$ of the optimal revenue when the distributions are regular. We prove that these upper bounds cannot be further improved, by providing matching lower bounds. Lastly, we derive sample complexity upper bounds for learning a near-optimal auction for both MHR and regular distributions.

First, we prove tight upper bounds on the revenue we can obtain with a corrupted distribution under a population model, for both regular valuation distributions and distributions with monotone hazard rate (MHR). We then propose new algorithms that, given only an ``approximate distribution'' for the bidder's valuation, can learn a mechanism whose revenue is nearly optimal simultaneously for all ``true distributions'' that are $\alpha$-close to the original distribution in Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance. The proposed algorithms operate beyond the setting of bounded distributions that have been studied in prior works, and are guaranteed to obtain a fraction $1-O(\alpha)$ of the optimal revenue under the true distribution when the distributions are MHR. Moreover, they are guaranteed to yield at least a fraction $1-O(\sqrt{\alpha})$ of the optimal revenue when the distributions are regular. We prove that these upper bounds cannot be further improved, by providing matching lower bounds. Lastly, we derive sample complexity upper bounds for learning a near-optimal auction for both MHR and regular distributions.

paragraphs: Learning a revenue-maximizing auction becomes harder when observed bidder valuations are corrupted or their distributions are adversarially perturbed. This paper studies auction learning under that uncertainty. It asks what revenue can still be guaranteed when the learner has only an approximate valuation distribution rather than an exact description of bidders' values.

The authors design algorithms whose revenue is nearly optimal simultaneously across all true distributions within a specified Kolmogorov-Smirnov distance of the approximation. Their guarantees extend beyond previously studied bounded distributions. For monotone-hazard-rate distributions, the revenue fraction is at least one minus a term of order alpha; for regular distributions, the loss term is of order the square root of alpha.

Here alpha measures the allowed distributional discrepancy. Matching lower bounds establish that the dependence on this discrepancy cannot be improved in the studied settings. The paper also derives sample-complexity upper bounds for learning nearly optimal auctions in both distribution classes. These results quantify how robustness depends on distributional structure and how much revenue uncertainty can force a learner to lose.
summary.tldr: Robust auction-learning algorithms achieve tight revenue guarantees when bidder valuation distributions are adversarially perturbed.

title: Robust Learning of Optimal Auctions

abstract: Among the most successful methods for sparsifying deep (neural) networks are those that adaptively mask the network weights throughout training. By examining this masking, or dropout, in the linear case, we uncover a duality between such adaptive methods and regularization through the so-called “η-trick” that casts both as iteratively reweighted optimizations. We show that any dropout strategy that adapts to the weights in a monotonic way corresponds to an effective subquadratic regularization penalty, and therefore leads to sparse solutions. We obtain the effective penalties for several popular sparsification strategies, which are remarkably similar to classical penalties commonly used in sparse optimization. Considering variational dropout as a case study, we demonstrate similar empirical behavior between the adaptive dropout method and classical methods on the task of deep network sparsification, validating our theory.

paragraphs: Adaptive dropout methods sparsify neural networks by changing which weights are masked during training. This paper asks what optimization effect those changing masks create. It begins with the linear case, where the authors connect adaptive masking to explicit regularization through a mathematical device called the η-trick.

The connection expresses both approaches as iteratively reweighted optimization procedures. Within the analyzed setting, any dropout strategy that adapts monotonically to the weights corresponds to an effective subquadratic penalty, leading to sparse solutions. The authors derive these effective penalties for several popular sparsification strategies and find close similarities to classical penalties used in sparse optimization.

The paper then uses variational dropout as a case study in deep-network sparsification. Its experiments show behavior similar to classical methods, providing empirical support for the theoretical connection. The distinction between the linear analysis and the deep-network experiment matters: the former establishes the duality, while the latter examines whether comparable behavior appears in a more complex setting. The result supplies a regularization-based interpretation of adaptive masking.
summary.tldr: A linear-case analysis links monotonic adaptive dropout to sparsity-inducing regularization, with supporting empirical behavior in deep-network sparsification.

title: The Flip Side of the Reweighted Coin: Duality of Adaptive Dropout and Regularization

abstract: Prior work on differential privacy analysis of randomized SGD algorithms relies on composition theorems, where the implicit (unrealistic) assumption is that the internal state of the iterative algorithm is revealed to the adversary. As a result, the R\'enyi DP bounds derived by such composition-based analyses linearly grow with the number of training epochs. When the internal state of the algorithm is hidden, we prove a converging privacy bound for noisy stochastic gradient descent (on strongly convex smooth loss functions). We show how to take advantage of privacy amplification by sub-sampling and randomized post-processing, and prove the dynamics of privacy bound for ``shuffle and partition'' and ``sample without replacement'' stochastic mini-batch gradient descent schemes. We prove that, in these settings, our privacy bound converges exponentially fast and is substantially smaller than the composition bounds, notably after a few number of training epochs. Thus, unless the DP algorithm converges fast, our privacy analysis shows that hidden state analysis can significantly amplify differential privacy.

The paper examines what changes when those internal states remain hidden.

For noisy stochastic gradient descent on strongly convex, smooth losses, the authors prove a privacy bound that converges instead of continuing to grow. Their analysis uses privacy amplification from subsampling together with randomized post-processing. It covers stochastic mini-batch schemes based on shuffling and partitioning, as well as sampling without replacement.

In these settings, the privacy bound approaches its limit exponentially quickly and becomes substantially smaller than composition-based bounds, notably after a few epochs. The result shows why the adversary's access to intermediate states can materially affect privacy accounting. Its guarantees depend on hidden state and the stated loss assumptions; they establish a sharper analysis for these training settings rather than an unrestricted claim about all neural-network training.
summary.tldr: With hidden internal states and strongly convex smooth losses, noisy SGD admits privacy bounds that converge rather than grow linearly with epochs.

title: Differentially Private Learning Needs Hidden State (Or Much Faster Convergence)

abstract: This paper presents OmniVL, a new foundation model to support both image-language and video-language tasks using one universal architecture. It adopts a unified transformer-based visual encoder for both image and video inputs, and thus can perform joint image-language and video-language pretraining. We demonstrate, for the first time, such a paradigm benefits both image and video tasks, as opposed to the conventional one-directional transfer (e.g., use image-language to help video-language). To this end, we propose a \emph{decoupled} joint pretraining of image-language and video-language to effectively decompose the vision-language modeling into spatial and temporal dimensions and obtain performance boost on both image and video tasks. Moreover, we introduce a novel unified vision-language contrastive (UniVLC) loss to leverage image-text, video-text, image-label (e.g., image classification), video-label (e.g., video action recognition) data together, so that both supervised and noisily supervised pretraining data are utilized as much as possible. Without incurring extra task-specific adaptors, OmniVL can simultaneously support visual only tasks (e.g., image classification, video action recognition), cross-modal alignment tasks (e.g., image/video-text retrieval), and multi-modal understanding and generation tasks (e.g., image/video question answering, captioning). We evaluate OmniVL on a wide range of downstream tasks and achieve state-of-the-art or competitive results with similar model size and data scale.

paragraphs: OmniVL brings image-language and video-language learning into one architecture. A shared transformer-based visual encoder handles both images and videos, enabling joint pretraining across the two input types. The paper reports benefits for both image and video tasks, extending beyond using image-language learning only to help video-language performance.

Its pretraining method separates spatial and temporal aspects of vision-language modeling. A unified contrastive loss also combines image-text, video-text, image-label, and video-label data. This allows the same training framework to use both supervised labels and noisier paired language data rather than relying on only one kind of supervision.

The resulting model supports visual classification, image or video retrieval from text, question answering, and captioning without additional task-specific adaptors. Across a broad range of downstream evaluations, it achieves state-of-the-art or competitive results at similar model sizes and data scales. The contribution is evidence that a shared architecture and coordinated training objective can support this variety while allowing image and video learning to benefit each other.
summary.tldr: OmniVL jointly learns from images, videos, text, and labels in one architecture that supports diverse visual and language tasks.

title: OmniVL: One Foundation Model for Image-Language and Video-Language Tasks

abstract: Motivated by the problem of learning with small sample sizes, this paper shows how to incorporate into support-vector machines (SVMs) those properties that have made convolutional neural networks (CNNs) successful. Particularly important is the ability to incorporate domain knowledge of invariances, e.g., translational invariance of images. Kernels based on the \textit{maximum} similarity over a group of transformations are not generally positive definite. Perhaps it is for this reason that they have not been studied theoretically. We address this lacuna and show that positive definiteness indeed holds \textit{with high probability} for kernels based on the maximum similarity in the small training sample set regime of interest, and that they do yield the best results in that regime. We also show how additional properties such as their ability to incorporate local features at multiple spatial scales, e.g., as done in CNNs through max pooling, and to provide the benefits of composition through the architecture of multiple layers, can also be embedded into SVMs. We verify through experiments on widely available image sets that the resulting SVMs do provide superior accuracy in comparison to well-established deep neural network benchmarks for small sample sizes.

paragraphs: When training examples are scarce, incorporating knowledge about the problem can be valuable. This paper brings several properties associated with convolutional neural networks into support-vector machines. A central example is transformation invariance: images related by a relevant transformation, such as translation, should retain an appropriate notion of similarity.

The proposed kernels use the maximum similarity over a group of transformations. Such kernels are not generally positive definite, a mathematical property important to the kernel formulation. The authors show that positive definiteness holds with high probability in the small-training-sample regime they study. The qualification matters: the result does not establish positive definiteness for arbitrary datasets.

The paper also incorporates local features at multiple spatial scales and composition through multiple layers into the SVM approach. Experiments on available image datasets show superior accuracy over established deep neural network benchmarks when sample sizes are small. Together, the theory and experiments support building relevant invariances and multiscale structure directly into models intended for limited-data learning.
summary.tldr: Transformation-aware, multiscale SVMs outperform tested deep-network benchmarks with few samples, with a qualified positive-definiteness result for their kernels.

title: Learning from Few Samples: Transformation-Invariant SVMs with Composition and Locality at Multiple Scales

abstract: Inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) aims to recover the reward function and the associated optimal policy that best fits observed sequences of states and actions implemented by an expert. Many algorithms for IRL have an inherent nested structure: the inner loop finds the optimal policy given parametrized rewards while the outer loop updates the estimates towards optimizing a measure of fit. For high dimensional environments such nested-loop structure entails a significant computational burden. To reduce the computational burden of a nested loop, novel methods such as SQIL \cite{reddy2019sqil} and IQ-Learn \cite{garg2021iq} emphasize policy estimation at the expense of reward estimation accuracy. However, without accurate estimated rewards, it is not possible to do counterfactual analysis such as predicting the optimal policy under different environment dynamics and/or learning new tasks. In this paper we develop a novel {\em single-loop} algorithm for IRL that does not compromise reward estimation accuracy. In the proposed algorithm, each policy improvement step is followed by a stochastic gradient step for likelihood maximization. We show that the proposed algorithm provably converges to a stationary solution with a finite-time guarantee. If the reward is parameterized linearly we show the identified solution corresponds to the solution of the maximum entropy IRL problem. Finally, by using robotics control problems in Mujoco and their transfer settings, we show that the proposed algorithm achieves superior performance compared with other IRL and imitation learning benchmarks.

Many methods repeatedly solve a policy problem inside a separate reward-estimation loop. That nested structure is expensive in high-dimensional environments, while shortcuts emphasizing policy estimation can sacrifice reward accuracy.

The paper proposes a single-loop method that follows each policy-improvement step with a stochastic gradient update for likelihood maximization. It is designed to reduce the nested computation without compromising reward estimation. Accurate rewards matter because they support counterfactual questions, such as how an optimal policy should change when the environment's dynamics change or when addressing new tasks.

The theoretical result thus pairs a general stationarity guarantee with a stronger identification result under a specific reward assumption.
summary.tldr: A single-loop inverse reinforcement learning algorithm preserves reward estimation and provides finite-time convergence to a stationary solution.

title: Maximum-Likelihood Inverse Reinforcement Learning with Finite-Time Guarantees

abstract: In this paper, we introduce \emph{data multiplexing} (DataMUX), a technique that enables deep neural networks to process multiple inputs simultaneously using a single compact representation. DataMUX demonstrates that neural networks are capable of generating accurate predictions over \emph{mixtures} of inputs, resulting in increased inference throughput with minimal extra memory requirements. Our approach uses two key components -- 1) a multiplexing layer that performs a fixed linear transformation to each input before combining them to create a "mixed" representation of the same size as a single input, which is then processed by the base network, and 2) a demultiplexing layer that converts the base network's output back into independent representations before producing predictions for each input. We show the viability of DataMUX for different architectures (Transformers, and to a much lesser extent MLPs and CNNs) across six different tasks spanning sentence classification, named entity recognition and image classification. For instance, DataMUX for Transformers can multiplex up to 20x/40x inputs, achieving up to 11x/18x increase in inference throughput with absolute performance drops of $<2\%$ and $<4\%$ respectively compared to a vanilla Transformer on MNLI, a natural language inference task. We also provide a theoretical construction for multiplexing in self-attention networks and analyze the effect of various design elements in DataMUX.

paragraphs: DataMUX explores whether a neural network can make separate predictions for several inputs after processing them together in one compact representation. Each input first undergoes a fixed linear transformation. The transformed inputs are combined into a mixture with the same size as one input, allowing the base network to process shared representational space.

A demultiplexing layer then turns the network’s output into separate representations for individual predictions. The objective is higher inference throughput with little additional memory. The paper evaluates six tasks spanning sentence classification, named entity recognition, and image classification. Its evidence is strongest for Transformers, with viability demonstrated to a much smaller extent for MLPs and CNNs.

The corresponding absolute performance drops are below two and four percentage points. These results show a measured throughput–accuracy tradeoff rather than cost-free acceleration. The paper also supplies a theoretical construction for self-attention multiplexing and examines how design choices affect the approach.
summary.tldr: DataMUX mixes multiple inputs into one compact network representation to increase inference throughput with measured accuracy tradeoffs.

title: DataMUX: Data Multiplexing for Neural Networks

abstract: We present an efficient approach for Masked Image Modeling (MIM) with hierarchical Vision Transformers (ViTs), allowing the hierarchical ViTs to discard masked patches and operate only on the visible ones. Our approach consists of three key designs. First, for window attention, we propose a Group Window Attention scheme following the Divide-and-Conquer strategy. To mitigate the quadratic complexity of the self-attention w.r.t. the number of patches, group attention encourages a uniform partition that visible patches within each local window of arbitrary size can be grouped with equal size, where masked self-attention is then performed within each group. Second, we further improve the grouping strategy via the Dynamic Programming algorithm to minimize the overall computation cost of the attention on the grouped patches. Third, as for the convolution layers, we convert them to the Sparse Convolution that works seamlessly with the sparse data, i.e., the visible patches in MIM. As a result, MIM can now work on most, if not all, hierarchical ViTs in a green and efficient way. For example, we can train the hierarchical ViTs, e.g., Swin Transformer and Twins Transformer, about 2.7$\times$ faster and reduce the GPU memory usage by 70%, while still enjoying competitive performance on ImageNet classification and the superiority on downstream COCO object detection benchmarks.

This paper enables those models to discard masked patches and compute only on visible ones. Its changes address both window-based attention and convolution layers.

These findings show that the proposed sparse processing can substantially reduce training resources while retaining strong evaluated performance, with the framework intended to cover most hierarchical vision transformers.
summary.tldr: Grouped attention and sparse convolutions let hierarchical vision transformers skip masked patches, substantially reducing training time and memory in reported examples.

title: Green Hierarchical Vision Transformer for Masked Image Modeling

abstract: Auxiliary learning is a widely adopted practice in deep learning, which aims to improve the model performance on the primary task by exploiting the beneficial information in the auxiliary loss. Existing auxiliary learning methods only focus on balancing the auxiliary loss and the primary loss, ignoring the module-level auxiliary influence, i.e., an auxiliary loss will be beneficial for optimizing specific modules within the model but harmful to others, failing to make full use of auxiliary information. To tackle the problem, we propose a Module-Aware Optimization approach for Auxiliary Learning (MAOAL). The proposed approach considers the module-level influence through the learnable module-level auxiliary importance, i.e., the importance of each auxiliary loss to each module. Specifically, the proposed approach jointly optimizes the module-level auxiliary importance and the model parameters in a bi-level manner. In the lower optimization, the model parameters are optimized with the importance parameterized gradient, while in the upper optimization, the module-level auxiliary importance is updated with the implicit gradient from a small developing dataset. Extensive experiments show that our proposed MAOAL method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines for different auxiliary losses on various datasets, demonstrating that our method can serve as a powerful generic tool for auxiliary learning.

paragraphs: Auxiliary learning improves a primary task by training with additional losses that provide useful information. A single auxiliary loss, however, can help some parts of a network while harming others. This paper argues that balancing losses only at the whole-model level overlooks these different effects and can waste useful auxiliary information.

MAOAL assigns a learnable importance to each auxiliary loss for each model module. It jointly learns these importance values and the model parameters through two levels of optimization. The lower level updates model parameters using gradients shaped by the importance values. The upper level adjusts those values through implicit gradients from a small development dataset.

This arrangement makes the influence of auxiliary learning depend on where it acts within the network. Experiments across multiple datasets and auxiliary losses consistently outperform the state-of-the-art baselines considered in the paper. The results support module-specific control as a broadly useful way to improve auxiliary learning, rather than relying on one shared balance of losses for every network component.
summary.tldr: MAOAL learns how strongly each auxiliary loss should influence each network module, improving auxiliary learning across the reported experiments.

title: Module-Aware Optimization for Auxiliary Learning

abstract: Many deep learning models involve optimizing multiple objectives. Since objectives are often conflicting, we aim to get diverse and representative trade-off solutions among these objectives. Gradient-based multi-objective optimization (MOO) algorithms using reference vectors have shown promising performance. However, they may still produce undesirable solutions due to mismatch between the pre-specified reference vectors and the problem's underlying Pareto front. In this paper, we propose a novel gradient-based MOO algorithm with adaptive reference vectors. We formulate reference vector adaption as a bilevel optimization problem, and solve it with an efficient solver. Theoretical convergence analysis is also provided. Experiments on an extensive set of learning scenarios demonstrate the superiority of the proposed algorithm over the state-of-the-art.

Gradient-based multi-objective optimization (MOO) algorithms using reference vectors have shown promising performance. However, they may still produce undesirable solutions due to mismatch between the pre-specified reference vectors and the problem's underlying Pareto front. In this paper, we propose a novel gradient-based MOO algorithm with adaptive reference vectors. We formulate reference vector adaption as a bilevel optimization problem, and solve it with an efficient solver. Theoretical convergence analysis is also provided. Experiments on an extensive set of learning scenarios demonstrate the superiority of the proposed algorithm over the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Deep learning can require optimizing several objectives that conflict with one another. In that setting, the aim is often a diverse set of representative compromises. Reference-vector methods guide optimization toward different trade-offs, but their usefulness depends on how those directions relate to the problem's Pareto front, the set of solutions where improving one objective requires sacrificing another.

This paper identifies a mismatch between preset reference vectors and the underlying front as a source of undesirable solutions. It proposes adapting the vectors during gradient-based multi-objective optimization. The adaptation is formulated as a bilevel problem, linking the choice of guiding vectors with the optimization they influence, and is handled using an efficient solver.

The authors provide a theoretical convergence analysis and evaluate the method across an extensive range of learning scenarios. They report better performance than leading alternatives in those experiments. The approach matters because it treats the directions used to seek diverse compromises as quantities to learn, rather than assuming that an initial set already suits the problem.
summary.tldr: The method adapts reference vectors during multi-objective learning to seek more representative trade-offs between conflicting objectives.

title: Multi-Objective Deep Learning with Adaptive Reference Vectors

abstract: Transfer learning aims to leverage knowledge from pre-trained models to benefit the target task. Prior transfer learning work mainly transfers from a single model. However, with the emergence of deep models pre-trained from different resources, model hubs consisting of diverse models with various architectures, pre-trained datasets and learning paradigms are available. Directly applying single-model transfer learning methods to each model wastes the abundant knowledge of the model hub and suffers from high computational cost. In this paper, we propose a Hub-Pathway framework to enable knowledge transfer from a model hub. The framework generates data-dependent pathway weights, based on which we assign the pathway routes at the input level to decide which pre-trained models are activated and passed through, and then set the pathway aggregation at the output level to aggregate the knowledge from different models to make predictions. The proposed framework can be trained end-to-end with the target task-specific loss, where it learns to explore better pathway configurations and exploit the knowledge in pre-trained models for each target datum. We utilize a noisy pathway generator and design an exploration loss to further explore different pathways throughout the model hub. To fully exploit the knowledge in pre-trained models, each model is further trained by specific data that activate it, which ensures its performance and enhances knowledge transfer. Experiment results on computer vision and reinforcement learning tasks demonstrate that the proposed Hub-Pathway framework achieves the state-of-the-art performance for model hub transfer learning.

Directly applying single-model transfer learning methods to each model wastes the abundant knowledge of the model hub and suffers from high computational cost. In this paper, we propose a Hub-Pathway framework to enable knowledge transfer from a model hub. The framework generates data-dependent pathway weights, based on which we assign the pathway routes at the input level to decide which pre-trained models are activated and passed through, and then set the pathway aggregation at the output level to aggregate the knowledge from different models to make predictions. The proposed framework can be trained end-to-end with the target task-specific loss, where it learns to explore better pathway configurations and exploit the knowledge in pre-trained models for each target datum. We utilize a noisy pathway generator and design an exploration loss to further explore different pathways throughout the model hub. To fully exploit the knowledge in pre-trained models, each model is further trained by specific data that activate it, which ensures its performance and enhances knowledge transfer. Experiment results on computer vision and reinforcement learning tasks demonstrate that the proposed Hub-Pathway framework achieves the state-of-the-art performance for model hub transfer learning.

paragraphs: Model hubs contain pretrained networks with different architectures, training data, and learning methods. Hub-Pathway aims to draw on this variety for a target task. Applying single-model transfer methods separately to every available network can be computationally costly and fails to make full use of the hub's combined knowledge.

The framework generates pathway weights that depend on the input. These weights determine which pretrained models process a particular example and how their outputs are combined into a prediction. Training uses the target task's loss end to end, so model selection and aggregation can adapt to the requirements of individual examples.

A noisy pathway generator and an exploration loss encourage trying different routes through the hub. Each pretrained model is also further trained on the examples that activate it, allowing its knowledge to adapt to those inputs. Experiments in computer vision and reinforcement learning report state-of-the-art model-hub transfer performance. The approach makes transfer a learned coordination problem across available models.
summary.tldr: Hub-Pathway learns input-dependent routes and output combinations across a hub of pretrained models for transfer learning.

title: Hub-Pathway: Transfer Learning from A Hub of Pre-trained Models

abstract: We propose an algorithm that compresses the critical information of a large dataset into compact addressable memories. These memories can then be recalled to quickly re-train a neural network and recover the performance (instead of storing and re-training on the full original dataset). Building upon the dataset distillation framework, we make a key observation that a shared common representation allows for more efficient and effective distillation. Concretely, we learn a set of bases (aka ``memories'') which are shared between classes and combined through learned flexible addressing functions to generate a diverse set of training examples. This leads to several benefits: 1) the size of compressed data does not necessarily grow linearly with the number of classes; 2) an overall higher compression rate with more effective distillation is achieved; and 3) more generalized queries are allowed beyond recalling the original classes. We demonstrate state-of-the-art results on the dataset distillation task across five benchmarks, including up to 16.5% and 9.7% accuracy improvement when distilling CIFAR10 and CIFAR100 respectively. We then leverage our framework to perform continual learning, achieving state-of-the-art results on four benchmarks, with 23.2% accuracy improvement on MANY.

These findings support shared, recombinable memories as a useful representation for both compact retraining data and retaining information across learning stages.
summary.tldr: Shared addressable memories compress datasets into reusable training information and improve reported distillation and continual-learning results.

title: Remember the Past: Distilling Datasets into Addressable Memories for Neural Networks

abstract: In many sequential tasks, a model needs to remember relevant events from the distant past to make correct predictions. Unfortunately, a straightforward application of gradient based training requires intermediate computations to be stored for every element of a sequence. This requires to store prohibitively large intermediate data if a sequence consists of thousands or even millions elements, and as a result, makes learning of very long-term dependencies infeasible. However, the majority of sequence elements can usually be predicted by taking into account only temporally local information. On the other hand, predictions affected by long-term dependencies are sparse and characterized by high uncertainty given only local information. We propose \texttt{MemUP}, a new training method that allows to learn long-term dependencies without backpropagating gradients through the whole sequence at a time. This method can potentially be applied to any recurrent architecture. LSTM network trained with \texttt{MemUP} performs better or comparable to baselines while requiring to store less intermediate data.

paragraphs: Learning from very long sequences can require remembering events far in the past. Standard gradient-based training stores intermediate computations along the sequence, which becomes prohibitively expensive for sequences containing thousands or millions of elements. The difficulty is therefore partly about the memory needed to train the model.

MemUP builds on the observation that local context usually suffices for many sequence predictions. Predictions that depend on distant events are comparatively sparse and remain uncertain when only nearby information is available. The method uses this connection between uncertainty and long-term dependence to learn without backpropagating through an entire sequence at once.

The authors report that an LSTM trained with MemUP matches or exceeds the evaluated baselines while storing less intermediate data. This supports uncertainty-guided training as a way to make long-term memory learning more economical. They also describe potential applicability to any recurrent architecture; that broader possibility is distinct from the reported LSTM result.
summary.tldr: MemUP uses locally uncertain predictions to guide long-term memory learning while reducing stored training intermediates in reported LSTM experiments.

title: Explain My Surprise: Learning Efficient Long-Term Memory by predicting uncertain outcomes

abstract: Unsustainable fishing practices worldwide pose a major threat to marine resources and ecosystems. Identifying vessels that do not show up in conventional monitoring systems---known as ``dark vessels''---is key to managing and securing the health of marine environments. With the rise of satellite-based synthetic aperture radar (SAR) imaging and modern machine learning (ML), it is now possible to automate detection of dark vessels day or night, under all-weather conditions. SAR images, however, require a domain-specific treatment and are not widely accessible to the ML community. Maritime objects (vessels and offshore infrastructure) are relatively small and sparse, challenging traditional computer vision approaches. We present the largest labeled dataset for training ML models to detect and characterize vessels and ocean structures in SAR imagery. xView3-SAR consists of nearly 1,000 analysis-ready SAR images from the Sentinel-1 mission that are, on average, 29,400-by-24,400 pixels each. The images are annotated using a combination of automated and manual analysis. Co-located bathymetry and wind state rasters accompany every SAR image. We also provide an overview of the xView3 Computer Vision Challenge, an international competition using xView3-SAR for ship detection and characterization at large scale. We release the data (\href{https://iuu.xview.us/}{https://iuu.xview.us/}) and code (\href{https://github.com/DIUx-xView}{https://github.com/DIUx-xView}) to support ongoing development and evaluation of ML approaches for this important application.

The contribution is an accessible, application-specific dataset and evaluation effort supporting automated identification of vessels that conventional monitoring may miss.
summary.tldr: xView3-SAR provides a large annotated satellite-radar dataset and challenge for detecting vessels missing from conventional monitoring.

title: xView3-SAR: Detecting Dark Fishing Activity Using Synthetic Aperture Radar Imagery

abstract: As deep neural networks are highly expressive, it is important to find solutions with small generalization gap (the difference between the performance on the training data and unseen data). Focusing on the stochastic nature of training, we first present a theoretical analysis in which the bound of generalization gap depends on what we call inconsistency and instability of model outputs, which can be estimated on unlabeled data. Our empirical study based on this analysis shows that instability and inconsistency are strongly predictive of generalization gap in various settings. In particular, our finding indicates that inconsistency is a more reliable indicator of generalization gap than the sharpness of the loss landscape. Furthermore, we show that algorithmic reduction of inconsistency leads to superior performance. The results also provide a theoretical basis for existing methods such as co-distillation and ensemble.

paragraphs: A neural network can perform well on its training examples while doing less well on unseen data. This difference is the generalization gap. The paper studies that gap through the randomness of training, focusing on properties of model outputs that the authors call inconsistency and instability.

The theoretical analysis bounds the generalization gap using these two quantities, which can be estimated on unlabeled data. That matters because the proposed indicators do not require labels for the data used to estimate them. The empirical study finds both quantities strongly predictive of generalization gaps across various settings, with inconsistency providing a more reliable indicator than loss-landscape sharpness in the reported comparisons.

The paper goes beyond using inconsistency as a diagnostic: algorithmically reducing it also produces better performance in the experiments. The authors further connect their analysis to co-distillation and ensembles, providing a theoretical basis for these existing approaches. The combined message is that output behavior associated with stochastic training can help both assess generalization and guide methods intended to improve it.
summary.tldr: Output inconsistency and instability predict generalization gaps in the reported settings, and reducing inconsistency improves performance.

title: Inconsistency, Instability, and Generalization Gap of Deep Neural Network Training

abstract: Language models of code (LMs) work well when the surrounding code provides sufficient context. This is not true when it becomes necessary to use types, functionality or APIs defined elsewhere in the repository or a linked library, especially those not seen during training. LMs suffer from limited awareness of such global context and end up hallucinating.Integrated development environments (IDEs) assist developers in understanding repository context using static analysis. We extend this assistance, enjoyed by developers, to LMs. We propose monitor-guided decoding (MGD) where a monitor uses static analysis to guide the decoding. We construct a repository-level dataset PragmaticCode for method-completion in Java and evaluate MGD on it. On models of varying parameter scale, by monitoring for type-consistent object dereferences, MGD consistently improves compilation rates and agreement with ground truth. Further, LMs with fewer parameters, when augmented with MGD, can outperform larger LMs. With MGD, SantaCoder-1.1B achieves better compilation rate and next-identifier match than the much larger text-davinci-003 model.We also conduct a generalizability study to evaluate the ability of MGD to generalize to multiple programming languages (Java, C# and Rust), coding scenarios (e.g., correct number of arguments to method calls), and to enforce richer semantic constraints (e.g., stateful API protocols). Our data and implementation are available at https://github.com/microsoft/monitors4codegen.

paragraphs: Code language models can struggle when completion requires knowledge of types or APIs defined elsewhere in a repository or library. Monitor-guided decoding gives these models access to assistance analogous to what static analysis provides developers in an IDE. A monitor uses that analysis to guide generation using repository context.

The authors construct PragmaticCode, a repository-level Java method-completion dataset. They evaluate monitors that enforce type-consistent object dereferences and find consistent improvements in compilation rates and agreement with reference code across model sizes. With monitoring, SantaCoder-1.1B exceeds the much larger text-davinci-003 model on compilation rate and next-identifier match in the reported comparison.

A further study examines generalization across Java, C#, and Rust, as well as constraints involving method argument counts and stateful API protocols. The work shows how repository-aware analysis can strengthen code generation during decoding. Its findings also demonstrate that, for the evaluated measures, a smaller model with this assistance can outperform a larger model.
summary.tldr: Monitor-guided decoding uses repository static analysis to improve code completion, sometimes enabling smaller models to outperform larger ones.

title: Monitor-Guided Decoding of Code LMs with Static Analysis of Repository Context

abstract: In this paper, we aim to model 3D scene dynamics from multi-view videos. Unlike the majority of existing works which usually focus on the common task of novel view synthesis within the training time period, we propose to simultaneously learn the geometry, appearance, and physical velocity of 3D scenes only from video frames, such that multiple desirable applications can be supported, including future frame extrapolation, unsupervised 3D semantic scene decomposition, and dynamic motion transfer. Our method consists of three major components, 1) the keyframe dynamic radiance field, 2) the interframe velocity field, and 3) a joint keyframe and interframe optimization module which is the core of our framework to effectively train both networks. To validate our method, we further introduce two dynamic 3D datasets: 1) Dynamic Object dataset, and 2) Dynamic Indoor Scene dataset. We conduct extensive experiments on multiple datasets, demonstrating the superior performance of our method over all baselines, particularly in the critical tasks of future frame extrapolation and unsupervised 3D semantic scene decomposition.
