paragraphs: This paper studies online classification into K classes when each example is a point in a d-dimensional space. The learner receives bandit feedback, making its learning problem more restricted than classification with full label information. The central question is whether efficient algorithms can make only finitely many mistakes when the classes are linearly separable with a positive margin.

The authors distinguish strong and weak forms of linear separability. Under the strong condition, they provide an efficient algorithm with a near-optimal mistake bound proportional to K divided by the square of the margin. This expresses how the guarantee depends on both the number of possible classes and the separation available between them.

Under weak separability, they also obtain an efficient algorithm with a finite mistake bound, but its dependence on the problem parameters is substantially larger and exponential. That method uses a kernel Perceptron approach. The results make progress on the broader challenge while preserving a crucial distinction: the stronger assumption supports a much tighter guarantee than the weaker one.
summary.tldr: Efficient bandit classifiers achieve finite mistake bounds under two separability conditions, with a near-optimal bound under the stronger condition.

title: Bandit Multiclass Linear Classification: Efficient Algorithms for the Separable Case

abstract: We introduce the bilinear bandit problem with low-rank structure in which an action takes the form of a pair of arms from two different entity types, and the reward is a bilinear function of the known feature vectors of the arms. The unknown in the problem is a $d_1$ by $d_2$ matrix $\mathbf{\Theta}^*$ that defines the reward, and has low rank $r \ll \min\{d_1,d_2\}$. Determination of $\mathbf{\Theta}^*$ with this low-rank structure poses a significant challenge in finding the right exploration-exploitation tradeoff. In this work, we propose a new two-stage algorithm called “Explore-Subspace-Then-Refine” (ESTR). The first stage is an explicit subspace exploration, while the second stage is a linear bandit algorithm called “almost-low-dimensional OFUL” (LowOFUL) that exploits and further refines the estimated subspace via a regularization technique. We show that the regret of ESTR is $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}((d_1+d_2)^{3/2} \sqrt{r T})$ where $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}$ hides logarithmic factors and $T$ is the time horizon, which improves upon the regret of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(d_1d_2\sqrt{T})$ attained for a naïve linear bandit reduction. We conjecture that the regret bound of ESTR is unimprovable up to polylogarithmic factors, and our preliminary experiment shows that ESTR outperforms a naïve linear bandit reduction.

Each item has known features, and the reward depends on how those features interact through an unknown matrix. The key assumption is that this matrix has low rank: its interactions have a much smaller underlying dimension than its full size suggests.

The proposed Explore-Subspace-Then-Refine algorithm separates learning into two stages. First, it deliberately explores to estimate the relevant subspace. Their further suggestion that the bound is essentially unimprovable remains a conjecture.
summary.tldr: A two-stage bandit algorithm learns and exploits low-rank interactions between paired actions to improve regret over a naïve linear formulation.

title: Bilinear Bandits with Low-rank Structure

abstract: Dropout regularization of deep neural networks has been a mysterious yet effective tool to prevent overfitting. Explanations for its success range from the prevention of "co-adapted" weights to it being a form of cheap Bayesian inference. We propose a novel framework for understanding multiplicative noise in neural networks, considering continuous distributions as well as Bernoulli noise (i.e. dropout). We show that multiplicative noise induces structured shrinkage priors on a network’s weights. We derive the equivalence through reparametrization properties of scale mixtures and without invoking any approximations. Given the equivalence, we then show that dropout’s Monte Carlo training objective approximates marginal MAP estimation. We leverage these insights to propose a novel shrinkage framework for resnets, terming the prior ’automatic depth determination’ as it is the natural analog of automatic relevance determination for network depth. Lastly, we investigate two inference strategies that improve upon the aforementioned MAP approximation in regression benchmarks.

paragraphs: Dropout helps prevent overfitting, but explaining why it works has motivated several different interpretations. This paper places dropout inside a broader framework for multiplicative noise in neural networks. It treats both Bernoulli noise, which corresponds to dropout, and continuous noise distributions, connecting these training procedures to probabilistic assumptions about network weights.

The authors show that multiplicative noise induces structured shrinkage priors: priors that encourage weights to shrink in a coordinated way. They derive this equivalence exactly through reparameterization properties of scale mixtures. A separate result concerns the training objective: dropout’s Monte Carlo objective approximates marginal maximum a posteriori estimation. The exact equivalence and the approximate estimation interpretation are distinct claims.

Using this connection, the paper introduces a shrinkage framework for residual networks called automatic depth determination. It extends the idea of automatically determining relevance to network depth. The authors also investigate two inference strategies that improve on the stated maximum a posteriori approximation in regression benchmarks, turning the interpretation into concrete alternatives for learning.
summary.tldr: An exact connection between multiplicative noise and shrinkage priors explains dropout and motivates new residual-network inference methods.

title: Dropout as a Structured Shrinkage Prior

abstract: We study the problem of detecting critical structures using a graph embedding model. Existing graph embedding models lack the ability to precisely detect critical structures that are specific to a task at the global scale. In this paper, we propose a novel graph embedding model, called the Ego-CNNs, that employs the ego-convolutions convolutions at each layer and stacks up layers using an ego-centric way to detects precise critical structures efficiently. An Ego-CNN can be jointly trained with a task model and help explain/discover knowledge for the task. We conduct extensive experiments and the results show that Ego-CNNs (1) can lead to comparable task performance as the state-of-the-art graph embedding models, (2) works nicely with CNN visualization techniques to illustrate the detected structures, and (3) is efficient and can incorporate with scale-free priors, which commonly occurs in social network datasets, to further improve the training efficiency.

In this paper, we propose a novel graph embedding model, called the Ego-CNNs, that employs the ego-convolutions convolutions at each layer and stacks up layers using an ego-centric way to detects precise critical structures efficiently. An Ego-CNN can be jointly trained with a task model and help explain/discover knowledge for the task. We conduct extensive experiments and the results show that Ego-CNNs (1) can lead to comparable task performance as the state-of-the-art graph embedding models, (2) works nicely with CNN visualization techniques to illustrate the detected structures, and (3) is efficient and can incorporate with scale-free priors, which commonly occurs in social network datasets, to further improve the training efficiency.

paragraphs: Graph representations can support prediction while still failing to identify precisely which structures matter for a particular task across the graph. This paper introduces Ego-CNNs to address that gap. The goal is to learn representations that help detect task relevant structures and make those structures available for explanation or discovery.

The model uses ego convolutions at each layer and stacks those layers in an egocentric manner. It can be trained jointly with the model performing the task, tying structure detection to the predictive objective. The authors also connect Ego-CNNs with convolutional network visualization techniques, allowing the detected structures to be illustrated rather than remaining only implicit in a learned representation.

Experiments report task performance comparable to leading graph embedding models, along with effective visualization and efficient operation. Incorporating scale free priors, which the authors associate with social network data, can further improve training efficiency. The stated benefit is therefore a combination of competitive prediction, more precise structure detection, and tools for examining what the model has found.
summary.tldr: Ego-CNNs learn graph representations that detect and visualize task relevant structures while achieving competitive predictive performance.

title: Distributed, Egocentric Representations of Graphs for Detecting Critical Structures

abstract: This paper considers generalized linear models using rule-based features, also referred to as rule ensembles, for regression and probabilistic classification. Rules facilitate model interpretation while also capturing nonlinear dependences and interactions. Our problem formulation accordingly trades off rule set complexity and prediction accuracy. Column generation is used to optimize over an exponentially large space of rules without pre-generating a large subset of candidates or greedily boosting rules one by one. The column generation subproblem is solved using either integer programming or a heuristic optimizing the same objective. In experiments involving logistic and linear regression, the proposed methods obtain better accuracy-complexity trade-offs than existing rule ensemble algorithms. At one end of the trade-off, the methods are competitive with less interpretable benchmark models.

paragraphs: Rule-based features let a prediction model express nonlinear relationships and interactions through conditions that people can inspect. This paper studies generalized linear models built from such rules for regression and probabilistic classification. Its formulation explicitly balances predictive accuracy against the complexity of the rule set, treating interpretability as part of the learning problem.

The challenge is that the space of possible rules is exponentially large. The authors use column generation to optimize over that space without first constructing a large candidate collection or greedily boosting individual rules. The associated rule-search subproblem can be solved with integer programming or with a heuristic that targets the same objective.

Experiments with linear and logistic regression show better accuracy–complexity trade-offs than existing rule-ensemble algorithms. At one end of that trade-off, the resulting models are competitive with less interpretable benchmarks. These findings suggest that carefully optimizing which rules enter a model can improve the balance between understandable structure and predictive performance.
summary.tldr: Column generation learns rule-based prediction models with improved empirical trade-offs between accuracy and rule-set complexity.

title: Generalized Linear Rule Models

abstract: Randomized sketching has been used in offline kernel learning, but it cannot be applied directly to online kernel learning due to the lack of incremental maintenances for randomized sketches with regret guarantees. To address these issues, we propose a novel incremental randomized sketching approach for online kernel learning, which has efficient incremental maintenances with theoretical guarantees. We construct two incremental randomized sketches using the sparse transform matrix and the sampling matrix for kernel matrix approximation, update the incremental randomized sketches using rank-$1$ modifications, and construct an time-varying explicit feature mapping for online kernel learning. We prove that the proposed incremental randomized sketching is statistically unbiased for the matrix product approximation, obtains a $1 + \epsilon$ relative-error bound for the kernel matrix approximation, enjoys a sublinear regret bound for online kernel learning, and has constant time and space complexities at each round for incremental maintenances. Experimental results demonstrate that the incremental randomized sketching achieves a better learning performance in terms of accuracy and efficiency even in adversarial environments.

paragraphs: Randomized sketching provides compact approximations that can make kernel learning more manageable. Applying it online creates an additional challenge: the sketch must be maintained as observations arrive, and that maintenance needs learning guarantees. The paper develops an incremental approach designed around these requirements instead of relying on an offline sketch.

The method constructs two randomized sketches, using a sparse transform matrix and a sampling matrix to approximate the kernel matrix. Rank-one modifications update these sketches incrementally. They then support an explicit feature mapping that changes over time, giving the online learner a representation derived from the evolving approximation.

The analysis establishes an unbiased matrix-product approximation, a kernel-matrix relative-error bound of 1 plus epsilon, and sublinear regret for online learning. It also gives constant time and space costs per round specifically for incremental maintenance. Experiments report better accuracy and efficiency, including in adversarial environments. Together, these results connect approximation quality, online predictive performance, and maintenance cost, showing why an incrementally updateable sketch can be useful beyond its ability to compress a matrix.
summary.tldr: Incrementally maintained randomized sketches support online kernel learning with approximation guarantees, sublinear regret, and constant per-round maintenance costs.

title: Incremental Randomized Sketching for Online Kernel Learning

abstract: We consider online allocation problems with concave revenue functions and resource constraints, which are central problems in revenue management and online advertising. In these settings, requests arrive sequentially during a finite horizon and, for each request, a decision maker needs to choose an action that consumes a certain amount of resources and generates revenue. The revenue function and resource consumption of each request are drawn independently and at random from a probability distribution that is unknown to the decision maker. The objective is to maximize cumulative revenues subject to a constraint on the total consumption of resources. We design a general class of algorithms that achieve sub-linear expected regret compared to the hindsight optimal allocation. Our algorithms operate in the Lagrangian dual space: they maintain a dual multiplier for each resource that is updated using online mirror descent. By choosing the reference function accordingly, we recover dual sub-gradient descent and dual exponential weights algorithm. The resulting algorithms are simple, efficient, and shown to attain the optimal order of regret when the length of the horizon and the initial number of resources are scaled proportionally. We discuss applications to online bidding in repeated auctions with budget constraints and online proportional matching with high entropy.

paragraphs: Online allocation requires deciding how to spend limited resources as requests arrive, without knowing future demand. Each action earns revenue and consumes resources. This paper considers concave revenue functions and assumes that requests' revenue and consumption characteristics are drawn independently from an unknown probability distribution. The objective is to maximize total revenue while respecting the overall resource budget.

The algorithms maintain a dual multiplier for each resource, which acts as a price reflecting its use in allocation decisions. These multipliers are updated through online mirror descent. Different choices of the method's reference function recover dual subgradient descent and dual exponential weights, placing several update strategies within one general framework.

The authors prove sublinear expected regret relative to the best allocation chosen with hindsight. They also establish the optimal order of regret when the time horizon and initial resource quantities grow proportionally. These guarantees connect simple resource-price updates to long-run allocation quality under the stated stochastic assumptions. Applications discussed include budget-constrained bidding in repeated auctions and online proportional matching with high entropy.
summary.tldr: Updating resource prices with dual mirror descent gives efficient online allocation algorithms with optimal-order regret under the stated stochastic scaling conditions.

title: Dual Mirror Descent for Online Allocation Problems

abstract: Marrying topic models and language models exposes language understanding to a broader source of document-level context beyond sentences via topics. While introducing topical semantics in language models, existing approaches incorporate latent document topic proportions and ignore topical discourse in sentences of the document. This work extends the line of research by additionally introducing an explainable topic representation in language understanding, obtained from a set of key terms correspondingly for each latent topic of the proportion. Moreover, we retain sentence-topic association along with document-topic association by modeling topical discourse for every sentence in the document. We present a novel neural composite language modeling (NCLM) framework that exploits both the latent and explainable topics along with topical discourse at sentence-level in a joint learning framework of topic and language models. Experiments over a range of tasks such as language modeling, word sense disambiguation, document classiﬁcation, retrieval and text generation demonstrate ability of the proposed model in improving language understanding.

paragraphs: A document’s topics provide context that extends beyond individual sentences. This paper develops a language-understanding framework that uses this broader context while retaining information about which topics relate to each sentence. The motivation is that a document-level mixture of topics alone leaves out the topical discourse occurring within the document.

The proposed neural composite language model jointly learns topic and language models. It combines latent topic proportions with an explainable representation consisting of key terms associated with each topic. It also models sentence-topic relationships alongside document-topic relationships. This gives the language model access both to an overall account of the document’s subject matter and to topic information tied to particular sentences.

Experiments cover language modeling, word sense disambiguation, document classification, retrieval, and text generation. Across these tasks, the authors report evidence that the combined framework improves language understanding. The approach matters because it brings interpretable topic content and sentence-level topical context into the same learning system, extending the use of topic information beyond a single document-wide representation.
summary.tldr: A joint topic-and-language model combines topic keywords, document context, and sentence-level topic associations to improve language-understanding tasks.

title: Explainable and Discourse Topic-aware Neural Language Understanding

abstract: The field of defense strategies against adversarial attacks has significantly grown over the last years, but progress is hampered as the evaluation of adversarial defenses is often insufficient and thus gives a wrong impression of robustness. Many promising defenses could be broken later on, making it difficult to identify the state-of-the-art. Frequent pitfalls in the evaluation are improper tuning of hyperparameters of the attacks, gradient obfuscation or masking. In this paper we first propose two extensions of the PGD-attack overcoming failures due to suboptimal step size and problems of the objective function. We then combine our novel attacks with two complementary existing ones to form a parameter-free, computationally affordable and user-independent ensemble of attacks to test adversarial robustness. We apply our ensemble to over 50 models from papers published at recent top machine learning and computer vision venues. In all except one of the cases we achieve lower robust test accuracy than reported in these papers, often by more than $10%$, identifying several broken defenses.

paragraphs: A defense can appear robust when the attack used to evaluate it is poorly configured or hindered by misleading gradients. This paper treats reliable attack evaluation as a prerequisite for measuring progress in adversarial defenses. It focuses on failures involving attack hyperparameters, gradient masking, and the attack's objective function.

The authors introduce two extensions of projected gradient descent attacks that address suboptimal step sizes and objective-function problems. They combine these with two complementary existing attacks into a parameter-free ensemble. The resulting evaluation is designed to be computationally affordable and independent of user-specific tuning choices, reducing opportunities for evaluation outcomes to hinge on those choices.

The ensemble is applied to more than 50 published models. In every case except one, it finds lower robust test accuracy than originally reported, often by more than 10%, and identifies several broken defenses. These results show that the tested defenses were frequently less robust than their reported evaluations suggested. The ensemble provides a stronger empirical assessment, rather than an exact certificate of robustness.
summary.tldr: A parameter-free ensemble of complementary attacks exposes overstated robustness in nearly all of more than 50 evaluated models.

title: Reliable evaluation of adversarial robustness with an ensemble of diverse parameter-free attacks

abstract: Neural networks utilize the softmax as a building block in classification tasks, which contains an overconfidence problem and lacks an uncertainty representation ability. As a Bayesian alternative to the softmax, we consider a random variable of a categorical probability over class labels. In this framework, the prior distribution explicitly models the presumed noise inherent in the observed label, which provides consistent gains in generalization performance in multiple challenging tasks. The proposed method inherits advantages of Bayesian approaches that achieve better uncertainty estimation and model calibration. Our method can be implemented as a plug-and-play loss function with negligible computational overhead compared to the softmax with the cross-entropy loss function.

paragraphs: Classification networks commonly use softmax to assign probabilities to class labels. The paper targets two problems with this building block: overconfidence and an inability to represent uncertainty about the categorical probabilities themselves. It proposes a Bayesian treatment in which those probabilities are modeled as a random variable.

A central part of the approach is its prior distribution. The prior explicitly represents presumed noise in the observed labels, bringing assumptions about label reliability into the learning framework. Instead of treating the probability assignment as a single fixed answer, the method provides a probabilistic representation of that assignment and its uncertainty.

The authors report consistent generalization gains across multiple challenging tasks, together with better uncertainty estimation and calibration. These findings concern both prediction quality and how well a model's confidence reflects its reliability. The approach is implemented as a replaceable loss function, with negligible computational overhead relative to softmax and cross-entropy, making the Bayesian formulation accessible without a costly change to the training setup.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian alternative to softmax models uncertainty and label noise while improving reported generalization and calibration.

title: Being Bayesian about Categorical Probability

abstract: The high sample complexity of reinforcement learning challenges its use in practice. A promising approach is to quickly adapt pre-trained policies to new environments. Existing methods for this policy adaptation problem typically rely on domain randomization and meta-learning, by sampling from some distribution of target environments during pre-training, and thus face difficulty on out-of-distribution target environments. We propose new model-based mechanisms that are able to make online adaptation in unseen target environments, by combining ideas from no-regret online learning and adaptive control. We prove that the approach learns policies in the target environment that can quickly recover trajectories from the source environment, and establish the rate of convergence in general settings. We demonstrate the benefits of our approach for policy adaptation in a diverse set of continuous control tasks, achieving the performance of state-of-the-art methods with much lower sample complexity. Our project website, including code, can be found at https://yudasong.github.io/PADA.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can require many interactions, making adaptation of a pretrained policy attractive. This paper focuses on adapting to unseen environments. It identifies a difficulty with approaches that sample target environments during pretraining: a new environment outside that sampled distribution can be challenging. The proposed approach instead introduces model-based mechanisms for online adaptation.

The mechanisms combine ideas from no-regret online learning and adaptive control. The authors prove that the approach learns policies in the target environment that can quickly recover trajectories from the source environment. They also establish a convergence rate in general settings. This gives the adaptation process a theoretical connection to recovering previously learned behavior under changed conditions.

Experiments examine a diverse set of continuous-control tasks. The approach achieves the performance of state-of-the-art methods while requiring substantially fewer samples. The practical significance is that an existing policy can be adapted with fewer new interactions in the evaluated tasks. The theoretical and empirical contributions support efficient transfer through online model-based adaptation, rather than requiring all relevant target environments to have been represented during pretraining.
summary.tldr: Model-based online adaptation combines learning and control principles to recover source behavior and match leading control methods with fewer samples.

title: Provably Efficient Model-based Policy Adaptation

abstract: We describe a framework for constructing nonstationary nonseparable random fields based on an infinite mixture of convolved stochastic processes. When the mixing process is stationary but the convolution function is nonstationary we arrive at nonseparable kernels with constant non-separability that are available in closed form. When the mixing is nonstationary and the convolution function is stationary we arrive at nonseparable random fields that have varying nonseparability and better preserve local structure. These fields have natural interpretations through the spectral representation of stochastic differential equations (SDEs) and are demonstrated on a range of synthetic benchmarks and spatio-temporal applications in geostatistics and machine learning. We show how a single Gaussian process (GP) with these random fields can computationally and statistically outperform both separable and existing nonstationary nonseparable approaches such as treed GPs and deep GP constructions.

paragraphs: This paper develops random fields for dependencies that vary across a domain and cannot be separated into independent component patterns. These properties matter in settings such as spatial and temporal modeling. The framework constructs such fields using an infinite mixture of convolved stochastic processes, providing different ways to control how dependence changes.

The authors distinguish two constructions. Stationary mixing combined with a nonstationary convolution function yields closed-form nonseparable kernels with constant nonseparability. Nonstationary mixing combined with a stationary convolution function instead produces varying nonseparability and better preservation of local structure. The distinction shows how assigning nonstationarity to different parts of the construction changes the resulting dependence patterns.

The fields also have interpretations through spectral representations of stochastic differential equations. Demonstrations span synthetic benchmarks and spatiotemporal applications in geostatistics and machine learning. The authors show that a single Gaussian process using these fields can outperform separable methods and existing nonstationary, nonseparable approaches, including treed and deep Gaussian processes, in both computational and statistical performance.
summary.tldr: Mixtures of convolved stochastic processes yield flexible random fields with constant or varying nonseparability.

title: Non-separable Non-stationary random fields

abstract: Deep Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are useful models for graph classification and graph-based regression tasks. In these tasks, graph pooling is a critical ingredient by which GNNs adapt to input graphs of varying size and structure. We propose a new graph pooling operation based on compressive Haar transforms — \emph{HaarPooling}. HaarPooling implements a cascade of pooling operations; it is computed by following a sequence of clusterings of the input graph. A HaarPooling layer transforms a given input graph to an output graph with a smaller node number and the same feature dimension; the compressive Haar transform filters out fine detail information in the Haar wavelet domain. In this way, all the HaarPooling layers together synthesize the features of any given input graph into a feature vector of uniform size. Such transforms provide a sparse characterization of the data and preserve the structure information of the input graph. GNNs implemented with standard graph convolution layers and HaarPooling layers achieve state of the art performance on diverse graph classification and regression problems.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks must often handle inputs with different numbers of nodes and different structures. Pooling helps turn these variable inputs into representations suitable for graph classification or regression. This paper proposes HaarPooling, a pooling operation based on compressive Haar transforms and a sequence of clusterings of the input graph.

Each HaarPooling layer reduces the number of nodes while keeping the feature dimension unchanged. The transform removes fine detail in the Haar wavelet domain, producing a compressed representation. Applying these operations in a cascade eventually yields a feature vector of uniform size. The authors describe the transforms as providing a sparse characterization of the data while preserving information about graph structure.

Networks combining standard graph convolution layers with HaarPooling achieve state-of-the-art performance on the graph classification and regression problems evaluated. The contribution is a structured route from variable-sized graphs to fixed-sized representations. Its design makes graph clustering and the removal of fine-scale detail explicit parts of the pooling process, with empirical results supporting its usefulness across diverse tasks.
summary.tldr: HaarPooling compresses graphs through clustered Haar transforms to produce fixed-sized representations while preserving structural information.

title: Haar Graph Pooling

abstract: Neural networks are often represented as graphs of connections between neurons. However, despite their wide use, there is currently little understanding of the relationship between the graph structure of the neural network and its predictive performance. Here we systematically investigate how does the graph structure of neural networks affect their predictive performance. To this end, we develop a novel graph-based representation of neural networks called relational graph, where layers of neural network computation correspond to rounds of message exchange along the graph structure. Using this representation we show that: (1) a “sweet spot” of relational graphs leads to neural networks with significantly improved predictive performance; (2) neural network’s performance is approximately a smooth function of the clustering coefficient and average path length of its relational graph; (3) our findings are consistent across many different tasks and datasets; (4) the sweet spot can be identified efficiently; (5) top-performing neural networks have graph structure surprisingly similar to those of real biological neural networks. Our work opens new directions for the design of neural architectures and the understanding on neural networks in general.

paragraphs: Neural networks can be viewed as graphs, but that viewpoint alone does not explain how their connection patterns affect prediction. This paper introduces a relational graph representation to investigate that relationship systematically. In this representation, a layer of network computation corresponds to a round of messages exchanged along the graph’s connections.

Using this formulation, the authors identify a region of graph structures associated with significantly better predictive performance. They report that performance varies approximately smoothly with two graph properties: the clustering coefficient, which describes local connectedness, and average path length, which describes how far apart nodes are through graph connections. This connects architecture quality to measurable structural characteristics.

The findings are consistent across many tasks and datasets, and the favorable region can be identified efficiently. The authors also observe that top-performing networks have graph structures similar to real biological neural networks. Together, these observations suggest a route to architectural design based on connectivity patterns, while the biological similarity remains an observed structural relationship.
summary.tldr: A relational graph representation reveals connectivity patterns associated with stronger neural-network prediction across multiple tasks and datasets.

title: Graph Structure of Neural Networks

abstract: Machine learning models trained with purely observational data and the principle of empirical risk minimization (Vapnik 1992) can fail to generalize to unseen domains. In this paper, we focus on the case where the problem arises through spurious correlation between the observed domains and the actual task labels. We find that many domain generalization methods do not explicitly take this spurious correlation into account. Instead, especially in more application-oriented research areas like medical imaging or robotics, data augmentation techniques that are based on heuristics are used to learn domain invariant features. To bridge the gap between theory and practice, we develop a causal perspective on the problem of domain generalization. We argue that causal concepts can be used to explain the success of data augmentation by describing how they can weaken the spurious correlation between the observed domains and the task labels. We demonstrate that data augmentation can serve as a tool for simulating interventional data. We use these theoretical insights to derive a simple algorithm that is able to select data augmentation techniques that will lead to better domain generalization.

paragraphs: A model can perform well on observed domains yet fail in a new one because domain membership is spuriously correlated with the labels it predicts. This paper focuses on that source of generalization failure. It argues that many domain-generalization methods do not explicitly address the correlation, while practical augmentation choices often rely on heuristics.

The authors develop a causal perspective to explain how augmentation can help. An augmentation can weaken the unwanted relationship between the observed domain and the task label, allowing it to simulate interventional data. This connects a practical training technique to an account of which statistical associations are responsible for poor transfer.

Using these theoretical insights, the paper derives a simple algorithm for selecting augmentation techniques that improve domain generalization. The central contribution is a principle for choosing transformations based on the spurious relationship they can disrupt. The claim is tied to the studied mechanism of domain-label correlation, giving augmentation selection a specific causal purpose.
summary.tldr: A causal account of augmentation leads to a selection algorithm that targets spurious domain-label correlations to improve generalization.

title: Selecting Data Augmentation for Simulating Interventions

abstract: As machine learning methods are deployed in real-world settings such as healthcare, legal systems, and social science, it is crucial to recognize how they shape social biases and stereotypes in these sensitive decision-making processes. Among such real-world deployments are large-scale pretrained language models (LMs) that can be potentially dangerous in manifesting undesirable representational biases - harmful biases resulting from stereotyping that propagate negative generalizations involving gender, race, religion, and other social constructs. As a step towards improving the fairness of LMs, we carefully define several sources of representational biases before proposing new benchmarks and metrics to measure them. With these tools, we propose steps towards mitigating social biases during text generation. Our empirical results and human evaluation demonstrate effectiveness in mitigating bias while retaining crucial contextual information for high-fidelity text generation, thereby pushing forward the performance-fairness Pareto frontier.
originalAbstract: As machine learning methods are deployed in real-world settings such as healthcare, legal systems, and social science, it is crucial to recognize how they shape social biases and stereotypes in these sensitive decision-making processes. Among such real-world deployments are large-scale pretrained language models (LMs) that can be potentially dangerous in manifesting undesirable representational biases - harmful biases resulting from stereotyping that propagate negative generalizations involving gender, race, religion, and other social constructs. As a step towards improving the fairness of LMs, we carefully define several sources of representational biases before proposing new benchmarks and metrics to measure them. With these tools, we propose steps towards mitigating social biases during text generation. Our empirical results and human evaluation demonstrate effectiveness in mitigating bias while retaining crucial contextual information for high-fidelity text generation, thereby pushing forward the performance-fairness Pareto frontier.

paragraphs: Pretrained language models can express stereotypes that propagate harmful generalizations about social groups. This paper focuses on these representational biases, including those involving gender, race, and religion. Its aim is to make the biases more clearly defined and measurable, then use that understanding to improve generated text.

The authors first distinguish several sources of representational bias. They then propose benchmarks and metrics for measuring them, providing an evaluation basis for mitigation. With those tools in place, they develop steps to reduce social bias during text generation. The approach treats preserving relevant contextual information as part of the objective, alongside reducing harmful representations.

Empirical results and human evaluation indicate that the proposed methods mitigate bias while retaining context needed for high-fidelity generation. The authors describe this as advancing the performance–fairness Pareto frontier: achieving better combinations of generation quality and fairness in their evaluation. The finding supports an improved tradeoff on the biases and tasks studied, rather than establishing that generated language is free of all social bias.
summary.tldr: The paper defines and measures representational biases, then demonstrates mitigation that preserves contextual information in generated text.

title: Towards Understanding and Mitigating Social Biases in Language Models

abstract: Training deep neural network models in the presence of corrupted supervision is challenging as the corrupted data points may significantly impact generalization performance. To alleviate this problem, we present an efficient robust algorithm that achieves strong guarantees without any assumption on the type of corruption and provides a unified framework for both classification and regression problems. Unlike many existing approaches that quantify the quality of the data points (e.g., based on their individual loss values), and filter them accordingly, the proposed algorithm focuses on controlling the collective impact of data points on the average gradient. Even when a corrupted data point failed to be excluded by our algorithm, the data point will have a very limited impact on the overall loss, as compared with state-of-the-art filtering methods based on loss values. Extensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets have demonstrated the robustness of our algorithm under different types of corruption. Our code is available at \url{https://github.com/illidanlab/PRL}.

paragraphs: Corrupted supervision can steer a deep network toward poor generalization. Many approaches respond by scoring individual examples, often using their loss values, and removing those judged unreliable. This paper develops a robust training algorithm that instead focuses on the collective influence of examples on the average gradient used for learning.

The distinction matters because identifying every corrupted example is difficult. The proposed method controls how much data points can affect the overall update, so a corrupted point that remains in training still has limited influence on the overall loss. The abstract contrasts this behavior with state-of-the-art filtering methods based on individual loss values.

The authors provide strong guarantees without imposing assumptions on the type of corruption and use one framework for both classification and regression. Experiments across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate robustness under different corruption types. The contribution is therefore both conceptual and practical: robust learning can be organized around limiting the aggregate effect of unreliable supervision, without making successful exclusion of every bad example the central requirement of the approach.
summary.tldr: The proposed robust trainer limits corrupted examples’ collective gradient influence across classification and regression.

title: Learning Deep Neural Networks under Agnostic Corrupted Supervision

abstract: Neural controlled differential equations (CDEs) are the continuous-time analogue of recurrent neural networks, as Neural ODEs are to residual networks, and offer a memory-efficient continuous-time way to model functions of potentially irregular time series. Existing methods for computing the forward pass of a Neural CDE involve embedding the incoming time series into path space, often via interpolation, and using evaluations of this path to drive the hidden state. Here, we use rough path theory to extend this formulation. Instead of directly embedding into path space, we instead represent the input signal over small time intervals through its \textit{log-signature}, which are statistics describing how the signal drives a CDE. This is the approach for solving \textit{rough differential equations} (RDEs), and correspondingly we describe our main contribution as the introduction of Neural RDEs. This extension has a purpose: by generalising the Neural CDE approach to a broader class of driving signals, we demonstrate particular advantages for tackling long time series. In this regime, we demonstrate efficacy on problems of length up to 17k observations and observe significant training speed-ups, improvements in model performance, and reduced memory requirements compared to existing approaches.

paragraphs: Neural controlled differential equations model time series by letting an input signal drive a continuously evolving hidden state. Existing approaches commonly interpolate the observations into a path and repeatedly evaluate that path during computation. This paper extends the formulation using rough path theory, with the specific goal of handling long time series more effectively.

The proposed Neural Rough Differential Equations represent each small interval of the input through its log-signature. These statistics describe how the signal drives a controlled differential equation. Changing to interval-level signal descriptions broadens the class of driving signals the model can use and provides a different computational route from directly evaluating an embedded input path.

Experiments demonstrate effectiveness on sequences containing up to 17,000 observations. In this long-sequence regime, the authors observe significant training speedups, improved model performance, and lower memory requirements relative to existing approaches. The findings connect the mathematical extension to practical computation: the new signal representation helps make continuous-time neural modeling more effective on the evaluated long time-series problems.
summary.tldr: Neural RDEs use interval log-signatures to model long time series, improving speed, memory use, and performance in reported experiments.

title: Neural Rough Differential Equations for Long Time Series

abstract: Optimal transport (OT) measures distances between distributions in a way that depends on the geometry of the sample space. In light of recent advances in computational OT, OT distances are widely used as loss functions in machine learning. Despite their prevalence and advantages, OT loss functions can be extremely sensitive to outliers. In fact, a single adversarially-picked outlier can increase the standard $W_2$-distance arbitrarily. To address this issue, we propose an outlier-robust formulation of OT. Our formulation is convex but challenging to scale at a first glance. Our main contribution is deriving an \emph{equivalent} formulation based on cost truncation that is easy to incorporate into modern algorithms for computational OT. We demonstrate the benefits of our formulation in mean estimation problems under the Huber contamination model in simulations and outlier detection tasks on real data.

paragraphs: Optimal transport compares distributions while accounting for the geometry of their sample space, making it useful as a machine-learning loss. However, standard transport losses can be highly sensitive to outliers. The paper highlights the severity of this problem: one adversarially selected outlier can make the usual W₂ distance arbitrarily large.

The authors propose a convex formulation of optimal transport that is robust to outliers. Although this formulation initially appears difficult to scale, they derive an equivalent version based on truncating transport costs. The equivalence is central: it makes the proposed robust objective easy to incorporate into modern computational transport algorithms while retaining the same underlying formulation.

The paper demonstrates benefits in simulated mean-estimation problems under the Huber contamination model and in outlier-detection tasks using real data. These evaluations connect the formulation to both estimation with contaminated observations and identifying unusual observations. The overall contribution joins a robustness objective with a computationally accessible expression, making the treatment of outliers part of the transport comparison itself.
summary.tldr: An outlier-robust transport objective has an equivalent cost-truncation formulation that fits readily into modern optimal-transport algorithms.

title: Outlier-Robust Optimal Transport

abstract: Contrastively trained text-image models have the remarkable ability to perform zero-shot classification, that is, classifying previously unseen images into categories that the model has never been explicitly trained to identify. However, these zero-shot classifiers need prompt engineering to achieve high accuracy. Prompt engineering typically requires hand-crafting a set of prompts for individual downstream tasks. In this work, we aim to automate this prompt engineering and improve zero-shot accuracy through prompt ensembling. In particular, we ask “Given a large pool of prompts, can we automatically score the prompts and ensemble those that are most suitable for a particular downstream dataset, without needing access to labeled validation data?" . We demonstrate that this is possible. In doing so, we identify several pathologies in a naive prompt scoring method where the score can be easily overconfident due to biases in pre-training and test data, and we propose a novel prompt scoring method that corrects for the biases. Using our proposed scoring method to create a weighted average prompt ensemble, our method overall outperforms equal average ensemble, as well as hand-crafted prompts, on ImageNet, 4 of its variants, and 11 fine-grained classification benchmarks. while being fully automatic, optimization-free, and not requiring access to labeled validation data.

paragraphs: Text-image models can classify images using descriptions of candidate categories, but the wording of those descriptions affects accuracy. Combining several prompts can help, yet choosing them often requires manual work. This paper asks whether a model can automatically select and weight useful prompts from a large pool without labeled validation examples.

The authors identify problems with a naive scoring approach: biases in pretraining and test data can make a prompt appear more reliable than it actually is. They introduce a scoring method that corrects for these biases, then use the scores to form a weighted prompt ensemble. The key idea is to distinguish apparent confidence from evidence that a prompt suits the downstream dataset.

The resulting method performs better overall than equal-weight prompt averaging and hand-crafted prompts across ImageNet, four variants, and eleven fine-grained classification benchmarks. The procedure is automatic and requires neither optimization nor labeled validation data. These findings support prompt weighting as a practical way to improve zero-shot classification, while the reported overall advantage does not imply that every individual dataset improves.
summary.tldr: Automatically correcting biased prompt scores improves weighted prompt ensembles without optimization or labeled validation data.

title: A Simple Zero-shot Prompt Weighting Technique to Improve Prompt Ensembling in Text-Image Models

abstract: In multi-goal Reinforcement Learning, an agent can share experience between related training tasks, resulting in better generalization for new tasks at test time. However, when the goal space has discontinuities and the reward is sparse, a majority of goals are difficult to reach. In this context, a curriculum over goals helps agents learn by adapting training tasks to their current capabilities. In this work, we propose Stein Variational Goal Generation (SVGG), which samples goals of intermediate difficulty for the agent, by leveraging a learned predictive model of its goal reaching capabilities. The distribution of goals is modeled with particles that are attracted in areas of appropriate difficulty using Stein Variational Gradient Descent. We show that SVGG outperforms state-of-the-art multi-goal Reinforcement Learning methods in terms of success coverage in hard exploration problems, and demonstrate that it is endowed with a useful recovery property when the environment changes.

paragraphs: Multi-goal reinforcement learning allows an agent to reuse experience across related tasks. Exploration becomes difficult, however, when rewards are sparse and discontinuities in the goal space leave many goals hard to reach. A curriculum can help by selecting training goals that fit the agent's current capabilities rather than presenting mostly unattainable tasks.

Stein Variational Goal Generation, or SVGG, learns a predictive model of the agent's ability to reach goals. It uses that model to identify goals of intermediate difficulty. A collection of particles represents the goal distribution, and Stein Variational Gradient Descent moves those particles toward regions with an appropriate level of challenge.

The curriculum thus adapts its goal distribution using estimates of what the agent can currently accomplish. Experiments show higher success coverage than state-of-the-art multi-goal reinforcement learning methods on the evaluated hard-exploration problems. The authors also demonstrate useful recovery when the environment changes. These findings support adaptive goal generation as a way to improve exploration and respond to changed task conditions.
summary.tldr: SVGG adapts a particle-based goal curriculum to the agent's capabilities, improving success coverage and demonstrating recovery after environmental changes.

title: Stein Variational Goal Generation for adaptive Exploration in Multi-Goal Reinforcement Learning

abstract: In a backdoor attack , an adversary inserts maliciously constructed backdoor examples into a training set to make the resulting model vulnerable to manipulation. Defending against such attacks involves viewing inserted examples as outliers in the training set and using techniques from robust statistics to detect and remove them. In this work, we present a different approach to the backdoor attack problem. Specifically, we show that without structural information about the training data distribution, backdoor attacks are indistinguishable from naturally-occuring features in the data—and thus impossible to "detect" in a general sense. Then, guided by this observation, we revisit existing defenses against backdoor attacks and characterize the (often latent) assumptions they make, and on which they depend. Finally, we explore an alternative perspective on backdoor attacks: one that assumes these attacks correspond to the strongest feature in the training data. Under this assumption (which we make formal) we develop a new primitive for detecting backdoor attacks. Our primitive naturally gives rise to a detection algorithm that comes with theoretical guarantees, and is effective in practice.

paragraphs: Backdoor attacks insert specially constructed examples into training data so that a learned model can later be manipulated. A common defense treats these examples as statistical outliers. This paper asks what information is actually needed to distinguish a maliciously introduced pattern from a naturally occurring feature.

The authors show that, without structural information about the training distribution, that distinction cannot be made in general. They use this observation to examine existing defenses and expose the assumptions those defenses rely on, including assumptions that may be implicit. The impossibility claim is conditional on the absence of structural information, rather than a claim that all backdoor detection is impossible.

The paper then adopts a different assumption: a backdoor corresponds to the strongest feature in the training data. After formalizing this premise, the authors develop a detection primitive that yields an algorithm with theoretical guarantees and practical effectiveness. The contribution clarifies both why general detection needs assumptions and how a particular explicit assumption can support a constructive defense.
summary.tldr: Backdoor detection requires structural assumptions, and a formal strongest-feature assumption enables a guaranteed and practically effective detector.

title: Rethinking Backdoor Attacks

abstract: Multivariate probabilistic time series forecasts are commonly evaluated via proper scoring rules, i.e., functions that are minimal in expectation for the ground-truth distribution. However, this property is not sufficient to guarantee good discrimination in the non-asymptotic regime. In this paper, we provide the first systematic finite-sample study of proper scoring rules for time series forecasting evaluation. Through a power analysis, we identify the “region of reliability” of a scoring rule, i.e., the set of practical conditions where it can be relied on to identify forecasting errors. We carry out our analysis on a comprehensive synthetic benchmark, specifically designed to test several key discrepancies between ground-truth and forecast distributions, and we gauge the generalizability of our findings to real-world tasks with an application to an electricity production problem. Our results reveal critical shortcomings in the evaluation of multivariate probabilistic forecasts as commonly performed in the literature.

paragraphs: Probabilistic forecasts describe distributions of possible outcomes, and proper scoring rules are commonly used to evaluate them. A proper rule favors the true distribution in expectation. This paper shows why that desirable property does not by itself ensure that an evaluation with a finite amount of data can distinguish forecasting errors reliably.

The authors conduct a systematic finite-sample study using statistical power analysis. For each scoring rule, they identify a region of reliability: practical conditions under which the rule can be trusted to detect discrepancies between a forecast distribution and the truth. This shifts attention from an ideal expectation-based property to the actual ability of an evaluation to reveal mistakes.

The analysis uses a synthetic benchmark designed around several important distributional discrepancies. An electricity-production application then examines how the findings carry over to a real task. The results expose substantial shortcomings in commonly used evaluations of multivariate probabilistic forecasts. Their implication is that a scoring rule’s theoretical propriety and its practical error-detection ability need to be assessed separately.
summary.tldr: Finite-sample power analysis reveals when proper scoring rules can reliably detect errors in multivariate probabilistic forecasts.

title: Regions of Reliability in the Evaluation of Multivariate Probabilistic Forecasts

abstract: Recent data-driven approaches based on machine learning aim to directly solve a downstream forecasting or projection task by learning a data-driven functional mapping using deep neural networks. However, these networks are trained using curated and homogeneous climate datasets for specific spatiotemporal tasks, and thus lack the generality of currently used computationally intensive physics-informed numerical models for weather and climate modeling. We develop and demonstrate ClimaX, a flexible and generalizable deep learning model for weather and climate science that can be trained using heterogeneous datasets spanning different variables, spatio-temporal coverage, and physical groundings. ClimaX extends the Transformer architecture with novel encoding and aggregation blocks that allow effective use of available compute and data while maintaining general utility. ClimaX is pretrained with a self-supervised learning objective on climate datasets derived from CMIP6. The pretrained ClimaX can then be fine-tuned to address a breadth of climate and weather tasks, including those that involve atmospheric variables and spatio-temporal scales unseen during pretraining. Compared to existing data-driven baselines, we show that this generality in ClimaX results in superior performance on benchmarks for weather forecasting and climate projections, even when pretrained at lower resolutions and compute budgets. Our source code is available at https://github.com/microsoft/ClimaX.

paragraphs: Many machine learning models for weather and climate are trained for a particular task using carefully standardized datasets. That specialization limits their generality when variables, locations, or time scales change. ClimaX aims to provide a reusable model that can learn from heterogeneous climate data and later be adapted to a range of forecasting and projection tasks.

The model extends the Transformer with encoding and aggregation components designed to handle datasets with different variables, spatial and temporal coverage, and physical foundations. It is pretrained through self-supervised learning on climate datasets derived from CMIP6. Fine-tuning then adapts the shared model to downstream tasks, including tasks with atmospheric variables or scales absent during pretraining.

On weather forecasting and climate projection benchmarks, the authors report better performance than existing data-driven baselines, even with pretraining at lower resolutions and compute budgets. This supports the value of sharing learning across diverse climate datasets. The reported transfer involves fine-tuning, so its generality includes adaptation to new tasks rather than requiring every task to match the pretraining setup.
summary.tldr: ClimaX learns from heterogeneous climate datasets and can be fine-tuned for varied weather and climate tasks, including previously unseen variables and scales.

title: ClimaX: A foundation model for weather and climate

abstract: In this work we identify the dormant neuron phenomenon in deep reinforcement learning, where an agent’s network suffers from an increasing number of inactive neurons, thereby affecting network expressivity. We demonstrate the presence of this phenomenon across a variety of algorithms and environments, and highlight its effect on learning. To address this issue, we propose a simple and effective method (ReDo) that Recycles Dormant neurons throughout training. Our experiments demonstrate that ReDo maintains the expressive power of networks by reducing the number of dormant neurons and results in improved performance.

Our experiments demonstrate that ReDo maintains the expressive power of networks by reducing the number of dormant neurons and results in improved performance.

paragraphs: This paper identifies a training phenomenon in deep reinforcement learning: an increasing number of neurons become inactive as learning progresses. The authors call these dormant neurons. Their accumulation affects network expressivity, meaning the network’s ability to represent useful functions can be impaired even though those neurons remain part of its architecture.

The authors demonstrate the phenomenon across several reinforcement learning algorithms and environments and examine its effect on learning. This makes neuron activity a relevant part of understanding how an agent’s network changes during training. The issue concerns how much of the available network continues to contribute, connecting internal activity to the network’s effective representational capacity.

To address the problem, the paper proposes ReDo, a method that recycles dormant neurons throughout training. Experiments show that it reduces the number of dormant neurons, maintains expressive power, and improves performance. These findings support actively reusing inactive network components as a simple intervention for preserving useful capacity during the evaluated reinforcement learning training processes.
summary.tldr: ReDo recycles neurons that become inactive during reinforcement learning, preserving network expressivity and improving performance in experiments.

title: The Dormant Neuron Phenomenon in Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Causal disentanglement seeks a representation of data involving latent variables that are related via a causal model. A representation is identifiable if both the latent model and the transformation from latent to observed variables are unique. In this paper, we study observed variables that are a linear transformation of a linear latent causal model. Data from interventions are necessary for identifiability: if one latent variable is missing an intervention, we show that there exist distinct models that cannot be distinguished. Conversely, we show that a single intervention on each latent variable is sufficient for identifiability. Our proof uses a generalization of the RQ decomposition of a matrix that replaces the usual orthogonal and upper triangular conditions with analogues depending on a partial order on the rows of the matrix, with partial order determined by a latent causal model. We corroborate our theoretical results with a method for causal disentanglement. We show that the method accurately recovers a latent causal model on synthetic and semi-synthetic data and we illustrate a use case on a dataset of single-cell RNA sequencing measurements.

paragraphs: Causal disentanglement aims to recover hidden variables, their causal relationships, and how they produce observed data. This paper studies a specific linear setting: the hidden causal model is linear, and the observations are a linear transformation of its variables. Identifiability asks whether those underlying components can be uniquely determined.

The authors establish complementary results about interventions. If even one latent variable lacks an intervention, distinct models can exist that the data cannot distinguish. Conversely, one intervention on each latent variable is sufficient for identifiability in the studied setting. The first statement describes a failure of general identification, rather than claiming that every individual case with a missing intervention is ambiguous.

The proof generalizes matrix RQ decomposition using conditions determined by the causal model's partial ordering. The authors also develop a disentanglement method that accurately recovers latent causal models on synthetic and semi-synthetic data, and illustrate its use with single-cell RNA sequencing measurements. The practical results accompany a precise account of when intervention coverage supports recovery.
summary.tldr: For linear latent causal models observed through linear mixtures, one intervention per latent variable is sufficient for identifiability.

title: Linear Causal Disentanglement via Interventions

abstract: We investigate online classification with paid stochastic experts. Here, before making their prediction, each expert must be paid. The amount that we pay each expert directly influences the accuracy of their prediction through some unknown Lipschitz “productivity” function. In each round, the learner must decide how much to pay each expert and then make a prediction. They incur a cost equal to a weighted sum of the prediction error and upfront payments for all experts. We introduce an online learning algorithm whose total cost after $T$ rounds exceeds that of a predictor which knows the productivity of all experts in advance by at most $\mathcal{O}\big(K^2(\ln T)\sqrt{T}\big)$ where $K$ is the number of experts. In order to achieve this result, we combine Lipschitz bandits and online classification with surrogate losses. These tools allow us to improve upon the bound of order $T^{2/3}$ one would obtain in the standard Lipschitz bandit setting. Our algorithm is empirically evaluated on synthetic data.

paragraphs: The paper studies online classification when experts must be paid before making predictions. Each expert's accuracy depends on payment through an unknown productivity function. On every round, the learner chooses payments and then predicts, balancing prediction errors against the total amount spent through a weighted cost.

The productivity functions are assumed to be Lipschitz, meaning their changes are bounded relative to changes in payment. The proposed algorithm combines tools from Lipschitz bandits with online classification using surrogate losses. This combination lets the learner exploit the classification structure while learning how payments affect expert accuracy.

After T rounds with K experts, the algorithm's total cost exceeds that of a predictor that knows all productivity functions by at most an order of K squared times log T times the square root of T. Its dependence on T improves on the T to the two-thirds order obtained from the standard Lipschitz-bandit approach discussed in the paper. Synthetic-data experiments evaluate the algorithm empirically.
summary.tldr: An online algorithm learns how to pay stochastic experts while bounding combined prediction and payment costs against a productivity-informed predictor.

title: Trading-Off Payments and Accuracy in Online Classification with Paid Stochastic Experts

abstract: Clustering (or community detection) on multilayer graphs poses several additional complications with respect to standard graphs as different layers may be characterized by different structures and types of information. One of the major challenges is to establish the extent to which each layer contributes to the cluster assignment in order to effectively take advantage of the multilayer structure and improve upon the classification obtained using the individual layers or their union. However, making an informed a-priori assessment about the clustering information content of the layers can be very complicated. In this work, we assume a semi-supervised learning setting, where the class of a small percentage of nodes is initially provided, and we propose a parameter-free Laplacian-regularized model that learns an optimal nonlinear combination of the different layers from the available input labels. The learning algorithm is based on a Frank-Wolfe optimization scheme with inexact gradient, combined with a modified Label Propagation iteration. We provide a detailed convergence analysis of the algorithm and extensive experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets, showing that the proposed method compares favourably with a variety of baselines and outperforms each individual layer when used in isolation.

paragraphs: A multilayer graph represents several kinds of relationships among the same objects. Different layers may contain different information about communities, making it difficult to decide beforehand how much each should contribute to classification. Simply relying on one layer or their union may fail to use the available structure effectively.

The paper assumes that labels are initially available for a small percentage of nodes. It proposes a parameter-free, Laplacian-regularized model that uses those labels to learn an optimal nonlinear combination of layers. The supplied labels therefore guide how the different relationship structures contribute to the resulting assignments.

The learning procedure combines Frank-Wolfe optimization with an inexact gradient and a modified label-propagation iteration. The authors provide a detailed convergence analysis and evaluate the method on synthetic and real-world datasets. It compares favorably with multiple baselines and outperforms each isolated layer in the reported experiments. These findings support learning the layer combination from limited supervision rather than choosing its contribution in advance.
summary.tldr: A parameter-free model uses a small set of node labels to learn a nonlinear graph-layer combination, outperforming isolated layers in experiments.

title: Learning the Right Layers a Data-Driven Layer-Aggregation Strategy for Semi-Supervised Learning on Multilayer Graphs

abstract: Training practical agents usually involve offline and online reinforcement learning (RL) to balance the policy’s performance and interaction costs. In particular, online fine-tuning has become a commonly used method to correct the erroneous estimates of out-of-distribution data learned in the offline training phase. However, even limited online interactions can be inaccessible or catastrophic for high-stake scenarios like healthcare and autonomous driving. In this work, we introduce an interaction-free training scheme dubbed Offline-with-Action-Preferences (OAP). The main insight is that, compared to online fine-tuning, querying the preferences between pre-collected and learned actions can be equally or even more helpful to the erroneous estimate problem. By adaptively encouraging or suppressing policy constraint according to action preferences, OAP could distinguish overestimation from beneficial policy improvement and thus attains a more accurate evaluation of unseen data. Theoretically, we prove a lower bound of the behavior policy’s performance improvement brought by OAP. Moreover, comprehensive experiments on the D4RL benchmark and state-of-the-art algorithms demonstrate that OAP yields higher (29% on average) scores, especially on challenging AntMaze tasks (98% higher).

paragraphs: An agent trained only on recorded experience can misjudge actions that fall outside that experience. Online fine-tuning can correct these estimates, but obtaining new interactions may be inaccessible or dangerous in settings such as healthcare and autonomous driving. This paper proposes Offline-with-Action-Preferences, or OAP, to improve offline training without additional environment interactions.

OAP queries preferences between actions in the collected data and actions proposed by the learned policy. It uses those preferences to strengthen or relax the constraint that keeps the policy close to recorded behavior. This helps distinguish an action whose apparent value is overestimated from one that represents a useful improvement, supporting more accurate evaluation of unseen data.

The authors prove a lower bound on the improvement over the behavior policy and evaluate OAP with leading algorithms on D4RL. They report scores averaging 29% higher, with a 98% increase on challenging AntMaze tasks. These results support action preferences as a potentially valuable alternative to online correction in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: OAP uses action-preference queries to improve offline reinforcement learning without collecting new environment interactions.

title: Boosting Offline Reinforcement Learning with Action Preference Query

abstract: We study a new non-stochastic federated multiarmed bandit problem with multiple agents collaborating via a communication network. The losses of the arms are assigned by an oblivious adversary that specifies the loss of each arm not only for each time step but also for each agent, which we call doubly adversarial. In this setting, different agents may choose the same arm in the same time step but observe different feedback. The goal of each agent is to find a globally best arm in hindsight that has the lowest cumulative loss averaged over all agents, which necessities the communication among agents. We provide regret lower bounds for any federated bandit algorithm under different settings, when agents have access to full-information feedback, or the bandit feedback. For the bandit feedback setting, we propose a near-optimal federated bandit algorithm called FEDEXP3. Our algorithm gives a positive answer to an open question proposed in (Cesa-Bianchi et al., 2016): FEDEXP3 can guarantee a sub-linear regret without exchanging sequences of selected arm identities or loss sequences among agents. We also provide numerical evaluations of our algorithm to validate our theoretical results and demonstrate its effectiveness on synthetic and real-world datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies agents that repeatedly choose among actions while collaborating through a communication network. An oblivious adversary assigns losses across both time and agents, so two agents choosing the same action simultaneously can receive different feedback. Each agent aims to compete with the single action that would have minimized cumulative loss averaged across the entire group.

That shared objective makes communication necessary: one agent’s observations do not directly reveal how an action performs for everyone. The authors establish lower bounds on achievable regret for settings with full-information feedback and settings where agents observe only feedback for their selected actions. These bounds characterize unavoidable difficulty in the problem.

For bandit feedback, the paper introduces FEDEXP3, a near-optimal algorithm. It guarantees sublinear regret without agents exchanging sequences of chosen-action identities or losses, answering an existing open question. Sublinear regret means the average performance gap to the hindsight benchmark diminishes over time. Numerical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical results and demonstrate effectiveness in the tested settings.
summary.tldr: FEDEXP3 achieves near-optimal federated bandit learning when losses vary across agents and time without exchanging action or loss sequences.

title: Doubly Adversarial Federated Bandits

abstract: Recently, subgraph GNNs have emerged as an important direction for developing expressive graph neural networks (GNNs). While numerous architectures have been proposed, so far there is still a limited understanding of how various design paradigms differ in terms of expressive power, nor is it clear what design principle achieves maximal expressiveness with minimal architectural complexity. To address these fundamental questions, this paper conducts a systematic study of general node-based subgraph GNNs through the lens of Subgraph Weisfeiler-Lehman Tests (SWL). Our central result is to build a complete hierarchy of SWL with strictly growing expressivity. Concretely, we prove that any node-based subgraph GNN falls into one of the six SWL equivalence classes, among which $\mathsf{SSWL}$ achieves the maximal expressive power. We also study how these equivalence classes differ in terms of their practical expressiveness such as encoding graph distance and biconnectivity. In addition, we give a tight expressivity upper bound of all SWL algorithms by establishing a close relation with localized versions of WL and Folklore WL (FWL) tests. Overall, our results provide insights into the power of existing subgraph GNNs, guide the design of new architectures, and point out their limitations by revealing an inherent gap with the 2-FWL test. Finally, experiments demonstrate that $\mathsf{SSWL}$-inspired subgraph GNNs can significantly outperform prior architectures on multiple benchmarks despite great simplicity.

paragraphs: Subgraph graph neural networks offer ways to recognize graph structure that simpler architectures may miss. Yet many different designs exist, making it difficult to tell which architectural choices actually increase expressive power. This paper develops a systematic comparison for node-based subgraph GNNs using Subgraph Weisfeiler-Lehman tests, or SWL.
