summary.tldr: The paper classifies node-based subgraph GNNs into six expressiveness levels, identifying a maximal class that inspires simple, effective architectures.

title: A Complete Expressiveness Hierarchy for Subgraph GNNs via Subgraph Weisfeiler-Lehman Tests

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have unlocked new capabilities and applications; however, evaluating the alignment with human preferences still poses significant challenges. To address this issue, we introduce Chatbot Arena, an open platform for evaluating LLMs based on human preferences. Our methodology employs a pairwise comparison approach and leverages input from a diverse user base through crowdsourcing. The platform has been operational for several months, amassing over 240K votes. This paper describes the platform, analyzes the data we have collected so far, and explains the tried-and-true statistical methods we are using for efficient and accurate evaluation and ranking of models. We confirm that the crowdsourced questions are sufficiently diverse and discriminating and that the crowd-sourced human votes are in good agreement with those of expert raters. These analyses collectively establish a robust foundation for the credibility of Chatbot Arena. Because of its unique value and openness, Chatbot Arena has emerged as one of the most referenced LLM leaderboards, widely cited by leading LLM developers and companies. The platform is publicly available at https://chat.lmsys.org.

paragraphs: Chatbot Arena evaluates language models through people's preferences between pairs of responses. This addresses a challenge that capability measurements alone do not settle: whether users prefer the behavior a model produces. The open platform crowdsources comparisons from a diverse user base and uses those comparisons to evaluate and rank models.

The paper describes the platform and analyzes more than 240,000 votes collected over several months. It also explains the statistical methods used to turn comparisons into efficient and accurate evaluations. A central part of the analysis concerns the quality of the inputs to that process: whether user questions meaningfully distinguish models and whether crowd judgments agree with expert judgments.

The authors find that the questions are sufficiently diverse and discriminating, and that crowd votes agree well with expert ratings. These findings support the credibility of the platform's preference-based rankings. The contribution combines a public evaluation mechanism with evidence about its collected data, making human preference a practical basis for comparing assistants.
summary.tldr: Chatbot Arena uses crowdsourced pairwise comparisons and statistical analysis to rank language models by human preference.

title: Chatbot Arena: An Open Platform for Evaluating LLMs by Human Preference

abstract: The problem of two-player zero-sum Markov games has recently attracted increasing interests in theoretical studies of multi-agent reinforcement learning (RL). In particular, for finite-horizon episodic Markov decision processes (MDPs), it has been shown that model-based algorithms can find an $\epsilon$-optimal Nash Equilibrium (NE) with the sample complexity of $O(H^3SAB/\epsilon^2)$, which is optimal in the dependence of the horizon $H$ and the number of states $S$ (where $A$ and $B$ denote the number of actions of the two players, respectively). However, none of the existing model-free algorithms can achieve such an optimality. In this work, we propose a model-free stage-based algorithm and show that it achieves the same sample complexity as the best model-based algorithm, and hence for the first time demonstrate that model-free algorithms can enjoy the same optimality in the $H$ dependence as model-based algorithms. The main improvement of the dependency on $H$ arises by leveraging the popular variance reduction technique based on the reference-advantage decomposition previously used only for single-agent RL. However, such a technique relies on a critical monotonicity property of the value function, which does not hold in Markov games due to the update of the policy via the coarse correlated equilibrium (CCE) oracle. Thus, to extend such a technique to Markov games, our algorithm features a key novel design of updating the reference value functions as the pair of optimistic and pessimistic value functions whose value difference is the smallest in the history in order to achieve the desired improvement in the sample efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper studies how much experience a model-free algorithm needs to learn an approximately optimal Nash equilibrium in a two-player zero-sum Markov game. In the finite-horizon episodic setting, the authors propose a stage-based algorithm matching the best stated model-based sample complexity: O(H³SAB/ε²), where H is the horizon, S counts states, and A and B count player actions.

The improvement comes from adapting a variance-reduction technique called reference-advantage decomposition. Previously used in single-agent reinforcement learning, this technique depends on a monotonicity property of value estimates. That property fails here because policies are updated through a coarse correlated equilibrium oracle, making a direct transfer of the technique insufficient.

The algorithm instead updates its reference values using the historical pair of optimistic and pessimistic value functions with the smallest gap. This design enables the desired sample-efficiency improvement despite the missing monotonicity. The result establishes that model-free methods can match model-based methods' optimal horizon dependence in this setting, with the stated bound also optimal in its dependence on the number of states.
summary.tldr: A stage-based model-free algorithm matches the best stated model-based sample complexity for learning approximate Nash equilibria in finite-horizon zero-sum Markov games.

title: Improving Sample Efficiency of Model-Free Algorithms for Zero-Sum Markov Games

abstract: Federated learning (FL) has enabled distributed learning of a model across multiple clients in a privacy-preserving manner. One of the main challenges of FL is to accommodate clients with varying hardware capacities; clients have differing compute and memory requirements. To tackle this challenge, recent state-of-the-art approaches leverage the use of early exits. Nonetheless, these approaches fall short of mitigating the challenges of joint learning multiple exit classifiers, often relying on hand-picked heuristic solutions for knowledge distillation among classifiers and/or utilizing additional layers for weaker classifiers. In this work, instead of utilizing multiple classifiers, we propose a recurrent early exit approach named ReeFL that fuses features from different sub-models into a single shared classifier. Specifically, we use a transformer-based early-exit module shared among sub-models to i) better exploit multi-layer feature representations for task-specific prediction and ii) modulate the feature representation of the backbone model for subsequent predictions. We additionally present a per-client self-distillation approach where the best sub-model is automatically selected as the teacher of the other sub-models at each client. Our experiments on standard image and speech classification benchmarks across various emerging federated fine-tuning baselines demonstrate ReeFL effectiveness over previous works.

paragraphs: Federated learning must accommodate devices with different computation and memory capacities. Early exits let clients make predictions using different portions of a model, but training several separate exit classifiers creates coordination problems. Existing approaches often use manually chosen distillation rules or extra layers to help weaker classifiers.

ReeFL replaces those multiple classifiers with a shared classifier that combines features from different sub-models. A transformer-based early-exit module is reused across them. It both uses representations from multiple layers for prediction and modifies the backbone's features for later predictions. This recurrent design connects predictions at different stages through a common module.

The authors also introduce self-distillation separately for each client, automatically selecting that client's best sub-model to teach the others. Experiments on image and speech classification benchmarks, across several federated fine-tuning baselines, demonstrate effectiveness over previous methods. The approach matters because it addresses the learning relationship among exits alongside hardware diversity, allowing clients' sub-models to share predictive machinery and exchange knowledge through automatically selected teachers.
summary.tldr: ReeFL uses a shared recurrent exit module and client-specific self-distillation to improve federated learning across devices with different capacities.

title: Recurrent Early Exits for Federated Learning with Heterogeneous Clients

abstract: Few-shot action recognition aims at quickly adapting a pre-trained model to the novel data with a distribution shift using only a limited number of samples. Key challenges include how to identify and leverage the transferable knowledge learned by the pre-trained model. We therefore propose CDTD, or Causal Domain-Invariant Temporal Dynamics for knowledge transfer. To identify the temporally invariant and variant representations, we employ the causal representation learning methods for unsupervised pertaining, and then tune the classifier with supervisions in next stage. Specifically, we assume the domain information can be well estimated and the pre-trained temporal dynamic generation and transition models can be well transferred. During adaptation, we fix the transferable temporal dynamics and update the image encoder and domain estimator. The efficacy of our approach is revealed by the superior accuracy of CDTD over leading alternatives across standard few-shot action recognition datasets.

paragraphs: Few-shot action recognition requires adapting a pretrained model to new data using only a small number of labeled examples, often with a distribution shift. The central question is which parts of the pretrained knowledge should carry over. CDTD addresses this by identifying temporal dynamics intended to remain useful across domains.

The method uses causal representation learning during unsupervised pretraining to distinguish temporally invariant and variant representations. A later stage tunes the classifier with supervision. During adaptation, the transferable temporal dynamics remain fixed, while the image encoder and domain estimator are updated. This assigns different adaptation roles to the components of the model.

The approach assumes that domain information can be estimated well and that the pretrained temporal generation and transition models transfer well. Under this formulation, experiments show higher accuracy than leading alternatives across standard few-shot action recognition datasets. The findings support preserving reusable temporal structure while adapting components that connect new visual inputs and domain information to that structure.
summary.tldr: CDTD improves few-shot action recognition by preserving transferable temporal dynamics while adapting visual and domain components, assuming those dynamics and domain estimates transfer well.

title: Learning Causal Domain-Invariant Temporal Dynamics for Few-Shot Action Recognition

abstract: Gaussian process latent variable models (GPLVMs) are a versatile family of unsupervised learning models commonly used for dimensionality reduction. However, common challenges in modeling data with GPLVMs include inadequate kernel flexibility and improper selection of the projection noise, leading to a type of model collapse characterized by vague latent representations that do not reflect the underlying data structure. This paper addresses these issues by, first, theoretically examining the impact of projection variance on model collapse through the lens of a linear GPLVM. Second, we tackle model collapse due to inadequate kernel flexibility by integrating the spectral mixture (SM) kernel and a differentiable random Fourier feature (RFF) kernel approximation, which ensures computational scalability and efficiency through off-the-shelf automatic differentiation tools for learning the kernel hyperparameters, projection variance, and latent representations within the variational inference framework. The proposed GPLVM, named advisedRFLVM, is evaluated across diverse datasets and consistently outperforms various salient competing models, including state-of-the-art variational autoencoders (VAEs) and other GPLVM variants, in terms of informative latent representations and missing data imputation.

paragraphs: Gaussian process latent variable models learn lower-dimensional representations without supervision. They can collapse into vague representations that fail to capture the structure of the data. This paper examines two contributing problems: insufficiently flexible kernels and poorly chosen projection noise. It first analyzes the influence of projection variance theoretically through a linear version of the model.

The proposed advisedRFLVM combines a spectral mixture kernel with a differentiable random Fourier feature approximation. The kernel addresses flexibility, while the approximation supports computational scalability and efficiency. Within variational inference, standard automatic differentiation tools learn the kernel hyperparameters, projection variance, and latent representations, bringing these quantities into the same learning framework.

Across diverse datasets, the authors report consistently better latent representations and missing-data imputation than competing models, including variational autoencoders and other GPLVM variants. These findings connect the model-design changes to both representation quality and a task that uses those representations. The contribution pairs a theoretical investigation of projection variance with a scalable, more flexible model intended to address the identified sources of collapse.
summary.tldr: advisedRFLVM combines a flexible kernel and differentiable approximation to address latent-representation collapse and improve reported missing-data imputation.

title: Preventing Model Collapse in Gaussian Process Latent Variable Models

abstract: In day-to-day communication, people often approximate the truth — for example, rounding the time or omitting details — in order to be maximally helpful to the listener. How do large language models (LLMs) handle such nuanced trade-offs? To address this question, we use psychological models and experiments designed to characterize human behavior to analyze LLMs. We test a range of LLMs and explore how optimization for human preferences or inference-time reasoning affects these trade-offs. We find that reinforcement learning from human feedback improves both honesty and helpfulness, while chain-of-thought prompting skews LLMs towards helpfulness over honesty. Finally, GPT-4 Turbo demonstrates human-like response patterns including sensitivity to the conversational framing and listener’s decision context. Our findings reveal the conversational values internalized by LLMs and suggest that even these abstract values can, to a degree, be steered by zero-shot prompting.
originalAbstract: In day-to-day communication, people often approximate the truth — for example, rounding the time or omitting details — in order to be maximally helpful to the listener. How do large language models (LLMs) handle such nuanced trade-offs? To address this question, we use psychological models and experiments designed to characterize human behavior to analyze LLMs. We test a range of LLMs and explore how optimization for human preferences or inference-time reasoning affects these trade-offs. We find that reinforcement learning from human feedback improves both honesty and helpfulness, while chain-of-thought prompting skews LLMs towards helpfulness over honesty. Finally, GPT-4 Turbo demonstrates human-like response patterns including sensitivity to the conversational framing and listener’s decision context. Our findings reveal the conversational values internalized by LLMs and suggest that even these abstract values can, to a degree, be steered by zero-shot prompting.

paragraphs: Useful communication does not always involve giving every detail with maximum precision. People may round a time or omit information to help a listener make a decision. This paper investigates how language models handle these nuanced tensions between honesty and helpfulness, using psychological models and experiments originally designed to characterize human behavior.

The researchers test multiple language models and examine two ways their responses can change: optimization for human preferences and reasoning during inference. In the studied settings, reinforcement learning from human feedback improves both honesty and helpfulness. Chain-of-thought prompting instead shifts responses toward helpfulness relative to honesty, showing that these interventions affect the balance differently.

GPT-4 Turbo also displays human-like response patterns, including sensitivity to conversational framing and the listener’s decision context. These findings describe observable communication choices in the experiments. They suggest that models internalize patterns associated with conversational values and that zero-shot prompts can steer even these abstract priorities to some degree, without establishing unrestricted control over honesty or helpfulness.
summary.tldr: Psychology-based experiments show that preference training and reasoning prompts affect how language models balance honesty and helpfulness.

title: How do Large Language Models Navigate Conflicts between Honesty and Helpfulness?

abstract: The objective in eXtreme Classification (XC) is to find relevant labels for a document from an exceptionally large label space. Most XC application scenarios have rich auxiliary data associated with the input documents, e.g., frequently clicked webpages for search queries in sponsored search. Unfortunately, most of the existing XC methods do not use any auxiliary data. In this paper, we propose a novel framework, Online Auxiliary Knowledge (OAK), which harnesses auxiliary information linked to the document to improve XC accuracy. OAK stores information learnt from the auxiliary data in a knowledge bank and during a forward pass, retrieves relevant auxiliary knowledge embeddings for a given document. An enriched embedding is obtained by fusing these auxiliary knowledge embeddings with the document’s embedding, thereby enabling much more precise candidate label selection and final classification. OAK training involves three stages. (1) Training a linker module to link documents to relevant auxiliary data points. (2) Learning an embedding for documents enriched using linked auxiliary information. (3) Using the enriched document embeddings to learn the final classifiers. OAK outperforms current state-of-the-art XC methods by up to $\sim 5 %$ on academic datasets, and by $\sim 3 %$ on an auxiliary data-augmented variant of LF-ORCAS-800K dataset in Precision@1. OAK also demonstrates statistically significant improvements in sponsored search metrics when deployed on a large scale search engine.

title: OAK: Enriching Document Representations using Auxiliary Knowledge for Extreme Classification

abstract: A significant amount of protein function requires binding small molecules, including enzymatic catalysis. As such, designing binding pockets for small molecules has several impactful applications ranging from drug synthesis to energy storage. Towards this goal, we first develop HarmonicFlow, an improved generative process over 3D protein-ligand binding structures based on our self-conditioned flow matching objective. FlowSite extends this flow model to jointly generate a protein pocket’s discrete residue types and the molecule’s binding 3D structure. We show that HarmonicFlow improves upon state-of-the-art generative processes for docking in simplicity, generality, and average sample quality in pocket-level docking. Enabled by this structure modeling, FlowSite designs binding sites substantially better than baseline approaches.

The contribution links improved docking generation to binding-site design, addressing two connected aspects of creating protein pockets for small molecules.
summary.tldr: HarmonicFlow improves binding-structure generation, and FlowSite extends it to jointly design pocket residues and molecular binding geometry.

title: Harmonic Self-Conditioned Flow Matching for joint Multi-Ligand Docking and Binding Site Design

abstract: We explore a Federated Reinforcement Learning (FRL) problem where $N$ agents collaboratively learn a common policy without sharing their trajectory data. To date, existing FRL work has primarily focused on agents operating in the same or “similar" environments. In contrast, our problem setup allows for arbitrarily large levels of environment heterogeneity. To obtain the optimal policy which maximizes the average performance across all potentially completely different environments, we propose two algorithms: FedSVRPG-M and FedHAPG-M. In contrast to existing results, we demonstrate that both FedSVRPG-M and FedHAPG-M, both of which leverage momentum mechanisms, can exactly converge to a stationary point of the average performance function, regardless of the magnitude of environment heterogeneity. Furthermore, by incorporating the benefits of variance-reduction techniques or Hessian approximation, both algorithms achieve state-of-the-art convergence results, characterized by a sample complexity of $\mathcal{O}\left(\epsilon^{-\frac{3}{2}}/N\right)$. Notably, our algorithms enjoy linear convergence speedups with respect to the number of agents, highlighting the benefit of collaboration among agents in finding a common policy.

The inverse dependence on N gives a linear speedup with additional agents in the theoretical result. This demonstrates how collaboration can improve learning efficiency even when the agents contribute experience from substantially different environments.
summary.tldr: Two momentum-based federated reinforcement learning algorithms converge to stationary points despite arbitrary environment heterogeneity and obtain linear speedups with more agents.

title: Momentum for the Win: Collaborative Federated Reinforcement Learning across Heterogeneous Environments

abstract: The maximal coding rate reduction (MCR$^2$) objective for learning structured and compact deep representations is drawing increasing attention, especially after its recent usage in the derivation of fully explainable and highly effective deep network architectures. However, it lacks a complete theoretical justification: only the properties of its global optima are known, and its global landscape has not been studied. In this work, we give a complete characterization of the properties of all its local and global optima as well as other types of critical points. Specifically, we show that each (local or global) maximizer of the MCR$^2$ problem corresponds to a low-dimensional, discriminative, and diverse representation, and furthermore, each critical point of the objective is either a local maximizer or a strict saddle point. Such a favorable landscape makes MCR$^2$ a natural choice of objective for learning diverse and discriminative representations via first-order optimization. To further verify our theoretical findings, we illustrate these properties with extensive experiments on both synthetic and real data sets.

paragraphs: Maximal coding rate reduction, or MCR², is an objective for learning compact representations that retain useful structure. Its global optima had already been studied, but those best possible solutions did not explain the rest of the optimization landscape. This paper addresses that gap by characterizing local optima, global optima, and the other critical points of the objective.

The authors show that every local or global maximizer corresponds to a representation that is low-dimensional, discriminative, and diverse. This matters because desirable representations are therefore associated with local maximizers as well as globally best solutions. They also prove that every critical point is either a local maximizer or a strict saddle point, giving a precise description of the remaining stationary configurations.

Together, these findings provide theoretical support for using MCR² with first-order optimization methods. The contribution concerns the geometry of the objective and the quality of its maximizers, rather than only examples of successful training. Experiments on synthetic and real datasets illustrate the established properties and complement the theoretical characterization.
summary.tldr: Every MCR² maximizer yields a compact, discriminative, diverse representation, and every other critical point is a strict saddle.

title: A Global Geometric Analysis of Maximal Coding Rate Reduction

abstract: Neural network training is inherently sensitive to initialization and the randomness induced by stochastic gradient descent. However, it is unclear to what extent such effects lead to meaningfully different networks, either in terms of the models’ weights or the underlying functions that were learned. In this work, we show that during the initial "chaotic" phase of training, even extremely small perturbations reliably causes otherwise identical training trajectories to diverge-an effect that diminishes rapidly over training time. We quantify this divergence through (i) $L^2$ distance between parameters, (ii) the loss barrier when interpolating between networks, (iii) $L^2$ and barrier between parameters after permutation alignment, and (iv) representational similarity between intermediate activations; revealing how perturbations across different hyperparameter or fine-tuning settings drive training trajectories toward distinct loss minima. Our findings provide insights into neural network training stability, with practical implications for fine-tuning, model merging, and diversity of model ensembles.

paragraphs: Neural-network training depends on initialization and the randomness of stochastic gradient descent. This paper asks how far those sensitivities extend: whether tiny changes simply alter numerical weights or lead training toward meaningfully different networks. The authors find an early chaotic phase in which extremely small perturbations reliably separate otherwise identical training trajectories.

They measure separation in several complementary ways. These include distances between parameter vectors, loss barriers along interpolations between networks, and the same comparisons after aligning permutations of parameters. They also examine similarity between intermediate activations. Together, these measurements investigate differences in both the weights and the internal representations learned by the models.

Across different hyperparameter and fine-tuning settings, the analysis shows how perturbations can steer trajectories toward distinct loss minima. This timing matters for understanding training stability: a perturbation's effect depends on when it occurs. The findings have implications for fine-tuning, combining model weights, and understanding the diversity available in model ensembles.
summary.tldr: Tiny perturbations can drive early neural-network training toward different minima, with sensitivity declining rapidly later in training.

title: The Butterfly Effect: Neural Network Training Trajectories Are Highly Sensitive to Initial Conditions

abstract: Remarkable progress in zero-shot learning (ZSL) has been achieved using generative models. However, existing generative ZSL methods merely generate (imagine) the visual features from scratch guided by the strong class semantic vectors annotated by experts, resulting in suboptimal generative performance and limited scene generalization. To address these and advance ZSL, we propose an inductive variational autoencoder for generative zero-shot learning, dubbed GenZSL. Mimicking human-level concept learning, GenZSL operates by inducting new class samples from similar seen classes using weak class semantic vectors derived from target class names (i.e., CLIP text embedding). To ensure the generation of informative samples for training an effective ZSL classifier, our GenZSL incorporates two key strategies. Firstly, it employs class diversity promotion to enhance the diversity of class semantic vectors. Secondly, it utilizes target class-guided information boosting criteria to optimize the model. Extensive experiments conducted on three popular benchmark datasets showcase the superiority and potential of our GenZSL with significant efficacy and efficiency over f-VAEGAN, e.g., 24.7% performance gains and more than $60\times$ faster training speed on AWA2. Codes are available at https://github.com/shiming-chen/GenZSL.

Existing methods often generate those features from expert-annotated semantic descriptions. GenZSL instead draws on similar seen classes and uses semantic vectors obtained from target class names through CLIP text embeddings, reducing reliance on detailed expert-provided class descriptions.

The method uses an inductive variational autoencoder to generate new class samples from this combination of familiar classes and target-name information. It adds two mechanisms to make those samples more useful for classifier training. Class diversity promotion increases diversity among semantic vectors, while a target-class-guided information objective directs optimization toward information relevant to the intended class.

Experiments on three benchmark datasets report improvements in both effectiveness and efficiency. On AWA2, the authors report a 24.7% performance gain and training more than 60 times faster than f-VAEGAN. These results support transferring information from similar seen classes as a productive basis for generating unseen-class features. The reported comparison also shows that replacing richer expert descriptions with class-name embeddings can work well within the tested approach.
summary.tldr: GenZSL generates unseen-class features from similar seen classes and class-name embeddings, improving benchmark performance and training efficiency.

title: GenZSL: Generative Zero-Shot Learning Via Inductive Variational Autoencoder

abstract: Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) is a popular format on the web and in the design industry. However, despite the great strides made in generative modeling, SVG has remained underexplored due to the discrete and complex nature of such data. We introduce GRIMOIRE, a text-guided SVG generative model that is comprised of two modules: A Visual Shape Quantizer (VSQ) learns to map raster images onto a discrete codebook by reconstructing them as vector shapes, and an Auto-Regressive Transformer (ART) models the joint probability distribution over shape tokens, positions and textual descriptions, allowing us to generate vector graphics from natural language. Unlike existing models that require direct supervision from SVG data, GRIMOIRE learns shape image patches using only raster image supervision which opens up vector generative modeling to significantly more data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method by fitting GRIMOIRE for closed filled shapes on the MNIST and Emoji, and for outline strokes on icon and font data, surpassing previous image-supervised methods in generative quality and vector-supervised approach in flexibility.

paragraphs: Vector graphics describe images through shapes, but their discrete and complex structure makes generative modeling challenging. GRIMOIRE generates SVG graphics from text while learning shapes from raster images. This supervision choice allows shape learning to draw on image data without requiring corresponding SVG examples.

The model contains two modules. A Visual Shape Quantizer reconstructs raster images as vector shapes and maps them into a discrete codebook. An autoregressive transformer then models the joint distribution of shape tokens, their positions, and textual descriptions. Together, these modules connect learned visual shape components with language-guided generation of complete vector graphics.

summary.tldr: GRIMOIRE learns vector shape tokens from raster images and uses a text-conditioned transformer to generate SVG graphics.

title: Vector Grimoire: Codebook-based Shape Generation under Raster Image Supervision

abstract: Accurately predicting user watch-time is crucial for enhancing user stickiness and retention in video recommendation systems. Existing watch-time prediction approaches typically involve transformations of watch-time labels for prediction and subsequent reversal, ignoring both the natural distribution properties of label and the instance representation confusion that results in inaccurate predictions. In this paper, we propose ProWTP, a two-stage method combining prototype learning and optimal transport for watch-time regression prediction, suitable for any deep recommendation model. Specifically, we observe that the watch-ratio (the ratio of watch-time to video duration) within the same duration bucket exhibits a multimodal distribution. To facilitate incorporation into models, we use a hierarchical vector quantised variational autoencoder (HVQ-VAE) to convert the continuous label distribution into a high-dimensional discrete distribution, serving as credible prototypes for calibrations. Based on this, ProWTP views the alignment between prototypes and instance representations as a Semi-relaxed Unbalanced Optimal Transport (SUOT) problem, where the marginal constraints of prototypes are relaxed. And the corresponding optimization problem is reformulated as a weighted Lasso problem for solution. Moreover, ProWTP introduces the assignment and compactness losses to encourage instances to cluster closely around their respective prototypes, thereby enhancing the prototype-level distinguishability. Finally, we conducted extensive offline experiments on two industrial datasets, demonstrating our consistent superiority in real-world application.

The authors observe that, among videos in the same duration bucket, watch ratio can have several distinct peaks. They argue that existing label transformations overlook this distribution and can leave individual example representations insufficiently distinguished.

ProWTP addresses these issues in two stages. A hierarchical vector quantised variational autoencoder converts the continuous label distribution into a high-dimensional discrete representation, providing prototypes for calibration. summary.tldr: ProWTP improves watch-time prediction by learning prototypes of watch-ratio patterns and aligning example representations with them.

title: Calibrating Video Watch-time Predictions with Credible Prototype Alignment

abstract: Macro placement, which involves optimizing the positions of modules, is a critical phase in modern integrated circuit design and significantly influences chip performance. The growing complexity of integrated circuits demands increasingly sophisticated placement solutions. Existing approaches have evolved along two primary paths (e.g., constructive and adjustment methods), but they face significant practical limitations that affect real-world chip design. Recent hybrid frameworks such as WireMask-EA have attempted to combine these strategies, but significant technical barriers still remain, including the computational overhead from separated layout adjustment and reconstruction that often require complete layout rebuilding, the inefficient exploration of design spaces due to random mutation operations, and the computational complexity of mask-based construction methods that limit scalability. To overcome these limitations, we introduce EGPlace, a novel evolutionary optimization framework that combines guided mutation strategies with efficient layout reconstruction. EGPlace introduces two key innovations: a greedy repositioning-guided mutation operator that systematically identifies and optimizes critical layout regions, and an efficient mask computation algorithm that accelerates layout evaluation. Our extensive evaluation using ISPD2005 and Ariane RISC-V CPU benchmarks demonstrate that EGPlace reduces wirelength by 10.8% and 9.3% compared to WireMask-EA and the state-of-the-art reinforcement learning-based constructive method EfficientPlace, respectively, while achieving speedups of 7.8$\times$ and 2.8$\times$ over these methods.

paragraphs: Macro placement determines where large modules sit within an integrated circuit, influencing chip performance. Existing search methods can spend substantial computation rebuilding layouts, making random changes, or evaluating placement masks. EGPlace addresses these costs within an evolutionary optimization framework that combines guided changes with efficient layout reconstruction.

Its first innovation is a mutation operator guided by greedy repositioning. This operator identifies critical regions of a layout and directs changes toward improving them, making exploration more targeted. It also achieves respective speedups of 7.8 and 2.8 times. These results indicate that the evaluated framework improves placement quality while reducing computation, rather than requiring more search time to obtain shorter wiring.
summary.tldr: EGPlace combines targeted evolutionary changes with faster layout evaluation to reduce both wirelength and placement runtime in chip-design benchmarks.

title: EGPlace: An Efficient Macro Placement Method via Evolutionary Search with Greedy Repositioning Guided Mutation

abstract: Multiwinner voting is the study of electing a fixed-size committee given individual agents’ preferences over candidates. Most research in this field has been limited to a static setting, with only one election over a fixed set of candidates. However, this approach overlooks the dynamic nature of applications, where candidate sets are subject to change. We extend the study of proportionality in multiwinner voting to dynamic settings, allowing candidates to join or leave the election and demanding that each chosen committee satisfies proportionality without differing too much from the previously selected committee. We consider approval preferences, ranked preferences, and the proportional clustering setting. In these settings, we either give algorithms making few changes or show that such algorithms cannot exist for various proportionality axioms. In particular, we show that such algorithms cannot exist for ranked preferences and provide amortized and exact algorithms for several proportionality notions in the other two settings.

paragraphs: Multiwinner voting selects a fixed-size committee from people’s preferences over candidates. This paper studies what happens when the candidate set changes as candidates arrive or leave. A committee must continue to satisfy a proportionality requirement, while avoiding excessive changes from the previous selection. Representation and continuity therefore become simultaneous algorithmic goals.

The authors examine three settings: approval preferences, ranked preferences, and proportional clustering. For different proportionality axioms, they either construct algorithms that make few changes or establish that such algorithms cannot exist. This makes the specific representation requirement central to determining whether a stable update procedure is possible.

For ranked preferences, the paper establishes impossibility of the desired low-change algorithms in the studied setting. For approval preferences and proportional clustering, it provides amortized and exact algorithms for several proportionality notions. Amortized guarantees concern behavior over a sequence of updates. The results map where proportional representation can be maintained with limited disruption as the available candidates change.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies when proportional committees can be updated with few changes as candidates join or leave, and when this is impossible.

title: Maintaining Proportional Committees with Dynamic Candidate Sets

abstract: Understanding the learning process and the embedded computation in transformers is becoming a central goal for the development of interpretable AI. In the present study, we introduce a hierarchical filtering procedure for data models of sequences on trees, allowing us to hand-tune the range of positional correlations in the data. Leveraging this controlled setting, we provide evidence that vanilla encoder-only transformers can approximate the exact inference algorithm when trained on root classification and masked language modeling tasks, and study how this computation is discovered and implemented. We find that correlations at larger distances, corresponding to increasing layers of the hierarchy, are sequentially included by the network during training. By comparing attention maps from models trained with varying degrees of filtering and by probing the different encoder levels, we find clear evidence of a reconstruction of correlations on successive length scales corresponding to the various levels of the hierarchy, which we relate to a plausible implementation of the exact inference algorithm within the same architecture.

We find that correlations at larger distances, corresponding to increasing layers of the hierarchy, are sequentially included by the network during training. paragraphs: This paper studies how transformers discover computations when the structure of their training data can be controlled. The authors introduce hierarchical filtering for sequence models built on trees. Filtering lets them adjust the range of positional correlations, creating a setting in which dependencies at different distances can be examined separately.

They train standard encoder-only transformers on root classification and masked language modeling. In this controlled setting, they find evidence that the networks can approximate the exact inference algorithm. During training, correlations over larger distances enter the learned computation sequentially, corresponding to progressively higher levels of the underlying hierarchy.

Comparisons of attention maps under different filtering settings, together with probes of encoder levels, support reconstruction of correlations at successive length scales. The authors relate these observations to a plausible implementation of exact inference within the transformer architecture. The result is evidence about how structured computation can emerge during learning: it connects training progression, internal representations, and known data structure without claiming that the proposed implementation is uniquely established.
summary.tldr: Controlled tree-structured data reveal evidence that encoder transformers learn increasingly distant correlations and approximate an exact inference procedure.

title: How Transformers Learn Structured Data: Insights From Hierarchical Filtering

abstract: The emergence of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) advances multimodal emotion recognition (MER) to the next level—from naive discriminative tasks to complex emotion understanding with advanced video understanding abilities and natural language description. However, the current community suffers from a lack of large-scale datasets with intensive, descriptive emotion annotations, as well as a multimodal-centric framework to maximize the potential of MLLMs for emotion understanding. To address this, we establish a new benchmark for MLLM-based emotion understanding with a novel dataset (MER-Caption) and a new model (AffectGPT). Utilizing our model-based crowd-sourcing data collection strategy, we construct the largest descriptive emotion dataset to date (by far), featuring over 2K fine-grained emotion categories across 115K samples. We also introduce the AffectGPT model, designed with pre-fusion operations to enhance multimodal integration. Finally, we present MER-UniBench, a unified benchmark with evaluation metrics tailored for typical MER tasks and the free-form, natural language output style of MLLMs. Extensive experimental results show AffectGPT’s robust performance across various MER tasks. We have released both the code and the dataset to advance research and development in emotion understanding: https://github.com/zeroQiaoba/AffectGPT.

Multimodal language models can describe emotions in natural language, but developing that ability requires descriptive training data and ways to evaluate open-ended answers. This paper addresses those needs together through a dataset, a model, and a unified benchmark.

The MER-Caption dataset contains 115,000 samples covering more than 2,000 fine-grained emotion categories. The authors construct it using a model-based crowd-sourcing strategy, providing a large resource for learning detailed emotional descriptions. Their AffectGPT model introduces pre-fusion operations intended to improve how information from different modalities is combined, making multimodal integration an explicit part of the design.

MER-UniBench evaluates both familiar emotion-recognition tasks and the free-form responses produced by multimodal language models. This matters because evaluating a descriptive answer differs from checking a fixed category prediction. The reported experiments show robust AffectGPT performance across multiple emotion-recognition tasks. Together, the three contributions provide training material, a modeling approach, and an evaluation framework for studying richer emotion understanding.
summary.tldr: AffectGPT combines descriptive emotion data, improved multimodal integration, and unified evaluation to support richer emotion understanding.

title: AffectGPT: A New Dataset, Model, and Benchmark for Emotion Understanding with Multimodal Large Language Models

abstract: Deep models have recently achieved remarkable performances in solving partial differential equations (PDEs). The previous methods are mostly focused on PDEs arising in Euclidean spaces with less emphasis on the general manifolds with rich geometry. Several proposals attempt to account for the geometry by exploiting the spatial coordinates but overlook the underlying intrinsic geometry of manifolds. In this paper, we propose a Curvature-aware Graph Attention for PDEs on manifolds by exploring the important intrinsic geometric quantities such as curvature and discrete gradient operator. It is realized via parallel transport and tensor field on manifolds. To accelerate computation, we present three curvature-oriented graph embedding approaches and derive closed-form parallel transport equations, and a subtree partition method is also developed to promote parameter-sharing. Our proposed curvature-aware attention can be used as a replacement for vanilla attention, and experiments show that it significantly improves the performance of the existing methods for solving PDEs on manifolds. Our code is available at https://github.com/Supradax/CurvGT.

paragraphs: Neural approaches to partial differential equations have largely emphasized Euclidean spaces. Equations defined on manifolds require attention to richer geometry, which spatial coordinates alone may not adequately capture. This paper builds geometric information into graph attention so that learned equation solvers can account for the underlying manifold more directly.

The proposed attention mechanism uses intrinsic quantities including curvature and a discrete gradient operator. Parallel transport and tensor fields provide the machinery for incorporating these quantities across the manifold. To make computation faster, the authors introduce three curvature-oriented graph embeddings, derive closed-form parallel transport equations, and develop a subtree partition method that encourages parameter sharing.

The resulting mechanism can replace ordinary attention in existing models. Experiments report significant improvements in those models’ performance on partial differential equations defined on manifolds. Its significance lies in linking the solver’s information-sharing mechanism to intrinsic geometry while also addressing computational cost, allowing geometric structure to influence attention without requiring an entirely separate solver framework.
summary.tldr: Curvature-aware attention incorporates intrinsic manifold geometry to improve existing neural PDE solvers.

title: Curvature-aware Graph Attention for PDEs on Manifolds

abstract: Subgraphs of a complete graph are usually distributed across multiple devices and can only be accessed locally because the raw data cannot be directly shared. However, existing node-level federated graph learning suffers from at least one of the following issues: 1) heavily relying on labeled graph samples that are difficult to obtain in real-world applications, and 2) partitioning a complete graph into several subgraphs inevitably causes missing links, leading to sub-optimal sample representations. To solve these issues, we propose a novel $\underline{\text{Fed}}$erated $\underline{\text{N}}$ode-level $\underline{\text{C}}$lustering $\underline{\text{N}}$etwork (FedNCN), which mends the destroyed cross-subgraph links using clustering prior knowledge. Specifically, within each client, we first design an MLP-based projector to implicitly preserve key clustering properties of a subgraph in a denoising learning-like manner, and then upload the resultant clustering signals that are hard to reconstruct for subsequent cross-subgraph links restoration. In the server, we maximize the potential affinity between subgraphs stemming from clustering signals by graph similarity estimation and minimize redundant links via the N-Cut criterion. Moreover, we employ a GNN-based generator to learn consensus prototypes from this mended graph, enabling the MLP-GNN joint-optimized learner to enhance data privacy during data transmission and further promote the local model for better clustering. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of FedNCN.

paragraphs: Federated graph learning distributes portions of a graph across devices that cannot directly share raw data. Splitting the graph can remove links between those portions, weakening node representations. Existing approaches can also depend heavily on labeled examples. FedNCN addresses these issues through node clustering and restoration of cross-subgraph relationships.

Each client uses an MLP-based projector to preserve important clustering properties through a denoising-like learning process. It uploads clustering signals described as difficult to reconstruct. The server estimates graph similarity from these signals to identify potential relationships between subgraphs, then uses the normalized-cut criterion to reduce redundant links.

A graph neural network learns shared consensus prototypes from the repaired graph. Joint optimization of the MLP and graph network then supports better local clustering and enhances privacy during transmission, according to the abstract. Extensive experiments report superior performance. The method's central idea is to use clustering structure as a shared basis for recovering relationships lost during graph partitioning while keeping the original data local.
summary.tldr: FedNCN shares clustering signals to repair missing cross-device graph links and improve local node clustering while keeping raw data local.

title: Federated Node-Level Clustering Network with Cross-Subgraph Link Mending

abstract: Large Language Models (LLM) alignment aims to prevent models from producing content that misaligns with human expectations, which can lead to ethical and legal concerns. In the last few years, Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) has been the most prominent method for achieving alignment. Due to challenges in stability and scalability with RLHF stages, which arise from the complex interactions between multiple models, researchers are exploring alternative methods to achieve effects comparable to those of RLHF. However, these methods often rely on large high-quality datasets. Despite some methods considering the generation of additional data to expand datasets, they often treat model training and data generation as separate and static processes, overlooking the fact that these processes are highly interdependent, leading to inefficient utilization of the generated data. To deal with this problem, we propose PLE, i.e., Progressively Label Enhancement for LLM Alignment, a framework that dynamically adjusts the model’s training process based on the evolving quality of the generated data. Specifically, we prompt the model to generate responses for both the original query and a set of carefully designed principle guided query, and then utilize a dynamic threshold to determine the appropriate training approach for both responses based on their corresponding reward scores. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of PLE compared to existing LLM alignment methods.

paragraphs: Aligning language models with human expectations often depends on high-quality training data. Methods that generate extra responses can expand that data, but the quality of generated material changes as the model learns. This paper argues that treating generation and training as separate, static processes overlooks their dependence on each other and wastes useful information.

Progressively Label Enhancement, or PLE, makes training decisions responsive to the evolving generated data. The model produces responses to an original query and to carefully designed versions guided by principles. Reward scores assess those responses, and a dynamic threshold determines the appropriate training approach for them. This makes the treatment of generated examples change with their assessed quality.

Experiments show that PLE is effective compared with existing alignment methods. Its contribution is a feedback-aware organization of data generation and model training: generated responses are evaluated within an adapting process instead of being assigned a fixed role throughout learning. The reported findings support this dynamic use of generated data as a practical approach to alignment.
summary.tldr: PLE adapts language-model alignment training using reward scores and a changing threshold for responses generated from original and principle-guided queries.

title: Progressively Label Enhancement for Large Language Model Alignment

abstract: The improved semantic understanding of vision-language pretrained (VLP) models has made it increasingly difficult to protect publicly posted images from being exploited by search engines and other similar tools. In this context, this paper seeks to protect users’ privacy by implementing defenses at the image compression stage to prevent exploitation. Specifically, we propose a flexible coding method, termed Privacy-Shielded Image Compression (PSIC), that can produce bitstreams with multiple decoding options. By default, the bitstream is decoded to preserve satisfactory perceptual quality while preventing interpretation by VLP models. Our method also retains the original image compression functionality. With a customizable input condition, the proposed scheme can reconstruct the image that preserves its full semantic information. A Conditional Latent Trigger Generation (CLTG) module is proposed to produce bias information based on customizable conditions to guide the decoding process into different reconstructed versions, and an Uncertainty-Aware Encryption-Oriented (UAEO) optimization function is designed to leverage the soft labels inferred from the target VLP model’s uncertainty on the training data. This paper further incorporates an adaptive multi-objective optimization strategy to obtain improved encrypting performance and perceptual quality simultaneously within a unified training process. The proposed scheme is plug-and-play and can be seamlessly integrated into most existing Learned Image Compression (LIC) models. Extensive experiments across multiple downstream tasks have demonstrated the effectiveness of our design.

paragraphs: Vision-language models make publicly shared images easier to interpret automatically, creating a privacy challenge. Privacy-Shielded Image Compression, or PSIC, places a defense within the compression process. It produces a compressed bitstream with multiple decoding options, retaining ordinary compression functionality while controlling which reconstructed version is produced.

By default, decoding aims to preserve satisfactory perceptual quality while preventing interpretation by vision-language models. A customizable input condition enables reconstruction that preserves the image’s full semantic information. A conditional latent trigger module supplies information that steers the decoder toward different versions, making the decoding condition part of how image content is exposed.

Training uses an uncertainty-aware objective informed by soft labels from the target vision-language model. An adaptive multi-objective strategy jointly balances protection and perceptual quality. The authors report effectiveness across multiple downstream tasks and describe integration with most existing learned image compression models. The contribution is a flexible compression-and-decoding design whose reported protection is demonstrated through those model-based evaluations.
summary.tldr: PSIC adds condition-dependent decoding to image compression to preserve visual quality while obstructing vision-language model interpretation.

title: Privacy-Shielded Image Compression: Defending Against Exploitation from Vision-Language Pretrained Models

abstract: Despite the popularity of transformers in practice, their architectures are empirically designed and neither mathematically justified nor interpretable. Moreover, as indicated by many empirical studies, some components of transformer architectures may be redundant. To derive a fully interpretable transformer architecture with only necessary components, we contend that the goal of representation learning is to compress a set of noisy initial token representations towards a mixture of low-dimensional subspaces. To compress these noisy token representations, an associated denoising operation naturally takes the form of a multi-head (subspace) self-attention. By unrolling such iterative denoising operations into a deep network, we arrive at a highly compact architecture that consists of only self-attention operators with skip connections at each layer. Moreover, we show that each layer performs highly efficient denoising: it improves the signal-to-noise ratio of token representations at a linear rate with respect to the number of layers. Despite its simplicity, extensive experiments on vision and language tasks demonstrate that such a transformer achieves performance close to that of standard transformer architectures such as GPT-2 and CRATE.

paragraphs: This paper develops a transformer architecture from an explicit view of representation learning: noisy token representations should be compressed toward a mixture of low-dimensional subspaces. Under this view, learning useful representations means progressively removing noise while retaining the structure described by those subspaces. The authors use this proposed objective to motivate the network’s components.

The associated denoising operation takes the form of multi-head subspace self-attention. Repeating that operation and expressing the iterations as network layers produces a compact architecture containing only self-attention and skip connections. Each layer therefore has an interpretable role as a denoising step, connecting the architecture directly to the mathematical process from which it was derived.

The authors show that signal-to-noise ratio improves at a linear rate with network depth in their analysis. Experiments on vision and language tasks find performance close to standard transformer architectures including GPT-2 and CRATE. The findings suggest that this simpler, mathematically motivated architecture can retain substantial practical capability, while the claim of comparable performance remains an empirical result from the reported tasks.
summary.tldr: Unrolling a subspace-denoising process yields an interpretable attention-only transformer with performance close to standard architectures in reported experiments.

title: Attention-Only Transformers via Unrolled Subspace Denoising

abstract: A key challenge in black-box adversarial attacks is the high query complexity in hard-label settings, where only the top-1 predicted label from the target deep model is accessible. In this paper, we propose a novel normal-vector-based method called Two-third Bridge Attack (TtBA). A innovative bridge direction is introduced which is a weighted combination of the current unit perturbation direction and its unit normal vector, controlled by a weight parameter $k$. We further use binary search to identify $k=k_\text{bridge}$, which has identical decision boundary as the current direction. Notably, we observe that $k=2/3 k_\text{bridge}$ yields a near-optimal perturbation direction, ensuring the stealthiness of the attack. In addition, we investigate the critical importance of local optima during the perturbation direction optimization process and propose a simple and effective approach to detect and escape such local optima. Experimental results on MNIST, FASHION-MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet datasets demonstrate the strong performance and scalability of our approach. Compared to state-of-the-art non-targeted and targeted attack methods, TtBA consistently delivers superior performance across most experimented datasets and deep learning models. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/TtBA-6ECF.

paragraphs: Decision-based adversarial attacks must find input changes that alter a model's prediction while seeing only its top predicted label. This limited feedback can require many queries. TtBA addresses that problem with a search method based on perturbation directions and normal vectors.

The method constructs a bridge direction by combining the current unit perturbation direction with its unit normal vector. Binary search finds a bridge weight associated with the same decision boundary as the current direction. The authors observe that using two-thirds of that weight gives a near-optimal perturbation direction. They also study local optima in this search and propose a mechanism for detecting and escaping them.

Evaluations cover MNIST, FASHION-MNIST, CIFAR10, CIFAR100, and ImageNet. TtBA outperforms state-of-the-art targeted and non-targeted attack methods across most tested datasets and models, with reported evidence of scalability. Its central contribution is a geometric rule that guides the search despite limited feedback, complemented by a way to avoid becoming trapped in locally favorable but inferior perturbation directions.
summary.tldr: TtBA uses a geometric bridge direction and local-optimum escape mechanism to improve adversarial attacks that receive only predicted labels.

title: TtBA: Two-third Bridge Approach for Decision-Based Adversarial Attack

abstract: The out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization challenge is a longstanding problem in graph learning. Through studying the fundamental cause of data distribution shift, i.e., the changes of environments, significant progress has been achieved in addressing this issue. However, we observe that existing works still fail to effectively address complex environment shifts. Existing practices place excessive attention on extracting causal subgraphs, inevitably treating spurious subgraphs as environment variables. While spurious subgraphs are controlled by environments, the space of environment changes encompass more than the scale of spurious subgraphs. Therefore, existing efforts have a limited inference space for environments, leading to failure under severe environment changes. To tackle this issue, we propose a negative inference graph OOD framework (NeGo) to broaden the inference space for environment factors. Inspired by the successful practice of prompt learning in capturing underlying semantics and causal associations in large language models, we design a negative prompt environment inference to extract underlying environment information. We further introduce the environment-enhanced invariant subgraph learning to effectively exploit inferred environment embedding, ensuring the robust extraction of causal subgraph in the environment shifts. Lastly, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of NeGo on real-world datasets and synthetic datasets across domains. NeGo outperforms baselines on nearly all datasets, which verify the effectiveness of our framework.

paragraphs: Graph models can struggle when the environment changes between training and use. Existing approaches often seek causal subgraphs while treating spurious subgraphs as representations of the environment. This paper argues that such a representation is too narrow: environmental changes can involve more than the variation expressed by spurious graph structure.

NeGo expands the space used to infer environmental factors. Its negative prompt environment inference component extracts underlying environment information, drawing inspiration from prompt learning. An environment-enhanced invariant subgraph learning component then uses the inferred environment embedding to support the extraction of causal subgraphs under distribution shifts.

This connects a broader account of the environment to the graph features intended to remain useful across environments. Evaluations cover synthetic and real-world datasets across domains, with NeGo outperforming baselines on nearly all datasets. The results support the paper’s diagnosis that restricting environmental information to spurious subgraphs can hinder generalization. They also support using richer inferred environment information to improve invariant graph learning under the evaluated shifts.
summary.tldr: NeGo broadens environmental inference beyond spurious subgraphs to improve graph generalization under distribution shifts.

title: Enhancing Graph Invariant Learning from a Negative Inference Perspective

abstract: Identifying and estimating causal relationships from data is a crucial component of empirical research. While large language model-powered tools have shown potential for assisting research workflows, their ability to perform end-to-end causal inference remains underexplored. We introduce CauSciBench, a benchmark that puts LLM-powered tools to the test on causality- driven research questions. Unlike previous related benchmarks that focus on coding alone, CauSciBench enables evaluation across the full pipeline of causal inference: from method and variable selection to computation of causal effects and statistical interpretation in the context of real-world research problems. We evaluated 7 frontier models on over 300 queries derived from scientific publications, textbook problems, sem- inal datasets, and synthetic scenarios. Results show that models consistently perform worse on real datasets, with the key bottleneck being the selection of an appropriate causal inference method.

paragraphs: CauSciBench examines whether language-model tools can carry out the full process of causal inference in scientific research. The central challenge is broader than writing working code: a system must choose an appropriate method, select variables, estimate causal effects, and interpret the statistical results in the context of the research question.

The benchmark includes more than 300 queries drawn from scientific publications, textbook exercises, established datasets, and synthetic scenarios. This range lets the authors assess performance across different kinds of research problems. Seven frontier models are evaluated on the pipeline, rather than judging their ability only through isolated programming tasks.

The models consistently perform worse on real datasets, and choosing the right causal inference method emerges as the main bottleneck. The finding locates a specific obstacle to automation: successful computation depends on first making suitable methodological choices. CauSciBench therefore measures research judgment alongside implementation, exposing failures that a coding-only evaluation would not directly target.
summary.tldr: CauSciBench tests complete causal inference workflows and finds that selecting the right method is a major obstacle for frontier models.

title: CauSciBench: Can LLMs Automate Causal Inference in Real-World Scientific Research?

abstract: Training Large Language Models (LLMs) to reason often relies on Reinforcement Learning (RL) with task-specific verifiers. However, many real-world reasoning-intensive tasks lack verifiers, despite offering abundant expert demonstrations that remain under-utilized for reasoning-focused training. We introduce RARO (Relativistic Adversarial Reasoning Optimization), which learns strong reasoning capabilities from expert demonstrations alone via Inverse Reinforcement Learning. Our method sets up an adversarial game between a policy and a relativistic critic: the policy learns to mimic expert answers, while the critic aims to identify the expert among (expert, policy) answer pairs. Both the policy and the critic are trained jointly and continuously via RL, and we identify key stabilization techniques required for robust learning. Empirically, RARO significantly outperforms strong verifier-free baselines across all evaluation tasks: $+13.7%$ accuracy on Countdown ($1.5$B), +8.2% on DeepMath ($7$B), and $+19.1%$ win-rate on Poetry Writing ($7$B) against expert poems. RARO also exhibits similar robust scaling trends as RL with verifiers. These results demonstrate that RARO effectively elicits strong reasoning performance from expert demonstrations alone, enabling robust reasoning learning even when task-specific verifiers are unavailable.

However, many real-world reasoning-intensive tasks lack verifiers, despite offering abundant expert demonstrations that remain under-utilized for reasoning-focused training. We introduce RARO (Relativistic Adversarial Reasoning Optimization), which learns strong reasoning capabilities from expert demonstrations alone via Inverse Reinforcement Learning. Our method sets up an adversarial game between a policy and a relativistic critic: the policy learns to mimic expert answers, while the critic aims to identify the expert among (expert, policy) answer pairs. Both the policy and the critic are trained jointly and continuously via RL, and we identify key stabilization techniques required for robust learning. Empirically, RARO significantly outperforms strong verifier-free baselines across all evaluation tasks: $+13.7%$ accuracy on Countdown ($1.5$B), +8.2% on DeepMath ($7$B), and $+19.1%$ win-rate on Poetry Writing ($7$B) against expert poems. RARO also exhibits similar robust scaling trends as RL with verifiers. These results demonstrate that RARO effectively elicits strong reasoning performance from expert demonstrations alone, enabling robust reasoning learning even when task-specific verifiers are unavailable.

paragraphs: Training reasoning models with reinforcement learning often depends on a task-specific verifier that judges answers. Many tasks lack such a verifier but have expert demonstrations. RARO uses those demonstrations as its learning foundation, applying inverse reinforcement learning to develop reasoning capabilities without a task-specific verification mechanism.

The method creates an adversarial interaction between an answer-generating policy and a relativistic critic. The policy learns to imitate expert answers, while the critic tries to identify the expert answer within an expert-policy pair. Both components train jointly and continuously through reinforcement learning. The authors also identify stabilization techniques required to make this coupled learning process robust.

Against strong verifier-free baselines, RARO reports accuracy gains of 13.7% on Countdown with a 1.5B model and 8.2% on DeepMath with a 7B model. It also reports a 19.1% win-rate gain against expert poems on Poetry Writing with a 7B model. Its scaling trends resemble those of verifier-based reinforcement learning, supporting demonstrations as a useful basis for reasoning-focused training.
summary.tldr: RARO trains a policy and comparative critic from expert demonstrations, improving reasoning and poetry results without task-specific verifiers.

title: Escaping the Verifier: Learning to Reason via Demonstrations

abstract: Code-as-Policy (CaP) is a paradigm in which a language or vision-language model generates executable robot control programs, yet its effectiveness as an autonomous controller for embodied manipulation remains underexplored. Prior CaP systems often rely on high-level, human-designed primitives, making it difficult to separate agent capability from designer-provided scaffolding. We present CaP-X, an open-access framework for systematically studying Code-as-Policy agents in robot manipulation. CaP-X includes four components. CaP-Gym is an interactive environment in which coding agents control robots by synthesizing and executing programs that compose perception and control primitives. Building on this foundation, CaP-Bench evaluates frontier language and vision-language models across varying levels of abstraction, interaction, and perceptual grounding. Across 12 models, the task success rates improve with human-crafted abstractions but degrade as these priors are removed, exposing a dependence on designer scaffolding. At the same time, we observe that scaling test-time computation with multi-turn interaction, structured execution feedback, visual differencing, automatic skill synthesis, and ensembled reasoning can substantially improve robustness even when agents operate over low-level primitives. These findings motivate CaP-Agent0, a training-free framework that achieves near human-level reliability on several manipulation tasks in simulation and on real embodiments. CaP-RL explores reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards to improve success rates and supports sim-to-real transfer through a shared code-as-action-space interface. Together, CaP-X provides an open-access platform for advancing embodied coding agents. Project page: https://capgym.github.io

title: CaP-X: A Framework for Benchmarking and Improving Coding Agents for Robot Manipulation

abstract: In this paper, we settle the problem of learning optimal linear contracts from data in the offline setting, where agent types are drawn from an unknown distribution and the principal’s goal is to design a contract that maximizes her expected utility. Specifically, our analysis shows that the simple Empirical Utility Maximization (EUM) algorithm yields an $\varepsilon$-approximation of the optimal linear contract with probability at least $1-\delta$, using just $O(\ln(1/\delta) / \varepsilon^2)$ samples. This result improves upon previously known bounds and matches a lower bound from (Dütting et al., 2025) up to constant factors, thereby proving its optimality. Furthermore, our result establishes the stronger guarantee of uniform convergence: the empirical utility of every linear contract is a $\varepsilon$-approximation of its true expectation with probability at least $1-\delta$, using the same optimal $O(\ln(1/\delta) / \varepsilon^2)$ sample complexity.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to learn a linear contract from existing data when agent types follow an unknown distribution. The principal wants a contract that maximizes expected utility. The central question is how many samples are needed to choose a contract whose utility is close to the best available linear contract.

The authors prove that Empirical Utility Maximization achieves an epsilon approximation with probability at least 1 minus delta using O(ln(1/delta)/epsilon²) samples. This procedure selects according to utility measured on the observed data. The sample bound improves previous guarantees and matches an existing lower bound up to constant factors, establishing optimal sample complexity for the stated setting.

The analysis also provides uniform convergence at the same sample complexity: empirical utility approximates expected utility for every linear contract simultaneously, with the stated probability. This is stronger than guaranteeing only that the selected contract performs well. It explains why optimizing the empirical objective is reliable even though the contract is chosen after observing the data, rather than fixed in advance.
summary.tldr: Empirical Utility Maximization learns near-optimal linear contracts with provably optimal sample complexity and a uniform utility-estimation guarantee.

title: The Optimal Sample Complexity of Linear Contracts

abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems commonly improve robustness via query-time adaptations such as query expansion and iterative retrieval. While effective, these approaches are inherently stateless: adaptations are recomputed for each query and discarded thereafter, precluding cumulative learning and repeatedly incurring inference-time cost. Index-side approaches like key expansion introduce persistence but rely on offline preprocessing or heuristic updates that are weakly aligned with downstream task utility, leading to semantic drift and noise accumulation. We propose Evolving Retrieval Memory (ERM), a training-free framework that transforms transient query-time gains into persistent retrieval improvements. ERM updates the retrieval index through correctness-gated feedback, selectively attributes atomic expansion signals to the document keys they benefit, and progressively evolves keys via stable, norm-bounded updates. We show that query and key expansion are theoretically equivalent under standard similarity functions and prove convergence of ERM’s selective updates, amortizing optimal query expansion into a stable index with zero inference-time overhead. Experiments on BEIR and BRIGHT across 13 domains demonstrate consistent gains in retrieval and generation, particularly on reasoning-intensive tasks, at native retrieval speed.
